hexagrams.name: Qián · The Creative
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Qian: Supreme success. Steadfast correctness is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary calls Qian the great origin from which all things take their start. The Xiang commentary reads the image as heaven in ceaseless motion, and asks the noble person to strengthen themselves without pause.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Six unbroken lines: pure initiating force. The hexagram carries four qualities — origin, flow, fitness and steadfastness. It describes a situation where you have real power to begin something and set its direction. The instruction is to move by honest means rather than quick ones, and to build for the long run. When your strength is at its fullest, that is exactly when to watch for overreach.
hexagrams.trendReason: Qian is entirely yang and embodies all four virtues. First among the 64 hexagrams, it symbolizes the highest initiating power. With origination, success, rightness, and steadfastness all present, its overall direction is extremely positive, hence the rating: Highest Favorability.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Begin honestly, keep going, hold your direction

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: A hidden dragon. Do not act.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary notes that the dragon lies hidden because the yang force is still at the bottom. The strength exists but the moment has not arrived.
lines.plainLanguage: Your capability is still gathering. The timing is not ripe, so this is not the moment to step forward or make yourself visible.
lines.lifeTranslation: Treat this as a build-up phase. Firm up the basics and hold off on big announcements or irreversible decisions.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your strength genuinely ready yet, and which foundations are still unfinished?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: A dragon appears in the fields. It is beneficial to meet a great person.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the dragon appearing in the field spreads its virtue widely. Ability has become visible, and it is fitting to seek out those who can recognise it.
lines.plainLanguage: What you can do is starting to show. There is an opening to meet someone who matters, so let your ability be seen and ask for guidance.
lines.lifeTranslation: A good time to talk with an experienced senior or mentor, show what you can do, and look for collaboration or direction.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your ability ready to be shown, and who is the experienced person worth approaching?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: The noble person works diligently all day and remains watchful at night. Danger, but no blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary describes working all day and returning again to the path. The noble person knows when to advance and when to hold back, and so passes through danger without fault.
lines.plainLanguage: This is the busiest, most pressured stretch. Stay alert and disciplined, neither slackening nor congratulating yourself, and mistakes stay avoidable.
lines.lifeTranslation: Give the day your full attention, then review it in the evening. Do not get careless just because things are going your way.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you still reflecting in the middle of all this busyness, and where do you most need care?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Perhaps leaping from the depths. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary reads the leap above the depths as advancing without fault. At the hinge between moving and waiting, either choice can be sound.
lines.plainLanguage: You are at a real decision point. Leaping forward and holding still are both defensible. What matters is reading the situation accurately.
lines.lifeTranslation: Facing an important choice, you can move boldly or wait a while. Either works if you follow judgement you can actually justify.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What is making you hesitate, and what does each option cost and offer?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: A flying dragon in Heaven. It is beneficial to meet a great person.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the flying dragon in the sky marks the great person at work. Strength is at its height, and meeting others of similar standing suits the moment.
lines.plainLanguage: You are in the most favourable position of the hexagram, with plenty in reserve. This suits working with people of comparable ability to build something together.
lines.lifeTranslation: Your condition is at its best. Reach for the significant partnership or the wider move, alongside capable people.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Where does your advantage actually lie, and who is capable enough to build with?

lines.original: Nine at the top: An overreaching dragon. There is regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary warns that the arrogant dragon has cause for regret, because fullness cannot last. What is too rigid breaks.
lines.plainLanguage: Things have reached their peak. Past that point the trend reverses, and forcing matters or refusing to moderate leads to regret.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you only ever advance, or dig in on your own view, there is a bill to pay. Adjust course while adjusting is still cheap.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Where have you already overextended or held on too hard, and what could you let go of?

useNine.original: Use of the Nines: A host of dragons appears without a head. Good fortune.
useNine.plainLanguage: When every force arrives at once, having no single figure in charge is the favourable arrangement. Shared judgement can carry more than one strong individual.
useNine.lifeTranslation: In a room full of capable people, do not rush to lead. Choosing cooperation over competition tends to produce the better outcome.

topicRules.career: Conditions favour moving your work forward. Push by legitimate means rather than grabbing credit or cutting past people.
topicRules.study: Progress comes from daily consistency. Accumulate solid ground instead of hunting for shortcuts.
topicRules.romance: Say what you feel, openly and honestly, then leave the other person room. Urgency and pressure work against you here.
topicRules.family: Let whoever can carry responsibility step up and lead with integrity, rather than passing the task along.
topicRules.relations: Be active and visible, but stay modest. Constant competition for the spotlight costs more than it returns.
topicRules.finance: A reasonable time to plan actively. Base decisions on sound principle rather than chasing quick returns.
topicRules.wellness: You have energy to spare. Spend it on keeping a steady routine, not on burning through your reserves.
topicRules.general: The overall direction is favourable. Move ahead honestly, hold your aim, and remember that peaks do not last.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: set a clear direction, take responsibility for it yourself, and keep improving steadily. Avoid: pushing ahead on momentum alone, or turning your own conviction into pressure on other people.

hexagrams.name: Kūn · The Receptive
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Kun: Supreme success. The mare's steadfastness is beneficial. The noble person has somewhere to go: leading brings confusion, following finds a guide. Beneficial to gain friends in the southwest and lose friends in the northeast. Peaceful steadfastness brings good fortune.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary praises Kun as the origin through which all things are given life, following heaven's lead. The Xiang commentary reads the earth's disposition as depth of character able to carry weight.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Six broken lines: the earth's capacity to hold and sustain. This hexagram is about receiving, accommodating and enduring rather than initiating. The image of the mare's steadfastness says it well — yielding yet strong, flexible yet lasting. Go with the larger current, treat others generously, and resist the urge to strike out alone. Quiet correctness serves you here.
hexagrams.trendReason: Kun offers supreme success, and “peaceful steadfastness brings good fortune” explicitly indicates a positive direction. Earth supports all things with generous virtue and is generally auspicious. Yet it requires correctness, with slightly less initiating force than pure-yang Qian, hence the rating: Highly Favorable, rather than Highest Favorability.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Carry what comes; steadiness beats forcing

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Treading on frost; solid ice is coming.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary notes that treading on frost means the cold has begun to gather. Follow that course and hard ice arrives.
lines.plainLanguage: Thin frost underfoot points to solid ice ahead. How something begins already contains where it is heading, so notice it early.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you can see the first signs of a small problem, deal with it now rather than waiting until it is serious.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which small problem are you ignoring, and what was the earliest warning sign?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Straight, square, great. Without practice, nothing is unfavorable.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the movement here is straight and square, and that needing no rehearsal shows the way of earth at its clearest.
lines.plainLanguage: Straight, square and broad. No special technique is needed; acting from plain honesty gets the work done well.
lines.lifeTranslation: Deal with people and tasks straightforwardly. No elaborate strategy required — do your part properly and results follow.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you being straight about this, or circling around something you would rather not say?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Concealed excellence allows steadfastness. Perhaps following the king's affairs: no personal achievement, but completion.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary explains that hidden brilliance waits for the right moment, and that serving another's undertaking still reflects a wide understanding.
lines.plainLanguage: Keep your talent inward for now, waiting for its moment. Joining someone else's work brings no personal glory, but you can see it through to a clean finish.
lines.lifeTranslation: Support an existing plan or team. Do not fight for headline credit; concentrate on doing your own part properly.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do you need to set aside the urge to lead and take a supporting role instead?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Tie the sack closed. No blame and no praise.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary reads the tied-up sack as caution that does no harm. Nothing is gained in reputation, but nothing is lost either.
lines.plainLanguage: Keep a low profile. Say little, move little, claim nothing. In a sensitive period, silence is the steady option.
lines.lifeTranslation: Do less and say less for now. You do not need to be noticed; getting through quietly is enough.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What would cause trouble if you said or did it right now?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: A yellow lower garment. Supreme good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the yellow lower garment brings great good fortune because the refinement is held within. Yellow is the central colour and the garment the lower robe.
lines.plainLanguage: Holding a supporting position with balance and integrity, with your quality kept inward rather than displayed. That combination is strongly favourable.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you can hold an important role modestly, without talking over people or showing off, the results tend to be good.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you staying modest and balanced in your current role, or reaching past it?

lines.original: Six at the top: Dragons battle in the fields. Their blood is dark and yellow.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says dragons fighting in the open marks a way that has run out. The yielding principle should not turn rigid.
lines.plainLanguage: The yielding force has built to its limit and tries to overstep. Both sides end up damaged. Hardening now only drains everyone.
lines.lifeTranslation: Grievance stored up until it bursts, or expansion past your remit, injures both sides. Learn to speak in time and to give way in time.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What resentment have you been holding down, and where are you tempted to overstep?

useSix.original: Use of the Sixes: Lasting steadfastness is beneficial.
useSix.plainLanguage: The way of Kun is best used through lasting correctness. The real advantage of yielding strength is that it endures, not that it flares.
useSix.lifeTranslation: When everything points to the receptive, hold to a sound course over the long term. Aim for something durable rather than something fast.

topicRules.career: Take a solid supporting role and fit into the larger plan. Steady contribution over time outperforms a brief star turn.
topicRules.study: Work with patience and care, and accept guidance. Going it alone or rushing ahead does not suit this period.
topicRules.romance: Make room for the other person and be gentle in how you handle things. Insisting on control costs you the long-term harmony.
topicRules.family: Lead with generosity, carry more and count less. Keeping things settled is the task that matters now.
topicRules.relations: Be accommodating and unhurried. Good relationships gather around you when you stop competing for position.
topicRules.finance: Stay conservative and protect what you already have. This suits long-range planning rather than quick returns.
topicRules.wellness: Prioritise rest and replenishment. Let yourself recover properly instead of drawing down further.
topicRules.general: Work with the current rather than against it. Quiet correctness now buys stability later.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: accept the situation as it stands, keep things stable, and look after the groundwork. Avoid: stepping out before conditions are ready, or letting accommodation slide into losing your principles.

hexagrams.name: Zhūn · Difficult Beginning
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Zhun: Supreme success; steadfast correctness is beneficial. Do not set out to proceed. It is beneficial to appoint lords.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says that when firm and yielding first meet, difficulty is born; there is movement inside danger. The Xiang commentary reads cloud and thunder as the image, and asks the noble person to bring order out of tangle.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Zhun is the image of a shoot forcing its way up through the soil. Thunder's energy sits beneath the water of danger — there is plenty of force, but the way out is blocked. The judgement says the start is fundamentally sound, yet also warns against setting off anywhere. Build a base first and let the timing catch up.
hexagrams.trendReason: Although Zhun offers supreme success, the judgment explicitly warns against setting out, indicating obstacles and risks in action. Many lines are difficult but not without an exit; hope remains amid hardship. Its overall direction is neutral with caution, hence the rating: Balanced.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Beginnings are hard; build roots before reach

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Lingering in hesitation. Remaining steadfast is beneficial; appointing lords is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that although there is hesitation, the intent remains correct. Placing the worthy below the common people wins them over.
lines.plainLanguage: You are circling rather than advancing, and that caution is right. Holding your position and building a base matters more than moving now.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you feel stuck in place, do not panic. This is a good stretch for accumulating strength — make the groundwork solid first.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do you need to charge ahead, or firm up what is under your feet, and what counts as your foundation?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Difficulty and turning back, horses separating. Not robbers, but suitors. The woman remains steadfast and does not marry; after ten years, she marries.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the difficulty here to the yielding line riding above a firm one. Ten years before the union says the delay is long but not permanent.
lines.plainLanguage: The road forward is full of obstacles and nothing goes as planned. What looks like a threat may be an opportunity, but clarity takes a long time to arrive.
lines.lifeTranslation: Things feel blocked and unresolved. You need real patience — do not walk away simply because the short term shows nothing.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Have you given up too early on something that needed a long wait, and was it worth waiting for?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Pursuing deer without a forester, only entering the woods. The noble person sees the signs: better to give up. Advancing brings regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says chasing deer without a forester is merely running after game. The noble person lets it go, since going on leads only to a dead end.
lines.plainLanguage: Chasing a target with no guide takes you deep into the woods with no way out. The wise choice is to stop; pressing on costs you.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you are pursuing something and still cannot find a route, pausing to reassess beats pushing blindly onward.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do you have a reliable method or guide for what you are chasing, or are you just going on instinct?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Horses separating. Seeking marriage, go forward. Good fortune; nothing unfavorable.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that to seek and then go forward shows clear sight. Reaching out for the right alliance is the sound move.
lines.plainLanguage: Go and seek the partnership or connection that fits. Moving forward here is favourable, with nothing working against you. This is the moment to take the initiative.
lines.lifeTranslation: If there is a collaboration or relationship worth pursuing, act now. Do not let earlier hesitation cost you this one.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which opportunity or relationship have you been hesitating over, and what is holding you back?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Hoarding the nourishing grease. Small steadfastness brings good fortune; great steadfastness brings misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the stored richness cannot yet shine out. The honoured position is hemmed in, so small matters succeed while large ones do not.
lines.plainLanguage: You hold resources but cannot deploy them widely. Holding firm on a small scale works; overreaching does not. Match the task to what you actually have.
lines.lifeTranslation: Your current energy and resources are enough for what is in front of you. Do not widen the scope or raise the target yet — finish what exists.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Has your target outgrown the capability and resources you actually have?

lines.original: Six at the top: Horses separating; tears of blood flow endlessly.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary asks how weeping tears of blood could possibly last. Hardship has piled up to its limit, and something has to change.
lines.plainLanguage: Long circling inside difficulty has worn your reserves to the edge. What matters now is asking for help or changing course, not gritting through.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you have been under heavy pressure for a long time with no improvement, reach out for support or rethink the strategy. Enduring alone is not the answer.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What long-running pressure are you carrying, and are you willing to ask someone for help?

topicRules.career: Work is in an early or obstructed phase. Consolidate the base and hold your ground rather than expanding now.
topicRules.study: Expect bottlenecks. Keep at it and find the method that actually suits you instead of forcing speed.
topicRules.romance: Obstacles or uncertainty are likely. Be patient and let things develop rather than pushing the pace.
topicRules.family: The household may be going through upheaval. Stabilise the basics and handle what is in front of you; add no new variables.
topicRules.relations: Misunderstandings are likely. Pick a few dependable people and move carefully rather than widening your circle.
topicRules.finance: Stay conservative. Early outlay is likely to be hard going, so build from small, steady steps rather than large moves.
topicRules.wellness: You may feel worn down. Rest more, stop spending reserves you do not have, and get proper support.
topicRules.general: You are still in the hard opening stretch. Be patient, stay sound, and build roots before thinking about reach.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: start small, get your resources in place, and find people you can rely on. Avoid: expanding from day one, or changing direction every time the picture looks messy.

hexagrams.name: Méng · Youthful Ignorance
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Meng: Success. I do not seek the inexperienced youth; the youth seeks me. At the first divination, I answer. Repeating it twice or three times is disrespectful; if disrespectful, I do not answer. Steadfast correctness is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary places danger below the mountain: facing it, one halts, and that is Meng. Nurturing what is correct in the unformed is described as sacred work. The Xiang commentary sees a spring emerging at the mountain's foot.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Meng is the state of not yet knowing, and the asking that follows. A spring hides beneath the mountain, waiting to be found. The judgement is blunt about how learning works: the student comes to the teacher, not the reverse. Ask sincerely once and you get an answer; ask carelessly again and again and nothing useful comes back. Approach this with an open, modest mind.
hexagrams.trendReason: Meng offers success but requires sincere seeking of instruction. A lack of initiative or a careless attitude brings no benefit. Overall this is a neutral stage of early learning, neither fortunate nor unfortunate. Benefit lies in steadfastness and sincerity, hence the rating: Balanced.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Ask honestly; openness is what teaches you

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Opening the inexperienced. It is beneficial to apply discipline and remove shackles. Continuing in this way brings regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that applying discipline here serves to establish the rule. Shackles have to come off before anyone can walk.
lines.plainLanguage: The first step in learning is setting the rules and removing what restricts you. Rushing ahead before clearing the obstacles only adds difficulty.
lines.lifeTranslation: Before starting something new, put the necessary structure in place and drop the old habits that get in the way.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which old habit or mistaken assumption do you need to clear out before you start?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Embracing the inexperienced brings good fortune; taking a wife brings good fortune. The son can manage the household.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the son manages the household because firm and yielding meet. Taking in learners of every level is what makes a house prosper.
lines.plainLanguage: Making room for learners at every level brings good results. Whoever shoulders the responsibility lifts the whole.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you teach or lead, be patient with people at different levels. If you are learning, accept the guidance. Either way it works out.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you tolerant enough here, and are you willing to accept guidance or carry the responsibility?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Do not take this woman as a wife. Seeing a man of wealth, she loses possession of herself. Nothing is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says not to take this bride, because the conduct is not in keeping. Drawn by wealth alone, one loses oneself.
lines.plainLanguage: Do not chase an arrangement built purely on material gain or surface shine. You lose your own footing and end up with nothing.
lines.lifeTranslation: If an opportunity attracts you only on the surface but asks you to give up your principles or yourself, it is not a good one.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Has a surface attraction pulled your attention away from what actually matters here?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Confined in inexperience. Regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the regret of trapped ignorance comes from standing alone, far from anything real.
lines.plainLanguage: Staying shut inside what you do not know, refusing to grow or ask, leads only to regret and loss.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you refuse to learn anything new or deny your own gaps, the present state keeps costing you. The attitude has to change first.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What have you been refusing to admit you do not understand, and why?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Childlike inexperience. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the good fortune of the childlike learner to being compliant and receptive.
lines.plainLanguage: Learning with a child's openness, without assuming you already understand, is the most favourable state this hexagram describes.
lines.lifeTranslation: Look at the problem as a beginner would. Drop your assumptions, ask plainly, and something useful comes back.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you modest enough here to look at this again as a beginner would?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Striking at inexperience. It is unfavorable to act as a raider, beneficial to defend against raiders.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that using force to repel intruders keeps those above and below in accord. Correction is for defence, not for attack.
lines.plainLanguage: Force applied to ignorance is useful for defending and guiding, harmful when used to invade. Influence should direct, not control.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you have influence, use it to clear obstacles for others and point them somewhere good, not to hold them down.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your influence over other people helping them grow, or quietly limiting them?

topicRules.career: You are in a learning or starting phase. Ask sincerely and find a good mentor or partner; that choice decides the outcome.
topicRules.study: Come to the material openly and modestly. Genuine engagement produces results; half-attention does not.
topicRules.romance: Be modest and sincere rather than swayed by surface appeal. Honest exchange and learning from each other build the bond.
topicRules.family: There is something here to understand better. Talk it through with an open mind instead of holding your ground.
topicRules.relations: Take the humbler position of the person asking. Find someone who can guide you, and offer acceptance in return.
topicRules.finance: Fill the knowledge gap before you act. Ask when you do not know, and keep decisions cautious rather than casual.
topicRules.wellness: Something here needs proper understanding. Consult a professional and take the advice rather than insisting you know.
topicRules.general: This phase is about learning. Ask sincerely and stay open, and the growth available here is considerable.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: admit what you do not know, ask a specific question, and follow a method you trust. Avoid: guessing cleverly without checking, or asking repeatedly while practising nothing.

hexagrams.name: Xū · Waiting
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Xu: With sincerity, bright success. Steadfastness brings good fortune; crossing the great river is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary defines Xu as waiting, with danger ahead: firm and strong, one does not fall in, and so is not driven to extremity. The Xiang commentary sees clouds rising to heaven, and the noble person eating, drinking and keeping good spirits.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Xu is the image of moisture gathering in the sky over dry ground. The creative force meets danger blocking the way, yet does not sink into it; instead it waits with confidence intact. Holding a sound course through the wait leads to things opening up, and when the moment ripens, even a large crossing becomes reasonable. This is active waiting, not stalling.
hexagrams.trendReason: Xu's judgment combines four positive statements: sincerity, bright success, steadfast good fortune, and beneficial river crossing. Those who maintain trust and constancy can ultimately progress through difficulty. Waiting is the main theme, but the overall trend is favorable, hence the rating: Highly Favorable.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Wait in good faith; timing opens the way

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Waiting in the outskirts. Constancy is beneficial. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says waiting in the meadow means not walking into danger, and that constancy here keeps one within the ordinary course.
lines.plainLanguage: You are still at the safe outer edge, well clear of the risky centre. Keep your patience and your routine, do nothing rash, and nothing goes wrong.
lines.lifeTranslation: Things are still forming. Do not rush to the front line — steady yourself at the back and wait for a clear signal.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does your waiting have a rhythm to it, and what preparation keeps you from getting restless?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Waiting on the sand. Some criticism; good fortune in the end.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says waiting on the sand keeps one broadly in the middle. Some words are exchanged, but holding the centre brings a good ending.
lines.plainLanguage: You are closer to the risky ground now. There is minor friction or sharp words, but keeping to a balanced course sees it end well.
lines.lifeTranslation: Small obstacles or a bit of friction with people may unsettle you. It does not need much attention — hold your direction and carry on.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Can you tell which of the small irritations deserve attention and which can be let go?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Waiting in the mud invites raiders.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says waiting in the mud puts the disaster outside; one has invited the trouble oneself, and only care and respect prevent defeat.
lines.plainLanguage: Impatience during the wait has already put you in a bind, and it has drawn in trouble you did not need. Careful handling matters more now than more pushing.
lines.lifeTranslation: If haste got you into this, stop and deal with it carefully rather than grinding on or speeding up.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Did rushing put you where you are, and what is making it hard to step back out?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Waiting amid blood. Emerging from the pit.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says waiting amid blood means yielding and listening. From that place one comes out of the pit.
lines.plainLanguage: You are inside real danger, and this is not the moment to strike out. Go with the flow, listen, work with the situation, and you get clear of it.
lines.lifeTranslation: When the position is genuinely risky, lowering your profile and fitting in with the current is the safe way out.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do you need to drop the urge to act and follow the external rhythm instead?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Waiting amid wine and food. Steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the good fortune of waiting over food and wine to holding the centre and staying correct.
lines.plainLanguage: From the most favourable position, waiting means enjoying the quiet pace you are in. A settled, balanced state is what makes this favourable.
lines.lifeTranslation: No need for anxiety right now. Enjoy the calm you have and keep yourself steady inside.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Can you enjoy the present while waiting, rather than worrying at the future?

lines.original: Six at the top: Entering the pit, three uninvited guests arrive. Treat them with respect; good fortune in the end.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that treating the uninvited guests with respect brings a good ending; the position is not ideal, but nothing much is lost.
lines.plainLanguage: In the last stage of waiting, something unexpected turns up. Meeting the unplanned person or event with respect produces a better ending than you expect.
lines.lifeTranslation: Events may not go the way you pictured, and unfamiliar people or turns appear. Meet them openly and the result usually improves.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How do you meet unexpected turns and uninvited guests — with resistance or with openness?

topicRules.career: The direction is favourable but the timing is not ripe. Hold your standards and prepare rather than forcing an early move.
topicRules.study: Work through it step by step. Accumulate patiently; the breakthrough comes when the groundwork is there.
topicRules.romance: Wait in good faith rather than pressing for progress. Keep being genuine and the closeness comes at its own pace.
topicRules.family: If there is friction at home, be patient and do not inflame it. A calm, balanced response gives things room to turn.
topicRules.relations: Be reliable and let connections form in their own time. Rushing to build a network works against you here.
topicRules.finance: Wait for a good opening rather than committing early. Protect what you hold and act when conditions are clearer.
topicRules.wellness: Rest and recover. Do not force change; let your body come back at its own pace while you stay settled.
topicRules.general: Wait with your confidence intact. Do not rush, hold a sound course, and the way opens when the timing arrives.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: use the waiting period to prepare, keep the commitments you have made, and watch for the turn. Avoid: hurrying the outcome, or acting while you still lack the information you need.

hexagrams.name: Sòng · Conflict
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Song: With sincerity, obstruction and vigilance. Stopping midway brings good fortune; pursuing to the end brings misfortune. Meeting a great person is beneficial; crossing the great river is unfavorable.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary places firmness above and danger below: danger met with strength produces dispute, and it warns that a dispute cannot be brought to completion. The Xiang commentary sees heaven and water moving apart, and asks the noble person to think a matter through before beginning it.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Song is heaven and water pulling in opposite directions — a structure at odds with itself. Trust gets blocked and dispute follows, and forcing the point only deepens the split. There may be a workable middle stretch, but carrying the quarrel to its end goes badly. The real lesson sits at the start: think the thing through before you begin. Giving ground and holding the centre beats fighting to the last.
hexagrams.trendReason: Song's judgment explicitly warns of misfortune at the end: litigation is unlikely to end well, giving an overall negative direction. Though some lines offer fortune, the meaning favors yielding and careful thought at the outset, hence the rating: Below Average.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Fights rarely end well; settle, do not escalate

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Do not prolong the affair. Some criticism; good fortune in the end.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says not prolonging the matter is right, because a dispute should not run long. There are some words, but the case is made clear.
lines.plainLanguage: You do not let the quarrel grow or drag. There is some argument and clarification, but because your position is clear, it ends well.
lines.lifeTranslation: If there is a small clash or misunderstanding, clear it up early. Do not let it harden into a long-running feud.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which small piece of friction could you settle now, before it accumulates?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Unable to prevail in litigation, return and flee. The town's three hundred households suffer no calamity.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that being unable to win the dispute, one retreats and hides. Contending upward from below simply invites disaster.
lines.plainLanguage: Forcing the dispute is not winnable, and stepping back protects both you and the people around you. Against a much stronger side, withdrawal is the intelligent move.
lines.lifeTranslation: When the power gap is obvious, backing off protects more people than holding out does.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does this conflict really need to continue, and what does stepping back protect?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Living on former virtue. Steadfastness amid danger; good fortune in the end. Perhaps serving the king's affairs, without personal achievement.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that living on established virtue and following those above brings good fortune. Serving another's affairs leaves little of one's own to show.
lines.plainLanguage: Live off the standing and resources you have already built, and hold to a sound course. There is risk, but it ends well. Throwing yourself into someone else's venture yields little personal credit.
lines.lifeTranslation: Do not trade away the advantages you have accumulated for something new. Hold your existing base and act carefully.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What have you already built up, and are you overlooking the advantage it gives you?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Unable to prevail in litigation, return to the mandate and change. Peaceful steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that turning back, accepting what is ordained and changing one's stance loses nothing when done with quiet correctness.
lines.plainLanguage: The dispute cannot be won. Turn instead, change your position, and handle things calmly and correctly. That is the favourable route.
lines.lifeTranslation: Once you see that fighting on is pointless, the best move is to shift your thinking and restart from a calmer place.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which position of yours could already be adjusted, if only you could let it go?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Litigation. Supreme good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the great good fortune here to holding the central and correct place. This is the arbiter, not the contestant.
lines.plainLanguage: When a balanced and impartial figure decides the matter, the outcome is strongly favourable. The point is neutrality, not victory.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you are the one holding the balance or mediating in this dispute, handling it even-handedly tends to produce a good result.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In this matter, are you one of the sides, or could you take the more neutral role?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Perhaps awarded a ceremonial belt, then stripped of it three times before morning ends.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says an honour received through litigation does not deserve respect. The sash is granted and stripped away three times in a morning.
lines.plainLanguage: What you seize through dispute can be lost again within a day. Gains taken by fighting rarely hold.
lines.lifeTranslation: Even if you win something in the quarrel, it tends not to last, and it rarely earns you anyone's respect.
lines.reflectionPrompt: If you got what you want by fighting for it, would it be worth having in the long run?

topicRules.career: Steer clear of head-on confrontation. Use strategy and concession to defuse things; forcing a win tends to backfire.
topicRules.study: Do not spend your energy arguing over who is right. Put it into your own progress instead.
topicRules.romance: Settle disagreements early. Letting resentment drag on turns friction into distance.
topicRules.family: Cool the dispute rather than raising the temperature. A neutral third party often helps more than another round.
topicRules.relations: Think it through before you begin. Set out terms and expectations clearly up front to prevent later disputes.
topicRules.finance: Stay out of legal or financial entanglements. If a dispute exists, settle early — fighting to the end usually costs more than it recovers.
topicRules.wellness: Sustained conflict takes a toll. Adjust your stance, find a way to put the fight down, and give yourself proper rest.
topicRules.general: Avoid confrontation. Think ahead, give ground, hold the centre — settling is the more practical route.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: get clear on where you actually differ and what your limits are, keep a record, and look for fair mediation. Avoid: enlarging the fight over pride, or treating a concession as defeat.

hexagrams.name: Shī · The Army
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Shi: Steadfastness under a venerable leader brings good fortune and no blame.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says Shi means the multitude and correctness means the right way; whoever can keep the multitude correct can rule. The Xiang commentary sees water within the earth, and the noble person sheltering the people and gathering the many.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Shi is the image of an army and of discipline — water held deep inside the earth, strength stored within a body of people. Leading a group means moving steadily through danger on the strength of clear rules and honest conduct. The hexagram is direct about the conditions: you need character, you need discipline, and you need the right person in charge. Without a sound basis, even great force does not last.
hexagrams.trendReason: Shi requires right conduct and the leadership of a virtuous elder for fortune without blame. Success depends on adequate leadership and discipline: with these, great undertakings are possible; without them, misfortune follows, hence the rating: Balanced.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Lead by discipline, and put the right people in place

lines.original: Six at the beginning: The army sets out with discipline. Without proper order, misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the army goes out under discipline; losing that discipline brings misfortune.
lines.plainLanguage: Any action has to start from clear rules. Where the standards are vague or ignored, the risk is serious.
lines.lifeTranslation: Whatever you are starting or organising, set the rules and the discipline first, or the failure is already built in.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does what you are running have clear rules, or is it being held together by instinct?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Amid the army, good fortune and no blame. The king grants commands three times.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says being at the centre of the army brings good fortune through the favour of heaven, and that threefold commission reflects care for all the territories.
lines.plainLanguage: Holding the central position and leading in a balanced, upright way is favourable and free of fault. Leaders with real character earn trust in both directions.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you are the core of a team, lead honestly and evenly. You gain trust and you can carry a larger responsibility.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you acting with integrity in your group, and does your conduct match the trust you have been given?

lines.original: Six in the third place: The army may carry corpses in wagons. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the army carrying corpses home has accomplished nothing at all.
lines.plainLanguage: Putting the wrong person in a key role, or moving at the wrong time, can lead to heavy defeat. Undisciplined action causes losses you cannot recover.
lines.lifeTranslation: Letting someone unsuited take it on, or taking on more than you can handle at the wrong moment, tends to end badly.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is anyone here, including you, carrying something beyond their capability or timing?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: The army camps to the left. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that camping to the left is without fault, because it does not depart from ordinary practice.
lines.plainLanguage: Knowing when to pull back, to shift ground rather than hold on by force, is no failure. Retreat here serves a steadier advance.
lines.lifeTranslation: If the situation has turned against you, stepping back to regroup is not losing. It is buying strength for the next move.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Where do you need to pull back and regroup before pushing on?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Game in the fields. Taking action is beneficial, without blame. The eldest son leads the army; the younger carries corpses. Persistence brings misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the eldest son leads the army because he holds to the middle way, while sending the unsuitable means employing the wrong person.
lines.plainLanguage: There is a legitimate reason to act, but the capable person has to lead. Handing the main responsibility to someone secondary tends to end badly.
lines.lifeTranslation: Have a proper reason to act, and let the genuinely capable person lead. Putting an underqualified person in the key role creates a mess that is hard to clean up.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the most suitable person in the most important role, or did convenience decide it?

lines.original: Six at the top: The great ruler issues commands, founding states and establishing households. Do not employ petty people.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the great ruler's commission rightly acknowledges merit, but that employing the small-minded is certain to throw the state into disorder.
lines.plainLanguage: When the work is done, credit should be distributed on merit. Keep people of poor character out of important positions, or disorder follows.
lines.lifeTranslation: Share the results fairly once it is finished, and do not let someone with a character problem take a key position. That one costs you later.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do you have a clear standard for sharing the results, and for who gets real influence afterwards?

topicRules.career: Build on integrity and discipline. Find the right leader or be one; the right person in the right seat decides this.
topicRules.study: Hold yourself to a routine and find a teacher who can guide you. Working through in order is what produces results.
topicRules.romance: Be straight with each other. Playing games works against you; respect and steadiness are what last.
topicRules.family: Set clear roles and expectations. Let each person do their part and do not load anyone beyond their capacity.
topicRules.relations: Make the norms and expectations explicit. Keep people of poor character out of your inner circle.
topicRules.finance: Manage by rules — write them down and follow them. Get someone experienced to check your decisions rather than delegating loosely.
topicRules.wellness: Build a regular routine. Be disciplined with yourself without being harsh; rhythm is what keeps you well.
topicRules.general: Discipline, integrity and the right people. Plan before you move, and lead by character rather than volume.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: define who is responsible for what, set the pace, model it yourself, and keep the group in order. Avoid: unclear instructions, uneven reward and sanction, or asking of others what you will not do.

hexagrams.name: Bǐ · Holding Together
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Bi: Good fortune. Consult the original divination for fundamental, lasting steadfastness; no blame. The unsettled come from all sides. The latecomer meets misfortune.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary calls Bi favourable and defines it as support, with those below following willingly. Those who arrive late find their way exhausted. The Xiang commentary sees water on the earth, and the early kings establishing states and drawing the lords close.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Bi is water spread over the earth — things resting on one another and nourishing each other in the process. It is the hexagram of alliance and mutual support, of the ties between people and between groups. Everything here turns on sincerity: only honest intent builds a real bond. Move towards the upright people first and commit for the long term. Those who hesitate and arrive late may find the moment gone.
hexagrams.trendReason: Bi's judgment begins with good fortune, and fundamental, lasting steadfastness without blame emphasizes the basis of enduring fortune. Its spirit is sincere connection and mutual help, creating a positive overall atmosphere, hence the rating: Highly Favorable.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Reach out sincerely; lasting bonds carry you

lines.original: Six at the beginning: With sincerity, join them. No blame. Sincerity fills the earthen jar; in the end, something more comes. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that for the first line of Bi, something unlooked-for turns out well. A sincere beginning brings unexpected reward.
lines.plainLanguage: Reach out on a basis of honesty, with sincerity full as an earthen jar. What follows is a gain you did not plan for.
lines.lifeTranslation: Build the relationship or partnership genuinely. However plain it looks at the start, sincerity tends to return more than expected.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there an ordinary-looking but genuine connection whose sincerity you have not yet expressed?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Joining from within. Steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that holding together from within means one does not lose oneself. Sincerity moves outward from the inside, without flattery.
lines.plainLanguage: Closeness that comes from inside you rather than from surface accommodation. It is genuine outward movement, and holding to it is favourable.
lines.lifeTranslation: You do not need to perform or shape yourself to someone else's preferences. Start from what you actually feel and stay yourself.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is this relationship coming from real feeling, or have you lost some of yourself in accommodating?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Joining the wrong people.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary asks whether holding together with the wrong people is not painful indeed.
lines.plainLanguage: Binding yourself closely to people of poor character or poor fit is a choice to regret. That kind of closeness only causes damage.
lines.lifeTranslation: If someone you have grown close to leaves you uneasy, or the relationship does not feel healthy, that deserves serious rethinking.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there someone you know you should not be this close to, and what has stopped you changing it?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Joining outwardly. Steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says holding together outwardly with the worthy means following those above. Correctness here is favourable.
lines.plainLanguage: Reach outward to people of ability and character, following better guidance with an honest attitude. This is the favourable direction.
lines.lifeTranslation: Go towards people wiser or more capable than you, and ask for guidance or collaboration. That is the right move here.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Who is worth approaching and learning from, and what has kept you from acting?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Open joining. The king drives game on three sides, letting animals ahead escape. The townspeople need no warning. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the good fortune of open holding together to the central and correct position. Letting the game ahead escape means releasing what turns away and keeping what comes willingly.
lines.plainLanguage: Gather people openly and fairly. Let those who want to leave go, and those who want to stay gather of their own accord. No coercion; balanced treatment draws people in.
lines.lifeTranslation: You do not need to force anyone to join or agree. Act openly and fairly; the people who genuinely value it stay, and those who leave need no chasing.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there any pressure in how you build relationships, and what would happen if you used only sincerity?

lines.original: Six at the top: Joining without a head. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says holding together without a beginning has no ending either. Without taking the lead, nothing comes to completion.
lines.plainLanguage: Hesitating instead of making the first move lets the opening pass. No firm bond forms, and the position is a poor one.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you keep waiting for the other side to reach out and never make a move yourself, you may lose a relationship or opportunity that mattered.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which connection have you been waiting on, and are you willing to take the first step?

topicRules.career: Build partnerships sincerely and early; moving beats waiting. Fair, honest dealing is what wins collaborators.
topicRules.study: Approach capable people and join a study group. Genuine connections bring you resources and support.
topicRules.romance: Say what you feel sincerely. Honesty matters more than technique, and closeness from the heart is what lasts.
topicRules.family: Hold the household together through real regard, so people feel they matter rather than merely gathering out of form.
topicRules.relations: Build genuine ties and act openly. That attracts like-minded people; do not press those who are not interested.
topicRules.finance: Look for partners you can trust and act in good faith. Taking the initiative helps, but assess the person carefully.
topicRules.wellness: Seek out community support and people who share your direction. Isolation works against you; real connection helps.
topicRules.general: Reach out sincerely and commit for the long term. Acting early helps; hesitating may cost you the opening.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: offer goodwill first, and commit long term to people whose values are close to yours. Avoid: attaching yourself to a group just to belong, or joining a circle that defines itself by exclusion.

hexagrams.name: Xiǎo Xù · Small Restraint
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Xiao Xu: Success. Dense clouds, no rain, from our western outskirts.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary reads the single yielding line holding five firm ones as restraint that is real but small, so progress is possible yet not yet released. The Xiang image of wind moving above heaven tells the noble person to refine culture and character while waiting.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: This is the state of dense cloud that has not yet turned to rain. Something is gathering, and the direction is sound, but the amount you have built up is still modest. A small obstruction holds back a much larger force, so effort goes in and little comes out. The reading is not that the work is wrong. It is that the release has not arrived. Keep accumulating, tend to craft and conduct, and resist the urge to force a breakthrough with strength you do not yet have.
hexagrams.trendReason: Although Xiao Xu offers success, dense clouds without rain clearly show conditions still accumulating before results can be released. Several lines face obstruction or require care. Overall it favors prudent waiting, hence the rating: Balanced.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Keep gathering quietly; the release has not come yet.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Returning by one's own path. What blame? Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says returning by one's own path is right in itself, and therefore favourable. The first line is firm and stands at the bottom, holding to its proper way without needing help.
lines.plainLanguage: Coming back to the path that was always yours is already the good outcome. You do not need a shortcut or a clever detour. Continuing in the direction you had is enough to stay clear of fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you sense you have drifted, simply turn back to the direction you believe in. No elaborate correction is needed. Returning is the whole move.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you still on the path you genuinely agree with, and is there anything you have drifted from that you should return to?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Drawn back together. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says being drawn back while holding the centre means you do not lose yourself. The second line sits in the middle, so even when pulled along it keeps its own balance.
lines.plainLanguage: Someone or something draws you back onto the right track. You did not initiate it, and that is fine. Holding your centre means the pull does not cost you your footing.
lines.lifeTranslation: Sometimes it is a friend's remark or an outside push that puts you back on course. Accepting that is not weakness. Not everything has to start with you.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is someone around you nudging you back towards a better state, and are you willing to accept that nudge?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: The wagon loses its wheel spokes. Husband and wife turn against each other.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary explains the quarrel at home as an inability to set the household right. The third line is firm but caught under the yielding fourth, so forward motion breaks like spokes coming off a wheel.
lines.plainLanguage: The spokes come loose and the cart stops. Friction shows up in the closest relationship, because the stored-up force has run straight into an obstruction. Pushing harder only grinds.
lines.lifeTranslation: When progress stalls and a partnership starts to crack, look at the underlying fault first. Forcing the pace from here widens the break rather than closing it.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there a relationship or partnership showing visible strain right now, and have you looked at the real cause or been avoiding it?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: With sincerity, blood departs and fear passes. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that sincerity dissolves alarm because your intent aligns with those above. The fourth line is yielding and rightly placed, holding the firm lines through honesty rather than force.
lines.plainLanguage: Act with sincerity and the fear around a situation loosens on its own. Wounds close, alarm passes, and no fault attaches. Honesty is what releases the pressure here, not manoeuvring.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you are carrying pressure or a sense of danger, meet it plainly and truthfully. Sincerity is not a soft option here. It is the thing that actually defuses the tension.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you meeting this pressure honestly, or has fear pushed you into avoidance and tactics?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Sincerity binds closely; sharing wealth with neighbors.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says bound together in good faith means not being rich alone. The fifth line is firm and in the place of honour, with enough trust and enough resource to share rather than hoard.
lines.plainLanguage: Trust binds you to the people around you, and what you have accumulated is worth sharing with them. Generosity backed by honesty is what turns a stock of resource into something that works.
lines.lifeTranslation: Ask whether what you have built is being kept to yourself. Connecting honestly and sharing what you hold is what lets the accumulation do any real work.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you willing to share what you have gathered with the people near you, and what is driving your answer?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Rain has fallen; rest has come. Honored virtue accumulates. The wife's persistence is dangerous. The moon is nearly full; the noble person's advance brings misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that once the rain has fallen and things are at rest, virtue has been carried to its full load, and setting out invites trouble because doubt remains. The moon is nearly full but not yet full.
lines.plainLanguage: What you were storing is close to complete, like a moon a night short of full. This is exactly the point to be careful. A large move made the moment the store peaks tends to cost you.
lines.lifeTranslation: The moment you feel almost fully prepared is the moment to slow down. Do not convert a nearly full reserve into a sudden large commitment. What fills also wanes.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Now that your reserves feel nearly full, are you itching to act big, and does that impulse deserve one more look?

topicRules.career: Your position is still in the accumulating stage, so deepen skills and contacts rather than chasing a visible win before the weight is behind you.
topicRules.study: Progress is real but not yet showing in results, so keep the routine steady and stop measuring yourself by immediate returns.
topicRules.romance: Something is forming but has not ripened, so keep tending it sincerely and resist pressing for a definite step right now.
topicRules.family: Build agreement first and settle the small unresolved details; this is not the moment for a major household change.
topicRules.relations: You are laying groundwork, so invest in conduct and honesty and do not expect deep trust to arrive in one meeting.
topicRules.finance: Treat this as a saving phase: preserve capacity, keep commitments small, and wait for conditions that actually favour a move.
topicRules.wellness: You are rebuilding reserves, so feed and rest yourself properly rather than adding load on top of a partly recovered system.
topicRules.general: The period favours quiet accumulation and refinement of character, not a large move; let conditions finish forming.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: build up small results, tidy your resources, and let conditions finish forming before you push. Avoid: underestimating how much a small obstacle can hold back, or scaling something up before it is ready.

hexagrams.name: Lǚ · Treading
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Lu: Treading on the tiger's tail, it does not bite the person. Success.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary describes the yielding treading on the firm, meeting strength with good humour, so one steps on the tiger's tail and is not bitten. The Xiang image of heaven above and marsh below tells the noble person to make rank clear and settle the people's intent.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: This is the picture of walking behind a tiger and not being bitten. The danger is real and close, but careful, courteous conduct carries you through it. The situation has tension in it, and the answer is not to shrink away. It is to keep your proportions right: know your place, keep your manners, watch where each step lands. Progress here comes from precision and respect rather than boldness. Caution is the skill being asked for, not timidity.
hexagrams.trendReason: Lu's judgment explicitly states “success”: careful, courteous action can progress. Its overall direction is positive, although the third line warns against recklessness. Good fortune is associated with care and restraint, hence the rating: Highly Favorable.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Step carefully and keep your manners; that is how you pass.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Simple conduct. Proceed; no blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says plain treading goes forward because it walks alone by its own wish. The first line moves with unadorned integrity, so no fault arises.
lines.plainLanguage: Go forward plainly, without packaging or tactics. What carries you is the substance of what you actually are, and that is enough to keep you clear of fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: You do not need extra polish or a clever angle. Act simply and truthfully, and if the direction is right, plainness itself is your pass.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Where are you over-packaging yourself right now, and what would change if you acted as plainly as you actually are?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Treading a level, open path. The secluded person's steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the retiring person is favoured in holding firm because the centre is not disturbed. The second line holds the middle, and the road ahead of it is level.
lines.plainLanguage: The path is broad and level. Even someone who chooses to stay quiet and out of view does well by holding to what is right. Outside noise does not have to set your pace.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you prefer a quiet life away from the crowd, that is a workable choice. Hold your own standard and the quietness itself carries you well.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you living to match other people's expectations rather than the pace that actually suits you?

lines.original: Six in the third place: The one-eyed can see; the lame can walk. Treading on the tiger's tail, one is bitten. Misfortune. A warrior acts as the great ruler.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the one-eyed cannot really see and the lame cannot really walk, and the harm comes from standing in a place that does not fit. Overreach, not bad luck, is the cause.
lines.plainLanguage: Someone half-equipped insists on acting anyway, overrates their own capacity, and steps where the tiger can reach. This is the price of not seeing your own limits clearly.
lines.lifeTranslation: Taking on a role beyond your current capacity tends to end badly. An honest read of what you can actually handle right now matters more than the role's appeal.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Where are you straining to carry something past your current ability, and is the pressure coming from outside or from your own reluctance to admit it?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Treading on the tiger's tail, trembling with fear. Good fortune in the end.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the wary person ends well because the intent is carried through. The fourth line is close to the tiger's tail yet acts with steady apprehension.
lines.plainLanguage: You are treading right behind the danger, alert and uneasy, and that very alertness is what brings you through. The caution is armour, not a symptom.
lines.lifeTranslation: In a high-risk situation, staying wary protects you. Do not let the tension tip into panic; let it keep you precise instead.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Where are you walking on eggshells right now, and is that carefulness moving you forward or holding you still?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Resolute treading. Steadfastness brings danger.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says decisive treading carries danger precisely because the position is the responsible one. The fifth line holds the place of honour, where being right is not the same as being safe.
lines.plainLanguage: Acting decisively from a senior position may be correct and still be risky. The more the seat matters, the more caution the decision needs. Being right does not remove the exposure.
lines.lifeTranslation: Your call may well be the right one, but the weight of your position means the consequences travel. Treat correctness and safety as two separate questions.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In the decision you are making, has being right let you stop looking at the risk or at who else it lands on?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Examine your conduct and assess its signs. Returning through the full cycle brings supreme good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says great favour at the top brings real cause for celebration. The sixth line looks back over the whole road travelled and weighs what it finds.
lines.plainLanguage: At the end of the road you look back over how you walked it and weigh whether it held to what is right. Completing the circle honestly is where the real good lies.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a stage closes, spend time reviewing the path you actually took and whether it matched your core values. The review itself is worth a great deal.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Looking back over your recent choices, do you see the person you actually wanted to be?

topicRules.career: Move carefully and stay within your remit; keeping to your proper role earns more trust here than reaching past it.
topicRules.study: Follow the proper sequence and skip no steps; solid ground covered in order beats jumping to material above your level.
topicRules.romance: Sincerity plus a sense of proportion is the foundation; pursue with care rather than intensity and give the other person room.
topicRules.family: Let each person hold their own role and keep the household's agreed order; upsetting the balance costs more than it gains.
topicRules.relations: Treat people with courtesy and respect the unspoken lines; modesty is what lets you move through a complicated group.
topicRules.finance: Stay cautious and keep away from high-risk positions; steady returns are worth more than a fast one right now.
topicRules.wellness: Keep a regular rhythm and stick to your health habits; avoid overspending yourself or taking chances with your body.
topicRules.general: Proceed step by step with courtesy and proportion; caution here is intelligence, not conservatism.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: confirm the rules and the boundaries, and watch how the other side reacts to each step. Avoid: trusting luck and overstepping, or letting a run of ease loosen your courtesy.

hexagrams.name: Tài · Peace
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Tai: The small departs, the great arrives. Good fortune and success.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary reads the small departing and the great arriving as heaven and earth in exchange, so all things move freely and those above and below share one intent. The Xiang image tells the ruler to shape the way of heaven and earth and assist what suits them, for the people's sake.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Heaven and earth are in contact and everything circulates. The strong and active part sits below and rises; the yielding part sits above and comes down. That is why communication works in this state: people above and below actually want the same thing. Sound conduct is gaining ground and its opposite is receding. The commentary adds a warning inside the good news. A favourable period asks to be governed and used, not simply enjoyed, and nothing at its height stays there.
hexagrams.trendReason: Tai says, “The small departs, the great arrives. Good fortune and success.” Heaven and Earth communicate and all things flow. One of the most open and auspicious states among the 64 hexagrams, it has an extremely positive overall direction, hence the rating: Highest Favorability.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Channels are open; use the window rather than bask in it.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Pulling up thatch with its connected roots, others of its kind follow. Advancing brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says pulling up the grass and going forth is favourable because the intent points outward. The first line is firm, low, and joined at the root to others of its kind.
lines.plainLanguage: Pull up one stalk of grass and the connected roots come with it. People of like mind move together, and going outward as a group works better than going alone.
lines.lifeTranslation: This is a good moment to act, and better still to act with people who want the same thing. A shared aim multiplies what each of you can do.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do you have people of like mind to push this forward with, or are you defaulting to doing it alone?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Embrace the uncultivated. Wade across the river; do not neglect the distant. Let factions fall away. Be honored for walking the middle path.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says embracing the wasteland and walking the middle way is what makes one great. The second line holds the centre, without faction and without neglecting what lies far off.
lines.plainLanguage: Take in even the barren ground. Cross the river when it must be crossed, do not neglect what is distant, and form no cliques. Holding the middle way is what makes the reach real.
lines.lifeTranslation: An easy stretch is exactly when breadth matters. Do not fall into a favoured circle, and do not let the people or tasks at the edges drop out of view.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Has the current ease pulled you into a small circle, and who or what have you stopped paying attention to?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: No level ground without a slope; no departure without return. Steadfastness through hardship brings no blame. Do not worry about trustworthiness; there is blessing in sustenance.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says nothing goes without returning, because that is the boundary of heaven and earth. The third line stands where the peaceful phase turns, and holding firm through difficulty keeps it free of fault.
lines.plainLanguage: No ground stays level and nothing only goes out without coming back. A good stretch has a turn in it. Holding to what is right through the hard part keeps you clear, and there is still real sustenance in it.
lines.lifeTranslation: While things are easy, do not assume they stay that way. Stay ready for the shift. People who hold their standards through the difficult stretch still come away with something solid.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you preparing for the harder stretch while things are good, or fully absorbed in how well it is going?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Fluttering together, not wealthy, with one's neighbors; trusting without admonition.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says fluttering without wealth means substance has been lost, and trusting without warning comes from the heart's own wish. The fourth line enters the closing phase of peace, where sincerity needs no policing.
lines.plainLanguage: People come together lightly, and what holds them is not wealth but honest trust. Believing each other without needing reminders is the truest form the bond can take.
lines.lifeTranslation: The best relationships are not tied together by money or by repeated pledges of loyalty. Sincerity that comes from the inside is the stronger link.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In your important relationships, how much rests on interest or obligation, and how much on plain good faith?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Di Yi gives his daughter in marriage. Through blessing, supreme good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the great favour of this blessing comes from holding the centre and acting on one's real wish. The image is a sovereign giving a daughter in marriage with humility rather than rank.
lines.plainLanguage: Someone in the higher position steps down in manner, blesses the arrangement sincerely, and does not stand on status. That humility is where the real good of this line sits.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you hold the advantage, using it to make something good happen for someone else, without leaning on your standing, is worth more than the standing was.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there a chance to help or make way for someone below you, and what is stopping you?

lines.original: Six at the top: The city wall falls back into the moat. Do not use the army. Proclaim commands from your own town. Steadfastness brings regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the wall falling back into the moat shows that command has become disordered. At the end of peace the wall collapses, and the answer is not troops but setting one's own town in order.
lines.plainLanguage: At the far end of a good phase the wall falls back into the ditch. This is not the time for an outward campaign. Start by putting your own core in order, and accept some regret, because the larger tide has already turned.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a favourable stretch runs out, do not try to hold it with a bigger push. Tidy your own base first, accept that the situation has changed, and stop forcing it.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do you sense cracks in something that used to run smoothly, and are you trying to hold it by force or ready to adjust?

topicRules.career: Communication up and down is unusually open, so push the important plans now, while remembering that no peak holds indefinitely.
topicRules.study: Conditions are working with you, so use this stretch for depth; progress made now goes further than the same effort later.
topicRules.romance: Understanding flows easily at the moment, so say the thing you have been holding back; this is a good window to deepen a bond.
topicRules.family: The household mood is warm, which makes it the right time to settle old issues and agree on shared plans.
topicRules.relations: Collaboration comes easily now, so build connections widely, but keep to the middle way rather than favouring a faction.
topicRules.finance: Conditions favour setting medium and long-term plans; plan carefully now while both your situation and the environment cooperate.
topicRules.wellness: Energy is good, which makes this the best moment to establish habits and a steady routine rather than to coast.
topicRules.general: The period is strongly favourable and suits active progress; hold to your standards so the open stretch lasts longer.
