hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: use the open channels to align people above and below and move the important things forward. Avoid: enjoying the ease while ignoring what could turn, or taking the credit alone.

hexagrams.name: Pǐ · Obstruction
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Pi: The blockage of unworthy people. Unfavorable to the noble person's steadfastness. The great departs, the small arrives.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary reads the great departing and the small arriving as heaven and earth failing to meet, so nothing circulates and those above and below share no intent. The Xiang image tells the noble person to avoid trouble through frugal virtue and not to be tempted by honour or salary.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: This is the reverse of Peace. Heaven rises, earth sinks, and the two move apart, so exchange stops and everything jams. What is substantial leaves and what is thin arrives; people above and below no longer want the same thing. The old reading is blunt about it being an unfavourable period. The advice is to draw in, live simply, keep out of trouble, and not to chase position or reward while the channels are shut. A closed stretch is for building character and holding your intent until it opens.
hexagrams.trendReason: Pi depicts Heaven and Earth failing to meet and all things blocked: “Unfavorable to the noble person's steadfastness; the great departs, the small arrives.” An image of adverse obstruction and one of the least favorable states among the 64 hexagrams, hence the rating: Lowest Favorability.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Channels are shut; draw in, keep your standards, wait it out.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Pulling up thatch with connected roots, others of its kind follow. Steadfastness brings good fortune and success.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that pulling up the grass and holding firm is favourable because the intent still points towards what is right. At the start of obstruction, like roots stay connected and keep their bearing.
lines.plainLanguage: Even in a blocked period, people of like mind stay joined at the root and hold to what is right, and that still goes well. Not changing colour under pressure is the base you keep.
lines.lifeTranslation: In a hard stretch, hold your core values and find the few people who share them. The wider environment may be against you; your own conduct need not be.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In this difficult situation, are you still holding what you actually value, or has the pressure started shifting you?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Accommodating and supporting. Good fortune for petty people; stagnation for the great person, yet success.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the greater person passes through obstruction because they do not mix into the crowd. The second line is yielding and central, keeping its character apart from the flatterers.
lines.plainLanguage: Flattery and accommodation do well in a closed period. Someone of real character does not join in, carries more of the difficulty, and keeps their own standing intact.
lines.lifeTranslation: In an unfair environment some people get ahead by pleasing the right people. Declining to do that costs you in the short run and preserves what you actually are.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Under this pressure, do you feel the pull to accommodate, and is that compromise worth what it costs you?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Harboring shame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the concealed shame comes from standing in a place that does not fit. The third line is yielding in a firm position, unable to act and left holding the awkwardness.
lines.plainLanguage: There is nothing to do but carry the embarrassment. The cause is the position itself: what is asked and what you can give do not match, so discomfort is the whole content of the line.
lines.lifeTranslation: If a role leaves you unable to act, or makes you do things you are not proud of, that is usually a sign the role was never a fit.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there a role right now that leaves you ashamed or powerless, and does it actually suit you?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: A mandate. No blame. Companions share the blessing.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says having a mandate and no fault means the intent can be carried out. The fourth line is firm and enters the upper trigram, and those of its kind share in the blessing.
lines.plainLanguage: There is a mandate behind what you are doing, so no fault attaches, and the people alongside you share in it. Even inside a closed period, a purpose can still be carried forward.
lines.lifeTranslation: Difficult times still have work with meaning in them. If your actions serve something larger, that sense of purpose gives you and the people with you a direction to hold.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there a larger purpose holding up what you are doing, and is it carrying you and the people beside you?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Stagnation comes to rest. Good fortune for the great person. “It may perish! It may perish!” Tie it to a cluster of mulberry roots.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the greater person's good fortune comes from standing in the right position. The fifth line is central and correct, able to end the obstruction while staying tied, as if to mulberry roots, by a sense of danger.
lines.plainLanguage: The blockage can be brought to an end from here. What makes that last is the repeated thought that it could all be lost, like a cord tied to deep mulberry roots. Vigilance is the anchor.
lines.lifeTranslation: Even as things start to improve, keep the awareness that it could still go. Do not loosen. A recovery only holds if the roots underneath it are secure.
lines.reflectionPrompt: When things start improving, do you let go too soon, and what are the roots that keep you steady?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Stagnation is overturned. First stagnation, then joy.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says obstruction at its end topples over, for how could it last? The sixth line stands where the closed period exhausts itself and turns.
lines.plainLanguage: Once blockage reaches its limit it overturns of itself: hardship first, relief after. A closed period running out is the ordinary way of things, not a reward.
lines.lifeTranslation: Difficulty does end. Past the darkest stretch the ground opens again. The thing not to do is give up in the last part of the dark.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Might you be in the final stretch of this difficulty, with the turn closer than it feels?

topicRules.career: Communication is blocked and force does not move it; step back, build capability, and wait for the situation to loosen.
topicRules.study: Progress is slower than you expected, so drop the demand for quick results and keep the effort steady as groundwork for later.
topicRules.romance: Understanding is hard to reach at the moment, so sort out your own state first rather than pressing for a resolution now.
topicRules.family: The atmosphere is stiff, so reduce friction, live simply, and look for a workable channel instead of meeting force with force.
topicRules.relations: The environment is closed and collaboration stalls easily; keep a low profile, hold plans back, and work only with people you trust.
topicRules.finance: Conditions are against you, so protect what you have, cut unnecessary spending, and hold off on new commitments.
topicRules.wellness: Things feel stuck and heavy, so rest, loosen the schedule, and stop pushing through on reserves you do not have.
topicRules.general: This is a closed period: live frugally, preserve strength, avoid head-on conflict, and hold your standards until it turns.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: keep a low profile, protect the quality of your work, and hold capacity in reserve for when conditions shift. Avoid: forcing a new venture through a closed system, or trading your principles for approval.

hexagrams.name: Tóng Rén · Fellowship
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Tong Ren: Fellowship in the open fields. Success. It is beneficial to cross the great river and beneficial for the noble person to remain steadfast.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says the yielding line finds its place and centre and responds to the creative, and that only the noble person can reach the intent of all under heaven. The Xiang image of heaven together with fire tells the noble person to sort kinds and distinguish things.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Heaven and fire answer each other: different people bound by a shared aim. The judgement deliberately sets the meeting in open country, which is a warning that fellowship should not shrink to a circle of intimates. What makes it work is being able to tell differences apart and still hold to a shared standard. The lines themselves show exclusion, suspicion and open conflict, so this is not a picture of people naturally getting along. It is a picture of what open principles and continued talking can hold together.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's “success” and “beneficial to cross the great river” favor cooperation and shared responsibility, hence the rating: Highly Favorable. The second line's regret, third line's defensiveness, and fourth line's confrontation still remind us that results depend on overcoming self-interest. This rating is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Unite around a shared aim, not around familiar faces.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Fellowship at the gate. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary asks who could find fault with meeting people outside the gate. The point of this line is that association is not confined to one's own doorway, and is open rather than partial.
lines.plainLanguage: Going out of the gate to meet people means not keeping the collaboration inside your own household. Being open and unbiased is what keeps this line free of fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: At the start of a new collaboration, say the purpose and the boundaries out loud and leave room for people from different backgrounds. There is no need to sort everyone into insiders and outsiders yet.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you willing to let people outside your circle understand this and take part in it?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Fellowship within the clan. Regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary calls fellowship confined to one's clan a narrow road. Association limited by private affection restricts the scope of what can be done, which is why the line carries regret.
lines.plainLanguage: Joining only with kin or close friends keeps the collaboration inside the bounds of private feeling. The line's note of regret is a warning that the view has become too narrow.
lines.lifeTranslation: Working with familiar people takes less effort, but choose partners on capability, principles and an actual division of work, and check who else you have overlooked.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you choosing partners for the shared aim, or simply because you already know them?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Concealing troops in the thickets, ascending the high hill. For three years, no rising to action.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says arms are hidden in the thicket because the opponent is strong, and three years pass without action. Suspicion and standoff hold the collaboration still.
lines.plainLanguage: Weapons are hidden in the undergrowth and the high ground is used for watching. Nobody moves for a long time. Mistrust and rivalry have brought the work to a halt.
lines.lifeTranslation: If communication has turned into guesswork and defence, establish the facts and name the disagreement before deciding whether to work together. Quiet manoeuvring is not a way to carry this forward.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Of the guardedness you feel, how much rests on confirmed facts and how much on assumption?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Mounting the wall, unable to prevail; attacking, good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that although the wall is mounted, the attack rightly does not go through, and the favourable turn comes from being pressed and returning to principle. Stopping is what is commended, not conquest.
lines.plainLanguage: The wall has been scaled and the attack is halted. What is favourable here is not taking the position by force but recognising the situation and stopping a fight that does not belong.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a dispute escalates, withdrawing an excessive demand or stopping an attack is not the same as losing your position. It leaves space to renegotiate.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Can you call off one unnecessary confrontation before this grows any further?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: In fellowship, first wailing, then laughing. Great armies overcome and meet.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the earlier weeping to centred honesty, and the eventual meeting to overcoming what stood between. The military imagery belongs to the old text and should not be read as a modern instruction.
lines.plainLanguage: First there is crying at the separation, then laughter at the meeting. A shared intent only connects after it has been through obstruction. The martial language is imagery, not advice.
lines.lifeTranslation: Even with a shared aim you may go through misunderstanding and resistance. Say the disagreement plainly and sort out the resources; a temporary clash is not a verdict on you.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What is the aim you and the other person genuinely share, and what has still not been said out loud?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Fellowship in the outskirts. No regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says fellowship in the outskirts means the intent has not yet been realised. Distance avoids entanglement, but it also leaves you short of the wider fellowship the hexagram describes.
lines.plainLanguage: Meeting people out at the edge of town reduces entanglement and leaves nothing to regret, but the commentary notes the aim is still unfulfilled. You remain at a distance from real fellowship.
lines.lifeTranslation: Keeping some distance lowers friction, but if you want to work closely with people you have to see the part of this that is withdrawal and decide how far you actually want to commit.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the distance you keep respect for a boundary, or avoidance of something you actually care about?

topicRules.career: Settle the shared aim, responsibilities and decision rights, and keep information open; cross-team work is worth considering, but not on the strength of friendship alone.
topicRules.study: Discussion and swapping solutions sharpens your view, but keep verifying independently rather than treating group consensus as the answer.
topicRules.romance: Speak openly about values and expectations and respect each other's separate circles; shared interests are not evidence of shared intent.
topicRules.family: Give each member a chance to state what they need and negotiate the division of work around a shared aim, rather than letting favouritism harden into camps.
topicRules.relations: The work here is openness and common ground, not uniformity; establish principles and boundaries first, then choose a workable way to cooperate.
topicRules.finance: If money is pooled, agree the purpose, the liability and the exit terms first; trust is not a substitute for records, however well you know the person.
topicRules.wellness: Lean on people you trust for company and support while keeping your own limits on rest; you do not have to match a pace that exhausts you.
topicRules.general: Connect with others through a shared aim, communicate openly, and make room for difference; surface harmony is not the same as a solved problem.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: gather people around a stated common aim, make the rules public, and leave room for difference. Avoid: allying only with the people you already know, or reading disagreement as hostility.

hexagrams.name: Dà Yǒu · Great Holding
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Da You: Supreme success.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says the yielding line holds the place of honour, is greatly central, and is answered by those above and below, with firmness and clarity acting in accord with the season. The Xiang image of fire in the sky tells the noble person to check what is harmful, bring forward what is good, and follow the mandate of heaven.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Fire sits high in the sky: clear discernment paired with real substance, enough to carry more resource and more responsibility than usual. The judgement is unambiguously favourable, yet nearly every line pushes back against complacency, display and hoarding. The question this hexagram asks is not how to get more. It is what you do with what you already hold: how you use it, how you share it, and what limits you place on yourself. Abundance still needs honesty, proportion and regular review.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment explicitly states “supreme success,” and its commentary explains progress through strength, clarity, and action aligned with Heaven and the times. The text's overall direction is very positive, hence the rating: Highest Favorability. The third and fourth nines still require generosity of spirit and self-restraint. This summarizes the text's direction, not a promise of wealth or achievement.
hexagrams.coreMessage: The more you hold, the more discernment and restraint it needs.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: No involvement with harm; no fault. Awareness of hardship brings no blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary notes that at the start of Great Holding there is as yet no entanglement with what is harmful. Freedom from fault still depends on treating the situation as difficult.
lines.plainLanguage: At the beginning of abundance you are not yet tangled up with anything harmful, but you still need to hold yourself to the discipline of difficulty. No fault does not mean no limits.
lines.lifeTranslation: When resources or opportunities first arrive, identify the risks and set basic ground rules; an easy start is not a reason to stop checking.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What boundaries do you have in place to keep new resources from turning into a burden?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: A great wagon for carrying. There is somewhere to go. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the great cart can carry because what is gathered at the centre does not collapse. Capacity comes before distance travelled.
lines.plainLanguage: A large cart can carry a heavy load, which stands for having the capacity and the base to take weight. Going somewhere with it still means matching the load to what you can carry.
lines.lifeTranslation: Before accepting a new assignment, check whether the time, the people and the resources are actually there. Carrying capacity first, more work second.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Can your current arrangements genuinely carry the next stage of the work?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: A duke presents offerings to the Son of Heaven. A petty person cannot do so.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the duke's offering to the sovereign is beyond someone who counts only private gain. Resource held at this level is bound to public order.
lines.plainLanguage: A lord makes an offering to the sovereign: what he holds is directed towards the common order. Anyone reckoning only in private advantage cannot carry that kind of responsibility.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you hold more of the team's resources, say how they feed back into the shared aim. Position and results are not simply yours.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Of the resources under your control, which should serve the common good rather than your own discretion?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Do not make a display of abundance. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary ties freedom from fault here to clear discrimination. Standing amid abundance without making a display of it is what the line commends.
lines.plainLanguage: You are in a period of plenty and do not present yourself as grand. Capability still calls for avoiding display, comparison and over-expansion.
lines.lifeTranslation: When your results get recognised, let the facts speak and keep some capacity in reserve. You do not have to make everything bigger to prove the point.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the commitment you are adding driven by need, or by measuring yourself against someone else?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Sincerity in mutual exchange, with dignity. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says sincerity in exchange awakens the intent of others, and the favourable dignity comes from being approachable without being unguarded. Warmth and principle stand together.
lines.plainLanguage: You deal with people in good faith while keeping a measured authority and clear limits. This is leading gently without giving up the principle.
lines.lifeTranslation: Goodwill and rules can coexist. State the commitment, the responsibility and the limit clearly, so that being kind does not become saying yes to everything.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do people feel your sincerity and also know exactly where your limits are?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Heaven itself gives support. Good fortune; nothing is unfavorable.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the great favour at the top to help from heaven. The old text uses this language for the ideal result of following the way, keeping faith and honouring the capable, and it should be read together with the conduct the earlier lines require.
lines.plainLanguage: Help from above and a favourable outcome describe the ideal result of following the way, keeping faith and valuing capable people. Read alongside the earlier lines, it is not unconditional protection.
lines.lifeTranslation: With results already in hand, keep valuing the support you have, listen to capable people and stay accountable. A good position is not evidence that you cannot err.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How do you answer the support others give you, and how do you keep a smooth run from deafening you to warnings?

topicRules.career: Inventory the resources and assign responsibility clearly so authority matches capability; favourable conditions suit important work, not blind expansion or hoarded credit.
topicRules.study: Make full use of the material, teachers and time you already have and turn broad exposure into depth; abundance of resource is not a substitute for practice.
topicRules.romance: Spend the time and attention on genuine exchange, and give without keeping a ledger; material provision does not replace respect and consent.
topicRules.family: Discuss the sharing of resources and caring duties openly and account for different needs; holding the purse is not a licence to decide everything.
topicRules.relations: Share experience and opportunities while keeping proportion; being trusted raises the bar on keeping your word rather than lowering it.
topicRules.finance: Map income, obligations and tolerable loss, and keep a reserve; having more does not remove the risk of concentrating it in one place.
topicRules.wellness: Allocate real time to rest, movement and daily care, and watch the load that added responsibility brings; a good stretch of energy is not a licence to overdraw.
topicRules.general: The direction here is about using what you hold: discern clearly, act in good faith and take on more responsibility with restraint.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: take stock of what you have, state the principles for allocating it, and let the results reach the people involved. Avoid: showing off your advantage, holding on to too much, or accepting responsibility beyond your capacity.

hexagrams.name: Qiān · Modesty
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Qian: Success. The noble person brings things to completion.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says the way of heaven reduces the full and adds to the modest, and the way of earth changes the full and flows towards the modest, so modesty is honoured and luminous, humble yet not to be overstepped. The Xiang image of a mountain within the earth tells the noble person to take from the excessive, add to the scant, and weigh things so distribution is even.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: A mountain hidden inside the earth: real substance that does not advertise itself. The judgement approves this direction and says the noble person carries it through to the end. The image adds a practical instruction: reduce where there is too much, top up where there is too little, and weigh things out fairly. Modesty here is not self-denial or endless yielding. It is knowing your limits and respecting other people, while still being able to carry out your responsibilities and enforce a boundary when one is needed.
hexagrams.trendReason: “Success; the noble person brings things to completion,” along with several lines' good fortune and “nothing unfavorable,” gives humility and proper restraint a positive direction, hence the rating: Highly Favorable. The fifth and top sixes still require corrective action. Modesty cannot mean yielding in everything or guaranteeing outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Hold real substance lightly and still carry the responsibility.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: A modest, modest noble person. Crossing the great river brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the doubly modest person tends themselves through humility. Even at the starting position, willingness to admit what is missing is what the line commends.
lines.plainLanguage: Staying modest at the very start means being willing to admit what you do not yet have. Facing a large undertaking with that attitude is the direction the line approves.
lines.lifeTranslation: Taking on a task for the first time, ask your questions and fill the gaps in your preparation. Make asking part of the work rather than pretending you already know.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What have you not yet mastered that you could simply ask about instead of covering up?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Modesty makes itself heard. Steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that modesty which becomes audible is favourable in holding firm because it is gained in the heart. The point is consistency, not the performance of humility.
lines.plainLanguage: Modesty shows through from the inside and other people feel it. What matters is that the inside and the outside match, not that you construct a humble image.
lines.lifeTranslation: Keeping your words and actions consistent, taking feedback and being willing to correct yourself says far more than repeatedly running yourself down.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the modesty you show real respect, or are you waiting for someone to contradict it?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: A noble person of achievement and modesty. Completion brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the person who works hard and stays modest has the people's allegiance. Achievement and continued responsibility are shown here as compatible.
lines.plainLanguage: You have done the work and you still stay low, not claiming the achievement as your standing, and you see the thing through. Credit and continued responsibility can hold together.
lines.lifeTranslation: After finishing something important, acknowledge your own contribution and other people's, and hand over the follow-up properly rather than stopping at the recognition.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Once the result is in, are you still willing to do the unglamorous work that follows?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Nothing unfavorable. Put modesty into action.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that applying modesty is favourable in every way because it does not breach the rule. This is modesty enacted in advance and retreat, not courtesy in words.
lines.plainLanguage: Modesty here shows up in how you move forward and step back, staying inside what is appropriate. It means knowing when to help and when to make way.
lines.lifeTranslation: When dividing work, be clear about your own authority and give others space where it is theirs. You do not have to decide for people to prove your ability.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which task is yours to support rather than to take over?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Not wealthy, with one's neighbors. It is beneficial to undertake corrective campaigns. Nothing unfavorable.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the campaign is directed at those who will not submit. Neighbours are joined by more than wealth, and modesty does not rule out enforcing order when it is needed.
lines.plainLanguage: You are not bound to those around you by wealth alone, and there are moments where disorder has to be dealt with. Modesty does not exclude principle or consequence.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a line keeps getting crossed, state the rule first and then apply a proportionate measure as agreed. Endurance is not the only option available to you.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Have you been calling your reluctance to set a boundary modesty?

lines.original: Six at the top: Modesty makes itself heard. It is beneficial to mobilize the army and bring one's own towns and state to order.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that the modesty now known by name still has an intent unfulfilled, and that the campaign is directed at one's own town. Action is turned inward, towards what you can answer for.
lines.plainLanguage: Your modesty has a reputation, but what you set out to do may still be unfinished. The old text points the action at your own town, which means putting your own ground in order first.
lines.lifeTranslation: If there is still a gap between the ideal and the reality, examine your own methods and your team's internal problems before asking the outside world to fall in.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which specific problem could you fix inside your own remit first?

topicRules.career: Acknowledge the edge of your ability, ask for input and report results plainly; neither inflate the credit nor drop the duty that came with it.
topicRules.study: Find the parts you do not understand and adjust your method from mistakes and feedback; modesty keeps the door open, but practice still has to happen.
topicRules.romance: Respect each other's feelings and be willing to apologise and adjust, while keeping your own needs; yielding does not mean accepting treatment that hurts.
topicRules.family: Reweigh chores, care duties and resources so whoever is overloaded gets help; seniority or past contribution should not close the discussion.
topicRules.relations: See what other people are good at and leave room to listen when you state your own view; neither belittle yourself nor compete over everything.
topicRules.finance: Live within your means and admit the limits of what you know about the risk; verify the terms of anything large rather than committing out of pride.
topicRules.wellness: Respect the limits of your current energy and mood and allow yourself rest and help; shouldering everything is not modesty.
topicRules.general: Hold substance without display, top up what is scant, and express modesty through sustained action while keeping your proper responsibilities and limits.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: assess yourself honestly and let credit and responsibility land where they belong. Avoid: talking yourself down to be liked, or letting a success stop you listening.

hexagrams.name: Yù · Enthusiasm
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Yu: It is beneficial to appoint lords and mobilize the army.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says the firm line is answered and the intent carried out, moving in accord with the situation, which is why heaven and earth act this way and why establishing lords and moving armies is possible. The Xiang image of thunder bursting from the earth tells the ancient kings to make music, honour virtue and offer it to the ancestors.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Thunder comes out of the ground: momentum with a group behind it. The judgement speaks of appointing leaders and moving armies, which is about organised, prepared, collective action rather than a mood. The image links feeling to order through music and rite. But the lines return repeatedly to self-congratulation, waiting on other people's approval, and sinking into comfort. So enthusiasm here needs restraint, and the energy has to land in arrangements someone can actually carry out.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment affirms conditions for organized action, but the first six warns of misfortune, the third of regret, and the top of dimmed awareness. Inspiration and excess coexist, hence the rating: Balanced. This is an editorial reading of tensions within the hexagram, not a definite forecast of good or bad conditions.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Match the enthusiasm with preparation and notice shifts early.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Proclaiming enthusiasm. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the enthusiasm that announces itself at the first line is exhausted in its intent, and so brings misfortune. Excitement before you are steady costs you proportion.
lines.plainLanguage: Broadcasting your delight before you are on solid ground is self-congratulation too early. The line's warning is that excitement can make you lose your sense of proportion.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a bit of good news arrives, confirm the conditions before making public promises. A burst of excitement is not the same as a finished thing.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Of the result you want to announce, what still needs checking or finishing?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Firm as a rock, not waiting out the day. Steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says not waiting out the day is favourable because of being central and correct. The line commends clear-headedness and timely adjustment over being swayed by excitement.
lines.plainLanguage: You stand as firm as stone, and when you notice a change you do not let the day run out before acting. Clarity and timely correction are what this line approves.
lines.lifeTranslation: In a loud or persuasive environment, hold your own criteria. If something is clearly off, check and adjust early rather than waiting for it to grow.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What concrete signal tells you it is time to stop or change your approach?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Looking upward for enthusiasm. Regret. Delay brings regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the regret in looking upward for enjoyment comes from an unsuitable position. Hesitating after you have noticed the problem adds a second layer of regret.
lines.plainLanguage: Looking up at someone else for your pleasure tends to cost you your own judgement. Noticing that and then hesitating anyway adds another round of regret.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you keep waiting for someone else to supply your motivation or approval, work out the next step you can take yourself rather than handing over the decision.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Have you staked your next move entirely on how one person responds?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: The source of enthusiasm brings great gain. Do not doubt. Friends gather like hair held by a clasp.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that being the source of the enthusiasm brings much gain because the intent is widely carried out. The weight falls on shared trust and a clear direction, not on one person's takings.
lines.plainLanguage: You are the source of other people's momentum, and that draws companions and support. What matters is mutual trust and a clear direction, not one person collecting the gains.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you launch something, spell out the aim, the division of work and how to take part, so people can commit properly rather than riding on atmosphere or your personality.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your call to action concrete enough for willing people to actually join in?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Persistent illness, yet continually not dying.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the persistent affliction comes from riding on what is firm, and that it does not end because the centre has not been lost. The affliction in the old text is an image of circumstance, not a medical reading.
lines.plainLanguage: You are stuck in a long, uncomfortable, constrained position, but the support underneath has not gone. The illness in the text is an image for the situation, not a statement about health.
lines.lifeTranslation: If an uncomfortable arrangement has lasted a long time, work out what is barely holding it up and address the constraints one at a time. Still coping is not a reason to leave it alone.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In the bind you are putting up with, which constraint is most worth tackling first?

lines.original: Six at the top: Darkened enthusiasm. Though established, it changes. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary asks how darkened enjoyment at the top could last. Willingness to change even at the closing stage is what leaves the line free of fault, and the point is an actual turn rather than further delay.
lines.plainLanguage: Sunk in comfort and no longer seeing clearly, yet still willing to change at the closing stage, which is why the line leaves room for no fault. The requirement is a real change of course.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you notice that comfort or habit has you tied up, start with one change you can actually make and look again at the responsibility you set aside.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which habit that helps you avoid reality are you willing to stop, and what will you do instead?

topicRules.career: Turn the team's energy into a defined aim, division of work and schedule, and get the conditions in place before expanding what you promise.
topicRules.study: Use the interest to build a regular practice and check early whether your understanding is solid; enjoying a lesson is not the same as having learnt it.
topicRules.romance: Enjoy the easy time together while confirming what each of you expects; intensity now is not a reason to skip boundaries or unfinished conversations.
topicRules.family: Shared activities do bring people together, but settle the preparation, the cost and the caring duties first so they do not land on one or two people.
topicRules.relations: Tell the difference between a shared aim and a passing buzz, and keep your own judgement inside the group; do not agree to more than you can do just to keep the mood up.
topicRules.finance: Hold your spending limits during excitement or celebration and verify the purpose and the burden first; do not let a wave of sentiment or a short-term tip decide for you.
topicRules.wellness: Use moderate activity and rest to regulate the rhythm and watch the load from overstimulation or from sinking into comfort; the illness imagery in the text is not a health reading.
topicRules.general: Move with the momentum, but pair the enthusiasm with preparation and restraint; notice shifts early and answer drift or delay with a concrete adjustment.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: turn enthusiasm into preparation and rehearsal, and plan for what could go wrong first. Avoid: living on anticipation while execution slips, or using the mood to paper over a problem.

hexagrams.name: Suí · Following
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Sui: Supreme success. Steadfast correctness is beneficial. No blame.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary reads Following as the strong placing itself below the yielding, so that movement and gladness answer each other. The Xiang commentary pictures thunder resting inside the lake and the wise retiring at dusk: following means keeping time with the hour, not agreeing with everyone.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Thunder lies inside the lake. This hexagram is about following the moment rather than following whoever is loudest. The judgement stacks four favourable phrases together, yet each one rests on staying straight. The lines keep returning to a cost: hold on to one side and you let the other go. The fourth line says plainly that gaining through following can turn dangerous. So the work here is choosing the right thing to follow, at the right time, without handing over your own judgement.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment includes supreme success, beneficial steadfastness, and no blame, giving movement with the times a positive direction, hence the rating: Favorable. Yet the second and third lines show unavoidable trade-offs, and the fourth explicitly warns that gain through following can lead to misfortune if boundaries are lost. The top line's binding also suggests constraint, so this is not the highest rating. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Follow the moment, not the crowd, and keep your own standard.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: One's responsibilities change. Steadfastness brings good fortune. Going out to connect with others brings achievement.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that when what you preside over changes, following the straight path brings good fortune, and that going out to meet others succeeds because nothing proper was given up.
lines.plainLanguage: The thing you were in charge of has shifted. The old shape no longer fits, so adjust with the change instead of guarding the form. Stepping outside your usual circle is where the result comes from.
lines.lifeTranslation: When your role or the division of work is rearranged, check first whether the new direction makes sense, then adapt your method to it and reach out to people and teams you have not worked with before.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you resisting this change, or have you already seen what it is asking you to adjust?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Bound to the boy, one loses the mature man.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary notes that binding yourself to the younger one means the two cannot both be held. The line is not ranking the two parties; it is naming the exclusive nature of following.
lines.plainLanguage: Attach yourself to one side and you lose the other. Following cannot be split two ways, and the choice itself carries a price.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you are trying to please two people or two plans that point in opposite directions, admit that you cannot serve both, pick one by your own real standard, and say why you chose it.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which two things are you holding at once, and which one should you have set down already?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Bound to the mature man, one loses the boy. In following, seeking brings benefit. Dwell in steadfast correctness.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that binding yourself to the elder means the will has released what stood below. The line then adds that even when following brings you what you sought, you must settle into what is straight.
lines.plainLanguage: You have chosen the weightier side, so the other one has to be released. Even if the choice pays off, stay settled in the straight path and do not let wanting the gain replace the principle.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you move resources towards the more important person or project, say clearly what is being set aside, and watch whether you are following because it is right or because it pays.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In this choice, do you value the other side being right, or what you stand to collect?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Following brings gain. Persistence brings misfortune. With sincerity on the Way and clear understanding, what blame can there be?
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary judges gaining through following as dangerous in principle, because the gain exceeds your proper share. Only sincerity held to the path, with a clear grasp of the limits, keeps you free of blame.
lines.plainLanguage: Following has brought you something, and the line still calls it dangerous, because gain tempts you past your proper share. Sincerity, conduct that matches the path, and a clear sense of the boundary are what keep it clean.
lines.lifeTranslation: When following a person or a team brings you an extra benefit, state where it came from and how it is being shared, so the gain does not become something held against you later.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What have you gained here that you would be willing to explain in full?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Sincerity toward what is good. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: Sincerity placed on what is excellent brings good fortune. Among the six lines this is the one where the object of following is most sound in both aim and conduct.
lines.plainLanguage: Your sincerity rests on something genuinely good. The direction is right and your manner is straight, so this is the steadiest place in the hexagram.
lines.lifeTranslation: Once you have checked that their aims and their methods both hold up under scrutiny, you can commit your trust and deal openly, without hedging every exchange.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does this person or project hold up against the standard you apply to yourself?

lines.original: Six at the top: Detain and bind them, then follow and tether them. The king makes offerings at the Western Mountain.
lines.ancientContext: Following reaches its limit and becomes binding: held fast and tied. The closing reference to a sacrifice on the western mountain shows that only sincerity and respect can settle matters now.
lines.plainLanguage: Following has gone as far as it can and turned into a knot. Both sides are held and tied, with no room left to advance. What remains is to close the situation honestly rather than push it further.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a relationship or a partnership has become mutual entanglement and neither side can move, stop expanding it and handle the aftermath through honest conversation instead of adding more.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do you still have a choice here, or has following become something you cannot leave?

topicRules.career: Adapt to the new timing and the new division of work, and reach beyond your usual circle. Keep your professional judgement even when following a lead, and do not let a gain push you past your proper role.
topicRules.study: A suitable teacher, text or rhythm is worth following, but fit it to your own hours. Do not chase several sources at once; once you settle on one, keep checking things independently.
topicRules.romance: Look at whether their direction actually matches yours, and deal honestly. Holding one side means releasing the other, so do not keep two options warm or let accommodation replace saying what you mean.
topicRules.family: Take on your share in line with the household's current rhythm and respect that different ages need different things. When an arrangement forces a choice, explain the reasoning rather than quietly favouring one side.
topicRules.relations: What matters is choosing whom to follow and when. Stay open but keep your principles. Following excludes, so state your position plainly instead of pleasing both camps on the surface.
topicRules.finance: Be careful with gains that come from following someone else's move. Check the source, the rules and your own capacity first, and keep records. Someone else's position is not a basis for yours.
topicRules.wellness: Take the hint about retiring at dusk and let your hours follow daylight and your own signals. You do not have to match anyone else's intensity, and persistent discomfort belongs with a professional.
topicRules.general: Move with the moment rather than agreeing by reflex. Once you have chosen, act honestly and carry the cost of what you let go. As the returns grow, watch the boundary so that following does not become a binding.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: read the situation, follow a direction you can genuinely respect, and review that choice at intervals. Avoid: drifting with whoever is nearest, changing position every week, or letting agreement erode your own limits.

hexagrams.name: Gǔ · Repairing What Has Decayed
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Gu: Supreme success. It is beneficial to cross the great river. Three days before the jia day, three days after the jia day.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says the flow here comes from decay being confronted and set right, and that the three days before and after the turning point mark time for preparation and for review. The Xiang commentary pictures wind under the mountain, and the wise rousing people and cultivating character.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Wind stirs beneath the mountain and scatters what grows there: this is spoilage that built up slowly. The name means damage waiting to be repaired, yet the judgement calls it richly favourable and good for crossing the great water, because once decay is faced it becomes a chance to start again. Most lines speak of taking on what a parent left behind, which is really about inheriting other people's unfinished problems. It asks for sincerity, for the middle way, and for tolerance of some regret along the way.
hexagrams.trendReason: The name means accumulated decay, and all six lines address inherited problems. The first warns of danger, the third of small regret, and the fourth of humiliation in advancing: the process is plainly difficult. Yet the judgment's supreme success and beneficial river crossing indicate that willingness to repair can restore progress. Danger and opportunity coexist, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Face the old damage, repair it in stages, and begin again.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Repairing the father's decay. Having a son honors the deceased father. No blame; danger, but good fortune in the end.
lines.ancientContext: Taking on what the father left behind. Because a capable successor continues the work rather than denouncing it, there is no blame; the way is hard, yet it ends well.
lines.plainLanguage: You are taking over someone else's unfinished mess. Because you are continuing the work rather than repudiating it, nothing is held against you. The road is risky, but it turns out well.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you inherit a role or a household task with old problems attached, say first that you intend to carry it forward properly, then work through the backlog step by step. The strain is normal.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you taking this on to prove someone was wrong, or to get it genuinely right?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Repairing the mother's decay. Do not persist rigidly.
lines.ancientContext: Taking on what the mother left behind: here one must not press straight through. The line warns that some decay is bound up with feeling and relationship, and calls for a gentler, middle course.
lines.plainLanguage: Some old damage is tangled up with feelings. Pushing hard until it yields will not work here, so the line steers you towards a milder, more measured approach.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you change a long-standing habit that touches an elder or a long-serving colleague, slow the pace, leave them their dignity, and adjust in stages rather than overturning it in one move.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the real resistance about the method, or about feelings no one has attended to?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Repairing the father's decay. Small regret, but no great blame.
lines.ancientContext: Taking on what the father left behind with slightly too much force. There is small regret, but because the direction is right, no great blame follows.
lines.plainLanguage: You pushed the repair a little too hard and left some regret behind. The direction was still correct, so this does not amount to a real fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you spoke too sharply or moved too fast while driving a change, add a word of explanation or an apology afterwards. One heavy-handed moment is not a reason to abandon the whole effort.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The regret you carry from doing this right, does it call for a change of method or a change of manner?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Indulging the father's decay. Advancing brings humiliation.
lines.ancientContext: Being indulgent towards what the father left behind. Going on this way brings humiliation: the line warns that leniency is not a remedy.
lines.plainLanguage: Endless tolerance of the decay looks generous but only lets it accumulate. The line names the shame that follows from leaving things alone.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you know a process or a habit is faulty and keep saying you will look at it later, set a firm date and name someone responsible, so the thing actually starts getting handled.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your patience with this problem consideration, or avoidance?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Repairing the father's decay. Receiving praise.
lines.ancientContext: Taking on what the father left behind and winning praise. The line shows that trust is earned by the character shown in handling the matter, not by force of will.
lines.plainLanguage: You repair the old damage through the way you conduct yourself, and that is what earns recognition. Character, not a forceful style, is what wins the confidence of others.
lines.lifeTranslation: When the repair starts working, put the credit back into the system and the team, and let trust accumulate through a consistent way of working rather than stories about your own skill.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is it your results people respect, or the way you go about things?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Not serving kings or lords, holding one's undertaking in high esteem.
lines.ancientContext: Not serving kings and princes, but holding one's own affairs high. The Xiang commentary treats this withdrawal as something others can take as a model.
lines.plainLanguage: The repair work has reached its end. This line steps out of position and authority altogether, keeping its aims clean. Withdrawal here is a considered choice, not a retreat.
lines.lifeTranslation: When something no longer needs you, or when staying would only pull you into a contest over power, you can leave and turn towards what you actually value.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you still in this post because there is work to do, or because you cannot let go of it?

topicRules.career: This suits confronting process problems that have built up for a long time. Prepare before you act and track the effect afterwards. Delay deepens the damage, but pace the repair with an eye on the people affected.
topicRules.study: Find the gaps in the basics that were never filled, put them in order, and repair them before pushing ahead. Covering old holes with new material rarely holds for long.
topicRules.romance: A good time to handle the issue you both keep shelving, gently but with a clear line. Avoid dragging up every past grievance, and do not keep avoiding it out of fear of hurting the relationship.
topicRules.family: You are often inheriting an older generation's habits or duties. Speak as someone continuing the work rather than passing judgement, and slow right down where an elder's feelings are involved.
topicRules.relations: Face the source of the friction that keeps recurring, and agree on a concrete fix with a date to review it. Endless tolerance and one forceful demand both make the long run harder.
topicRules.finance: A good period for clearing unsettled accounts, forgotten subscriptions or debts. Take an inventory first, handle it in phases, and keep records. Neither ignore it nor make a large change in haste.
topicRules.wellness: Look at the sleep pattern or the discomfort you have postponed and arrange a check or an adjustment early. Repeated signals are not worth ignoring, and any diagnosis or treatment belongs with a professional.
topicRules.general: The task is to inherit and repair what has accumulated. Leave time to prepare before the change and time to review after it. The work is tiring and some regret is likely, but facing it is the way back in.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: trace the decay to its source, repair it in sections, and check both what led in and what follows out. Avoid: treating only the visible symptom, or handing the whole problem back to whoever created it.

hexagrams.name: Lín · Approaching
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Lin: Supreme success. Steadfast correctness is beneficial. By the eighth month, misfortune.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says the strong is steadily growing, glad and compliant, so the flow is great; the warning about the eighth month stands because the peak is not far from its decline. The Xiang commentary speaks of teaching without end and protecting people without limit.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Earth stands above the lake: you are high up and looking down on what lies below. The two strong lines at the bottom are growing upward, which is why the judgement is favourable. But it also adds that by the eighth month there is misfortune, stating plainly that this momentum has a time limit and turns after its peak. The six lines move from approaching by feeling, through approaching with sweetness, arriving in person, approaching with discernment, to approaching with generosity. Position is not what makes this work; sincerity and room for others are.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment gives supreme success and beneficial steadfastness, while many lines mention good fortune and no blame. Rising yang is clearly positive, hence the rating: Favorable. Yet the explicit eighth-month warning, explained as approaching decline, makes this a time-limited opportunity. The third line also warns that sweet-talking approach brings no benefit, so this is not the highest rating. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Draw near with sincerity while the tide is still rising.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Responsive approach. Steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: Approaching through genuine feeling. Staying straight brings good fortune, and the good fortune rests on the motive being sound rather than on clever handling.
lines.plainLanguage: From a starting position, you approach people and matters with real feeling. Hold to what is straight and it goes well, because the motive is right, not because the technique is smart.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you first take on a team or enter a new relationship, build the connection through honest interest and state your position and limits clearly. That works better than rushing to show authority.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does your reason for approaching this person hold up when you examine it yourself?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Responsive approach. Good fortune; nothing unfavorable.
lines.ancientContext: Approaching through genuine feeling once more, now with nothing unfavourable. The Xiang commentary notes this is not mere compliance with instruction; judgement is kept within the sincerity.
lines.plainLanguage: The sincerity goes a step further and nothing stands against you. Even so, this line is not simple obedience: your own judgement stays alive inside the goodwill.
lines.lifeTranslation: When cooperation is going smoothly, keep your independent judgement. If a request is unreasonable you can explain your reasoning honestly, rather than going along with it to preserve the mood.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Now that things are going well, how much of your own judgement is still in play?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Sweet approach. Nothing is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: Approaching with sweetness: nothing is gained by it. The line adds that once you are genuinely troubled about it and correct course, the fault does not last.
lines.plainLanguage: Leading with flattery and sweeteners gains nothing at all. The line does leave a way out: the moment you see it clearly and set about correcting it, the fault stops spreading.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you notice you are holding a relationship or a team together by pleasing people, go back to plain explanations and clear standards, and acknowledge that the earlier approach was not right.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which of the agreements you bought with sweeteners should have been plain honesty instead?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Arriving in person to approach. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: Arriving in person to approach the matter, therefore without blame. The point of the line is that you do not direct things from a distance.
lines.plainLanguage: You come in person and meet the situation as it actually is, so nothing goes wrong. What matters here is refusing to command across a gap.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a situation resists explanation, go and look at it yourself and talk to the people directly involved. That handles it better than reports and second-hand accounts.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Have you seen this for yourself, or only heard about it?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Wise approach, fitting for a great ruler. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: Approaching with discernment, as befits a great ruler: knowing people and placing them well rather than doing everything personally. Good fortune rests on holding the middle.
lines.plainLanguage: You lead with discernment, matching people to work instead of handling every part yourself. This suits the measure of someone in charge, and the key is staying balanced.
lines.lifeTranslation: Give the right work to the right person, hold the direction and the principles yourself, and resist stepping into every detail.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which task are you carrying that really belongs to someone better placed for it?

lines.original: Six at the top: Generous approach. Good fortune and no blame.
lines.ancientContext: Approaching with generosity. Although this line stands at the top of the hexagram, it still treats those below with a substantial, warm-hearted care, and so is fortunate and blameless.
lines.plainLanguage: You have reached the top of the hexagram and still treat those below you generously. Decency is both where Approaching ends and what it was built on.
lines.lifeTranslation: Even after you have stepped back from the front line, you can support your old colleagues generously, leaving your experience behind without competing for credit.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you still as generous with the people who can no longer help you?

topicRules.career: Momentum is rising, so this suits pushing forward and positioning yourself. Remember the time limit in the judgement and plan for when the heat fades. Lead by showing up in person and placing people well.
topicRules.study: You absorb material more easily now, so make use of the good stretch. At the same time build a fixed rhythm that does not depend on enthusiasm, or everything stops when the drive does.
topicRules.romance: Sustain this with sincerity rather than sweet words, and be willing to show up and listen. Where it goes still depends on what both people want over time, not on one warm stretch.
topicRules.family: A good time to take an interest and be personally involved in family matters, with a generous manner. Keep your patience with elders and children alike, and do not buy surface harmony with appeasement.
topicRules.relations: Suited to widening your influence and building trust, which rest on sincerity and room for others rather than rank. Kindness has to be sustainable; avoid a burst of warmth followed by sudden distance.
topicRules.finance: You have some slack now, which suits tidying the structure and setting aside a reserve. Heed the warning about timing and do not treat the current improvement as the permanent state.
topicRules.wellness: Condition tends to be on the rise, so build exercise and sleep habits you can keep for the long run. Do not overdraw on feeling good, and take persistent discomfort to a professional.
topicRules.general: Use the rising tide to get close to people and to the work, with sincerity and generosity instead of authority. Also remember that a good season is finite, so arrange the way out while things are strong.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: get close to where the work actually happens, lead patiently, and use the favourable stretch to build something that lasts. Avoid: talking down from above, chasing short-term expansion, or forgetting that a strong season turns.

hexagrams.name: Guān · Contemplating
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Guan: Hands washed, but offerings not yet presented. Sincerity inspires reverent attention.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary describes the one above contemplating the world from a centred and correct position, so that those below are transformed simply by watching. The Xiang commentary shows early kings touring the regions, observing how people live, and shaping their teaching from what they see.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Wind moves across the earth and reaches everywhere: this hexagram is about seeing and being seen. The judgement uses a sacrifice as its image. The hands have been washed and the offering not yet presented, and at that moment the reverence is at its fullest, so onlookers are moved without anything being performed. Real influence comes from the bearing people observe in you, not from the gestures you stage for them. The lines run from a child's shallow look and a glance through a crack, to examining your own conduct and reading the character of a whole community. How shallow your seeing is sets how narrow your road becomes.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment gives no verdict of good or bad fortune, only a sincerely reverent state worthy of contemplation. The lines emphasize observation and reflection: the first line's “regret for the noble person” and the second's “peering” show narrow vision's limits. The fifth and top nines give the noble person “no blame,” rather than gain, and the top Image adds that the purpose is not yet at peace. The focus is examination and preparation rather than effective action, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: See clearly first, starting with yourself, then act.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Childlike observation. No blame for a petty person; regret for the noble person.
lines.ancientContext: Contemplating like a child. For someone of small responsibility this is not a fault; for someone who carries responsibility it is a real shortcoming.
lines.plainLanguage: You judge from the surface alone. With little at stake that is not quite a fault, but for anyone carrying responsibility such shallow seeing is a genuine failing.
lines.lifeTranslation: On matters you are answerable for, do not take a position from a first impression or a fragment. Gather the key facts before you speak.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your view here built on the full picture, or only on the most visible corner?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Peering through a crack. A woman's steadfastness is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: Contemplating through a crack in the door. Holding steady this way does no harm, yet the Xiang commentary still marks the narrowness of the view as a deficiency.
lines.plainLanguage: Peering through a gap shows you only a part. Keeping to your place like this does no damage, but the narrow field of view is itself the limitation.
lines.lifeTranslation: If all you can do is pick up news about something from the side, look for a way to take part or ask the people involved directly. Do not assemble fragments into a verdict.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Could you actually go and see this clearly, and are you choosing to watch from a distance instead?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Observe my life and actions; advance or withdraw.
lines.ancientContext: Contemplating one's own conduct in order to decide whether to advance or withdraw. Self-examination of this kind keeps you from straying off the straight path.
lines.plainLanguage: You turn the looking back on yourself and decide whether to go on or pull back based on what you have actually produced. Self-examination of this kind keeps you on course.
lines.lifeTranslation: Before deciding whether to keep investing in something, look honestly at what you have actually produced over this period, then judge whether to commit more or stop.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Looking only at what you have actually produced, is it telling you to advance or to withdraw?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Observe the nation's splendor. It is beneficial to be the king's guest.
lines.ancientContext: Contemplating the brilliance of a country, which makes it fitting to be received as a guest of the king. The line is about recognising an environment worth entering.
lines.plainLanguage: You see where a community's real quality lies, which makes it right to take part as a welcomed guest. The work is recognising an environment worth joining.
lines.lifeTranslation: When considering a new organisation or circle, observe how it actually works and what it actually values. If you agree with what you find, join as a collaborator.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What is genuinely admirable about the place you want to join?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Observe my life and actions. No blame for the noble person.
lines.ancientContext: Contemplating one's own conduct from a high position: the noble person is without blame. The Xiang commentary says that to know how you are doing, look at what the people around you have become.
lines.plainLanguage: From a position of responsibility you examine your own conduct, and that keeps you clear of blame. To know how you are doing, look at how the people near you have been shaped.
lines.lifeTranslation: To find out whether your way of leading works, look at the actual state of your team or your family. It is usually the echo of what you have been doing for a long time.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What does the current state of the people around you reflect back about your own conduct?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Observe their life and actions. No blame for the noble person.
lines.ancientContext: Contemplating the conduct of others. No longer in charge, this line stays upright and so is without blame, though the Xiang commentary hints that the heart has not entirely let go.
lines.plainLanguage: You are no longer the one in charge and now watch what others do. Because your own conduct stays upright there is no blame, though something in you has not fully let go.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you still follow the work after stepping down, put your attention into offering experience when it is needed, rather than commenting on every decision.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The thing you cannot let go of, does it still need you, or do you still need it?

topicRules.career: Observe the whole picture and how the organisation really operates before deciding to advance or step back. Judge an opportunity by its culture and results rather than its slogans, and fill the information gap before choosing.
topicRules.study: Understand the overall structure before drilling into detail, and check periodically how much you have actually grasped. Do not conclude from a partial impression that you have learned it.
topicRules.romance: Watch what they consistently do day to day, and look back at who you are inside the relationship. Do not read their feelings from fragments or from what someone else reports.
topicRules.family: Let the current state of your family tell you something about your own long-standing way of relating. Where you want to improve things, understand the real need before adjusting, and hold back the advice.
topicRules.relations: See the relationship as it actually is, and notice the bearing others see in you. Influence comes from consistent conduct, not from gestures arranged for an audience.
topicRules.finance: Take stock and observe the whole picture, understanding the shape of income and spending before adjusting anything. Do not move important arrangements on a fragment of news or someone else's example.
topicRules.wellness: Observe your moods and physical signals and keep a record so patterns emerge. If something abnormal persists, let a professional assess it rather than inferring the cause yourself.
topicRules.general: See clearly before acting, and turn the observation from the world back onto yourself. Your range of choice matches your range of sight, so this favours careful review over hurried advance.
