hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: take in the whole picture and your own part in it, then build trust through consistent action. Avoid: judging fast on surfaces, or asking others to change while you stay as you are.

hexagrams.name: Shì Kè · Biting Through
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Shi He: Success. It is beneficial to administer justice.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary uses something lodged in the mouth that must be bitten through before anything can pass, so the obstruction has to be cleared. The Xiang commentary takes thunder and lightning as the image, and early kings making penalties clear and the law plain.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Thunder and lightning meet: something is stuck in the mouth and has to be bitten through before things can move again. The name is about removing what sits in the way, and the judgement's reference to legal judgement points at deciding right and wrong openly rather than fighting quietly. The lines run from light fetters, through cured meat that turns out tainted and dried flesh that yields a metal arrow, to the heavy punishment at the top. Left alone, a problem raises its own price. What opens the way is acting with clarity: establish the facts, then judge by reason.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's “success” and “beneficial to administer justice” indicate a way through. Yet the third line encounters poison, the fifth warns of danger in steadfastness, and the top explicitly brings misfortune. Friction and costs remain; effectiveness depends on factual discernment rather than emotional force, hence the rating: Balanced. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Name the obstruction and clear it by the rules, in proportion.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Feet in stocks, the toes injured. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: Fetters on the feet, injuring the toes: a light correction. The Xiang commentary places the point on not walking on, since being stopped early is what averts a worse course.
lines.plainLanguage: A restraint at the foot marks a mild correction. Because it stopped you from walking further in the wrong direction, the small injury buys you a clean outcome.
lines.lifeTranslation: An early warning, a minor reprimand or a small setback can be read as a signal to adjust. Correct your approach while the cost is still low, rather than arguing or pressing on.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which small warning sign have you not actually stopped to look at?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Biting soft flesh, the nose injured. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: Biting through tender flesh and cutting into the nose: force applied past the measure. The Xiang commentary ties this to the position held; the direction was not wrong, so no fault results.
lines.plainLanguage: Something that should have been easy to deal with got a heavier hand than it needed. The mark is left, but because the direction of the response was sound, it does not become a fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: Problems that look easy are the ones people overreact to. Weigh the real size of the matter first, then decide how much force and how strong a word it calls for.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the strength of your reaction in proportion to the size of the problem?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Biting dried meat, encountering poison. Small humiliation, no blame.
lines.ancientContext: Biting into dried meat and meeting something tainted. The Xiang commentary attributes this to standing in an unsuitable position, so a small humiliation follows without becoming real blame.
lines.plainLanguage: Working on a stale, hard old matter, you hit a part that will not go down. The awkwardness is small, and recognising that something is off in time stops it growing into a fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: Taking on a long-deferred problem can land you in trouble you did not create. Check whether you are the right person to handle it, and bring in whoever actually holds the authority.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is this really yours to bite into?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Biting dried meat with bones, obtaining metal arrows. Steadfastness in hardship is beneficial. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: Biting through dried flesh on the bone and obtaining a metal arrow. The Xiang commentary notes that the light has not yet spread, so good fortune stands only on holding straight through difficulty.
lines.plainLanguage: You chew through the hardest part and come away with something solid. The situation is not yet fully clear, so the good outcome depends on staying straight while it is difficult.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you pursue a difficult matter properly to the end, you often come away with the decisive evidence or agreement. Keep records, use the formal route, and do not relax the standard because progress feels easy.
lines.reflectionPrompt: On the hardest part of this, is there something worth putting on record?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Biting dried meat, obtaining yellow gold. Steadfastness amid danger. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: Biting through dried meat and obtaining yellow gold. Holding straight, there is still danger; the Xiang commentary says the absence of blame rests on handling the matter appropriately.
lines.plainLanguage: You judge from the centre and something real comes of it, yet caution remains inside the correctness. Not easing off because you gained something is what keeps this clean.
lines.lifeTranslation: In a position where you have to decide, results and pressure usually arrive together. Stay careful, hear the other accounts, and do not let one success become a reason to shorten the process next time.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does your current judgement rest on grounds that survive being questioned?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Bearing the cangue, the ears injured. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: A heavy cangue that covers the ears: misfortune. The Xiang commentary traces it to not hearing counsel; with the ears blocked, the chance to correct things early is gone.
lines.plainLanguage: The problem has piled up to its limit, and what you carry now is not a light restraint but a heavy consequence. The cause lies in advice that was never heard, which is what removed the early chance to correct.
lines.lifeTranslation: Warnings ignored for a long time tend to arrive at last at full price. Stop arguing, acknowledge the situation, ask for help and start repairing, rather than continuing to defend yourself.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Who warned you long ago that you have still not listened to?

topicRules.career: Face the obstruction you have been leaving aside and handle it through the proper channel. Collect facts and keep records before judging; avoid emotional or private pressure, and do not wait until the cost grows.
topicRules.study: Find the concept that is actually blocking you and work through exactly where the error lies, instead of skipping the hard part. A record of mistakes and corrections shows progress better than a filled-in schedule.
topicRules.romance: If something unspoken has sat between you for a long time, pick a calm moment and address that one thing without reopening old ground. Both people need willingness and time; one confrontation will not change someone.
topicRules.family: Make the recurring rules explicit, such as chores, money and boundaries. Reach them by discussion rather than punishment or silence, and repair it afterwards if words came out too hard.
topicRules.relations: Aim at getting it right, not at winning. Establish the facts before you take a position. Do not dodge the point that needs making, but leave room in how you say it so one dispute does not set into a standing feud.
topicRules.finance: Go through the accounts, the contracts and anything still outstanding, and clear up the grey areas. Where there is a dispute, use formal channels and professional help; this text gives no specific investment or legal advice.
topicRules.wellness: Notice the small signals you have been overlooking, such as sleep, pain or swings in mood, adjust your routine early and seek a professional assessment when needed. This text offers no diagnosis or treatment advice.
topicRules.general: Clear what sits in the way, using explicit standards and open communication. Handled early the cost is low; delayed, it rises. Keep a sense of proportion and do not swing harder than the matter deserves.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: state the obstruction plainly, handle it through the agreed rules, and keep the response proportionate. Avoid: letting a problem sit in vague terms, or using excessive force to discharge your own feelings.

hexagrams.name: Bì · Adornment
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Bi: Success. A small benefit in having somewhere to go.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary explains adornment through the interweaving of firm and yielding, in nature as pattern and among people as culture. The Xiang commentary shows fire beneath the mountain, and the wise clarifying ordinary affairs while refusing to settle legal cases on outward polish.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Fire below the mountain lights up its shape: this is ornament and style. The judgement calls it favourable, yet grants only a small advantage in going forward, because presentation makes a thing easier to understand and accept without changing what it actually is. The lines move from leaving the carriage and walking, through adorning the beard, the white horse arriving, and the meagre roll of silk, to the plain white ornament at the top. The point is not to refuse decoration but to let the outside show the inside accurately.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's “success,” the third nine's lasting steadfast good fortune, the fifth six's eventual good fortune, and the top nine's no blame are broadly positive. Yet the small benefit in proceeding and the Image's caution against deciding legal cases limit adornment's role, while the fifth six first has regret. Hence the rating: Highly Favorable, rather than the highest. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Let the surface show what is really there, nothing more.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Adorn the feet. Leave the carriage and walk.
lines.ancientContext: Adorning the toes, and leaving the carriage to go on foot. The Xiang commentary says riding that carriage would not have been right; declining a convenience that does not match your place is how this hexagram begins.
lines.plainLanguage: The adornment starts at the lowest point, and the act chosen is to leave the carriage and walk. Giving up a convenience that does not match your place is the right opening move here.
lines.lifeTranslation: If resources or trappings beyond your position come with the start of something, you can decline them and travel the solid way instead of taking on an unequal obligation to look respectable.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which piece of your current standing does not actually belong to the position you hold?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Adorn the beard.
lines.ancientContext: Adorning the beard, which has meaning only while attached to the face. The Xiang commentary says it moves with what is above, marking this adornment as supporting rather than standing alone.
lines.plainLanguage: A beard only means anything attached to a face. This adornment is supportive; separated from what it belongs to, it has nothing to hold on to.
lines.lifeTranslation: In a supporting role, point your effort and your presentation at the main goal and keep pace with whoever is leading. There is no need to make your own style stand out separately yet.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your effort aimed at what this thing is actually about?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Adorned and glistening. Lasting steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: Adorned and glossy. The line ties the good fortune to lasting correctness, and the Xiang commentary adds that only long-held uprightness keeps others from slighting you.
lines.plainLanguage: Things look polished and attractive, which is a comfortable place to be. The good outcome is tied to holding straight over time, because appearance alone will not carry the weight.
lines.lifeTranslation: When circumstances are favourable and opinion of you is good, hold to your original standard and honesty. Consistency over time earns more respect than one bright presentation.
lines.reflectionPrompt: If the shine came off, what would be left?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Adorned in plain white; a white horse comes flying. Not a robber, but a suitor.
lines.ancientContext: Adornment fading to white, a white horse coming as if in flight. The Xiang commentary attributes the doubt to the position held; once it is clear these are not raiders but suitors, the misgiving clears and no blame follows.
lines.plainLanguage: The decoration fades to plain white and a white horse arrives at speed, which is unsettling at first. Once you can see the arrivals are not raiders but people coming in good faith, the doubt clears.
lines.lifeTranslation: When someone approaches suddenly or proposes working together, do not assume bad intent. Ask directly about their aim and their terms, and decide once you have enough information.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your guard here based on facts, or on what you imagine?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Adornment among hills and gardens, meager bundles of silk. Regret, but good fortune in the end.
lines.ancientContext: Adornment among the hills and gardens, with only a meagre roll of silk to offer: humiliating, yet ending well. The Xiang commentary calls this cause for gladness, since plain sincerity serves better than lavish display.
lines.plainLanguage: You want to do the thing properly but the gift you can offer is slight, which feels shabby. Even so, this ends well, because plain sincerity is worth more here than an impressive spread.
lines.lifeTranslation: When resources are short, do not strain to keep up appearances. Get the intent and the quality right. Something simple and honest is usually remembered longer than one lavish occasion.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the expense you are considering for doing this well, or for not losing face?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Plain white adornment. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: Plain white as adornment, without blame. The Xiang commentary says the aim is fulfilled here: when the display falls away and the natural colour returns, the logic of the hexagram is complete.
lines.plainLanguage: Adornment reaches its end in plain white, where adding no colour is itself the finest ornament. The ornate falls away, the plain returns, and the hexagram has run its course.
lines.lifeTranslation: After going through every kind of packaging and performance, try taking the surplus off: speak and work directly, and let the results explain themselves.
lines.reflectionPrompt: With every bit of decoration removed, what is left here that is worth looking at?

topicRules.career: Suited to tidying how you present things, such as decks, portfolios and external explanations, so your ability reads clearly. Packaging cannot replace delivery, so confirm the substance before working on the image.
topicRules.study: Organise the structure of your notes and how you express things, which helps understanding and revision. Watch that time spent on neat layout does not replace actually understanding; the test is explaining the principle.
topicRules.romance: Worth investing in the small details and shared rituals, and equally worth letting them see the real you. Attraction can open a relationship; over time it runs on honesty and consistent behaviour.
topicRules.family: A pleasant setting, festivals and shared rituals add warmth. Remember that the actual caring and talking are the foundation, and do not push family into performances for other people's benefit.
topicRules.relations: Pay attention to courtesy and phrasing so your goodwill is received as intended. Do not stop at politeness, though; say the thing that needs saying, and do not polish it until the sincerity is gone.
topicRules.finance: Watch spending that exists for appearances, and separate need from want. A budget can be presentable but capped. For investments or contracts, verify independently and consult a professional; this text gives no specific advice.
topicRules.wellness: Start with tidying your environment, your grooming and your routine so life has some order. This is ordinary upkeep; for a specific physical complaint seek a professional assessment, as this text gives no medical advice.
topicRules.general: Let the outside show the inside accurately: measured form, substance before shine. This hexagram grants only a small advantage in going forward, so it suits refining and tending, not leaning on packaging to drive a big change.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: get the substance right first, then use a measured form to organise and present it. Avoid: letting packaging stand in for substance, or hiding a serious flaw to keep the surface attractive.

hexagrams.name: Bō · Stripping Away
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Bo: Unfavorable. There is somewhere to go.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary describes five yielding lines pressing on one firm line, so the strong is being stripped and going forward is unfavourable. The Xiang commentary turns to governance: the mountain rests on the earth, and those above secure their dwelling by dealing generously with those below.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: The mountain rests on the earth, and the ground beneath is being worn away layer by layer. Five yielding lines below and one firm line above make this the clearest picture of decline, which is why going forward is unfavourable. The lines strip the bed from its legs, then its frame, and finally reach the skin itself; each advance is dangerous. But the Xiang commentary offers the response: deal generously with those below and make the dwelling secure. The top line leaves one great fruit uneaten, so that even at the end of the stripping something can still grow.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment explicitly discourages proceeding, explained by the growing influence of petty people. The first, second, and fourth sixes all declare misfortune, so the dominant tone is unfavorable. Yet the third six has no blame, the fifth nothing unfavorable, and the top nine preserves an uneaten great fruit as an opening for change. It is not total extinction, hence the rating: Unfavorable, rather than the lowest. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: In decline, protect the base and keep one seed uneaten.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Stripping the bed at its legs. Disregarding steadfastness brings misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The bed is stripped at the legs. The Xiang commentary says the foundation is being destroyed; treating the straight path with contempt because the damage is out of sight is what plants the misfortune.
lines.plainLanguage: The stripping begins at the legs of the bed, in the lowest and least visible place. Treating what is straight with contempt because you cannot see the damage is where the danger takes root.
lines.lifeTranslation: Problems usually show up first in the foundations: cash flow, health habits, trust. Repair the base while the loss is still small, rather than leaving it because the surface still holds.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Where in your foundations has something already started to loosen?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Stripping the bed at its frame. Disregarding steadfastness brings misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The bed is stripped at the frame, closer now to the person. The Xiang commentary notes the absence of any answering support, so contempt for the straight path again brings misfortune.
lines.plainLanguage: The stripping moves up to where the bed joins together, closer to the person on it. There is no answering support anywhere, which is what makes disregarding the straight path dangerous here.
lines.lifeTranslation: When the losses widen and no support is at hand, ask for help and describe the situation to someone you trust. Do not hold out alone until there is no room left to manoeuvre.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Have you told anyone what is actually happening?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Stripping away. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: Stripping away, yet without blame. The Xiang commentary attributes this to keeping a distance from the lines above and below: not decaying along with everyone else preserves this one.
lines.plainLanguage: This line sits inside the same decline yet takes no blame, because it has put distance between itself and those on either side. Not eroding along with everyone else is what saves it.
lines.lifeTranslation: When the whole environment is sliding, you can still decline to cut corners or give up along with it. Keeping your distance from a bad culture may spare you from being dragged into it.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you willing to be a little out of step in order to hold your principles?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Stripping the bed reaches the skin. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The stripping reaches the skin: misfortune. The Xiang commentary says calamity is close at hand. This line has no buffer left and must meet the matter directly.
lines.plainLanguage: The stripping spreads from the bed to the skin. This is no longer damage to an object but harm to the person. There is no buffer left, only the thing itself to face.
lines.lifeTranslation: When the damage has reached your health, your livelihood or the relationship itself, stop the loss at once and get outside help. Deal with the most immediate thing first and set the rest aside.
lines.reflectionPrompt: If you could only save one thing first, what would it be?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: A string of fish. Favor through the palace attendants. Nothing unfavorable.
lines.ancientContext: Fish strung in a line, palace attendants cared for in order: nothing is unfavourable. The Xiang commentary says no fault remains, since orderly places for everyone hold the situation during a decline.
lines.plainLanguage: Like fish strung in a row, everyone is attended to in turn. During a decline, giving each person a clear place in the order is what keeps things from going wrong.
lines.lifeTranslation: When resources are tight, set out a clear order and a rule for distribution so everyone knows when their turn comes. That steadies things far better than letting people compete for what is left.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Have you made the order of priority for your limited resources explicit?

lines.original: Nine at the top: A great fruit remains uneaten. The noble person gains a carriage; the petty person's dwelling is stripped away.
lines.ancientContext: One great fruit is left uneaten. The Xiang commentary separates two endings: the one who deals generously with those below is carried by them, while the one who only strips loses even the roof overhead.
lines.plainLanguage: At the end of the stripping, one large fruit is left uneaten, and with it the chance to grow again. Two endings part here: the generous are carried by others, while those who only take lose even their own roof.
lines.lifeTranslation: In the hardest stretch, keep the one thing that matters most, whether that is your credit, your core skill or a particular relationship. Treat the people still supporting you well and do not burn the last of what you have.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which fruit is the one you must not eat, whatever happens?

topicRules.career: Contract rather than expand. Protect the core business and the key people, and look at which costs are quietly draining you. This suits stopping losses and consolidating, not opening a new front.
topicRules.study: If both motivation and results are falling, narrow the scope and hold on to the most important subject and the basics. Restore a steady rhythm before worrying about volume.
topicRules.romance: This may be a depleting stretch. Reduce arguments and testing, and look after each other's basic needs first. Major commitments and decisions can wait until you are both steadier.
topicRules.family: Deal generously with whoever is in the weakest position and put limited resources into the essentials of daily life. Set an order for tasks and spending so competition does not damage trust.
topicRules.relations: Keep your distance from relationships that drain you, and value the people still willing to back you. There is no need to widen your network; holding a few trustworthy connections matters more.
topicRules.finance: The tendency is towards depletion. Review fixed costs and debts and keep a cash buffer. This favours defence over adding more; verify any specific decision independently and consult a professional, as this text gives no investment advice.
topicRules.wellness: Watch for accumulating fatigue and depletion. Put sleep, food and rest back at the centre and shed unnecessary load. If discomfort persists seek a professional assessment; this text gives no medical advice.
topicRules.general: This is a time of decline, so stop where the current says stop, look after those below you, and protect the foundation. It does not favour starting new things. Reduce the loss and keep one seed for later.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: reduce the drain, protect what is fundamental, and stop the commitments that are working against you. Avoid: expanding against the current, straining to save face, or giving up the core resources along with the rest.

hexagrams.name: Fù · Returning
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Fu: Success. Coming and going without affliction; friends arrive without blame. Returning along the path, return comes in seven days. It is beneficial to have somewhere to go.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says the firm line returns and moves in accord, which is why coming and going bring no trouble; the cycle has its own timing. The Xiang commentary shows thunder within the earth and early kings closing the passes at the solstice, since new life needs quiet rather than driving.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Thunder lies within the earth and a single firm line is born beneath five yielding ones: life returning after the stripping away. The judgement says coming and going bring no trouble and friends arrive without blame, and the seven-day return marks a cycle that runs to its own timing and cannot be hurried. All six lines are about how you come back: returning before going far, returning gracefully, returning again and again, returning alone, returning with substance, and at the top losing the way entirely. What decides this is whether you notice the drift early, and whether the first shoot is given cover.
hexagrams.trendReason: “Success,” “no blame,” and “beneficial to proceed,” reinforced by supreme good fortune in the first nine, clearly favor turning back and correcting course. Yet repeated return in the third six carries danger, while confused return at the top brings misfortune and a warning of great defeat. Repetition or stubborn refusal to return can reverse the outcome, hence the rating: Highly Favorable, rather than the highest. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Turn back early, then restart at a pace you can keep.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Returning before going far. No cause for regret. Supreme good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: Returning before going far, so no deep regret is left; the line is judged highly fortunate. The Xiang commentary treats this as the work of self-cultivation.
lines.plainLanguage: You turned back before straying far, so no heavy regret remains. Catching a mistake while it is still small costs the least of any option here.
lines.lifeTranslation: The moment you see your approach is wrong, adjust, even if it means admitting a misjudgement. The earlier you turn back, the less there is to repair.
lines.reflectionPrompt: At which step did the road you are on start to bend away?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Restful return. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: A fine, unhurried return, and therefore fortunate. The Xiang commentary explains it by the willingness to be humble and stay close to people of character.
lines.plainLanguage: You come back to the straight path calmly and well, which goes fortunately. The reason is closeness to people of character, and good influence makes turning back feel natural rather than forced.
lines.lifeTranslation: When changing a habit, getting near people who do it well and joining a healthy setting usually works better than willpower alone, and it lasts longer.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Whose way of living around you is the one you would want to move closer to?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Repeated return. Danger, but no blame.
lines.ancientContext: Returning repeatedly: there is danger, but no blame. The Xiang commentary affirms that in principle the one who keeps coming back is not at fault; the risk lies in the repetition, not in the return.
lines.plainLanguage: You drift and return, drift and return, and the repetition itself carries risk. Still, the line clears you of fault: what is dangerous is the relapsing, not the coming back.
lines.lifeTranslation: Breaking an old habit or rebuilding a routine usually involves repeated failure. What counts is being willing to start again after each break, while looking at which situation keeps pulling you back.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which recurring situation keeps returning you to the old pattern?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Walking among others, returning alone.
lines.ancientContext: Walking in the midst of others and returning alone. The Xiang commentary says this follows reason rather than numbers; turning alone takes judgement and the capacity to be misunderstood.
lines.plainLanguage: You are among others and the only one who turns back. That follows reason rather than numbers, and it takes both judgement and the willingness not to be understood.
lines.lifeTranslation: When everyone around you carries on as before, being the first to change direction feels lonely. Explain your reasons clearly and accept that not everyone will follow.
lines.reflectionPrompt: If nobody turns with you, can you still keep going?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Generous return. No regret.
lines.ancientContext: A substantial, generous return, and so no regret. The Xiang commentary places the key in holding the centre and examining oneself, rather than waiting to be corrected by others.
lines.plainLanguage: You come back to the straight path in a solid, unshowy way, so nothing is left to regret. The key is staying centred and checking yourself instead of waiting for someone else to point it out.
lines.lifeTranslation: Build a habit of regular self-review, such as looking over your progress and condition once a week, so correction becomes routine rather than something you improvise after a failure.
lines.reflectionPrompt: When did you last seriously review the direction you are going in?

lines.original: Six at the top: Confused return. Misfortune, calamity, and error. Mobilizing an army ends in great defeat, with misfortune for the ruler. For ten years, unable to campaign.
lines.ancientContext: Losing the way and still not returning: the most unfortunate line of the hexagram, carrying calamity. It speaks of an army defeated and ten years unable to march again; the Xiang commentary traces it to going against the straight path.
lines.plainLanguage: You have lost the way and still will not turn back, which is the worst place in this hexagram. The image of a defeated army and ten years without a campaign shows how long the cost lasts. Persisting takes a very long time to repair.
lines.lifeTranslation: When every signal says the direction is wrong, putting more in stretches the loss out for years. Stop and reassess, and put withdrawing or changing route on the list of options.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you still adjusting, or have you stopped admitting the direction is wrong?

topicRules.career: A good time to return to your original purpose and the basics, and correct where you have drifted. New plans can start, but keep them small and give them time to grow before raising the volume.
topicRules.study: Suited to starting again, picking up the interrupted work in small portions. The aim is restoring regularity, not making up the total. What counts is being willing to begin again after breaks.
topicRules.romance: There is room to repair and move closer again, built from small daily exchanges. Repair takes willingness and time from both sides; do not expect one long conversation to settle the past.
topicRules.family: A good time to reach out to a relationship that has grown distant, starting with a phone call or a meal. Allow each other time to adjust and do not demand an immediate return to the old closeness.
topicRules.relations: You can reconnect with people who once mattered and have faded, and it is a fitting time to acknowledge past mistakes. Be sincere without pressure, and leave space for their response.
topicRules.finance: Return to basic tracking and budgeting and bring disordered spending back into line. Order comes before returns; verify any specific investment decision independently and consult a professional, as this text gives no advice.
topicRules.wellness: Suited to rebuilding basic sleep and exercise rhythms, starting small and allowing relapse. Early on this needs nurturing rather than driving. If discomfort persists seek a professional assessment; this text gives no medical advice.
topicRules.general: Life is coming back. Notice the drift early, turn back onto the straight path, and move with the natural rhythm. The first shoot needs protection, and pushing too hard now damages it.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: get back on course early and restart with one small step you can sustain. Avoid: delaying the correction out of embarrassment, or pushing for results the moment things start to recover.

hexagrams.name: Wú Wàng · Without Pretence
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Wu Wang: Supreme success. Steadfast correctness is beneficial. What is not right brings calamity; proceeding is unfavorable.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary reads this as firmness arriving from outside and taking charge within: movement that is strong, great success through correctness. The Xiang image is thunder rolling under heaven, each thing growing true to its own nature, and rulers nourishing all things in step with the season.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Qian above, Zhen below. Thunder moves across the land and everything grows according to what it actually is, without contrivance. The judgement grants the four virtues of sublime success through correctness, then immediately adds a warning: stray from an honest motive and you invite fault. The lines cover both sides of this. Some speak of solid work done without counting the harvest; others speak of trouble you did not cause at all. You can hold your own conduct steady. You cannot hold every outcome.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment contains the four virtues of origination, success, rightness, and steadfastness, with a positive overall direction, hence the rating: Favorable. Yet “what is not right brings calamity” and the top line's “action brings calamity; nothing beneficial” explicitly warn against flawed motives or forcing forward, so it is not the highest rating. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Act from an honest motive and accept what you cannot control.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Innocence. Going forward brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that going forward without pretence lets the will find its range. Because the starting point is honest, the line is read as favourable movement.
lines.plainLanguage: You set out from a state that is neither false nor contrived. The motive is clean, so your intent can extend itself, and the line reads well.
lines.lifeTranslation: At the start of something, ask yourself plainly why you are doing it. When the reason is clear and carries no performance or calculation, the action stands on firmer ground.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What is the most honest reason you are pushing this forward?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Not plowing for the harvest, nor clearing new land for cultivated fields; then it is beneficial to proceed.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary notes that not reaping while ploughing means wealth is not the point. You do not tally the harvest while sowing, nor expect rich fields while clearing rough ground.
lines.plainLanguage: Do not count the yield while the seed is still going in. Put your attention on the work in front of you rather than on the return you have already imagined. That is what makes going forward suitable.
lines.lifeTranslation: In work or study, make the current step solid instead of re-estimating results that have not happened yet. Daily recalculation eats the hours the work needs.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How much of your energy goes into the work itself, and how much into predicting the payoff?

lines.original: Six in the third place: An undeserved calamity. A tethered ox is a traveler's gain and the villagers' misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: An ox is tethered by the road. A passing traveller leads it away, and the townspeople carry the suspicion and the loss. The Xiang commentary marks this as trouble arriving through no fault of your own.
lines.plainLanguage: The traveller gains, the locals pay. This is the situation where you did nothing wrong and are caught in it anyway. Undeserved misfortune is real and the text says so plainly.
lines.lifeTranslation: Some losses come from other people's behaviour or from a gap in the system. Work out where responsibility actually sits and keep records that show it, rather than starting with self-blame.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In this loss, what did you actually cause, and what were you simply caught by?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: One may remain steadfast. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary explains that steadfastness without fault comes from holding what is already yours. You keep to your own correct ground and make no extravagant claim outward.
lines.plainLanguage: You can hold firm, and there is no fault in it. The point is not to gain more but to keep a steady grip on the principles and the position that are properly yours.
lines.lifeTranslation: When things shift around you and you are unsure whether to follow, keep your existing rhythm and standards first. Do not move your own limits to match whichever way the wind turns.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which of your principles do you want to keep no matter how the situation changes?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: An undeserved illness. Without medicine, there is joy.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary warns that medicine for an affliction not of your own making should not be tried. Reaching for a remedy can itself create the trouble. This is read as a textual image, not as health advice.
lines.plainLanguage: An ailment you did not bring on yourself does not need an urgent intervention. Letting it settle is the better course here. The medicine in the original is a figure of speech, not a medical instruction.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a small setback was not caused by you, watching and waiting is often the right handling. Adding activity just to look like you are dealing with it tends to make more work.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which of your recent fixes created more trouble than the original problem?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Innocence, yet action brings calamity. Nothing is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary calls this the misfortune of exhaustion: movement at the final position, when the situation has already run to its limit, brings its own trouble.
lines.plainLanguage: Even with no false intent, pushing on after the momentum is spent produces fault and brings no advantage. When the timing is finished, the right move is to stop.
lines.lifeTranslation: Once something has been taken as far as the conditions allow, withdrawing suits better than raising the stake. A good motive does not substitute for reading the timing.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you continuing because the conditions still hold, or because you do not want to admit it is over?

topicRules.career: Return to the substance of your role and do the work properly rather than dressing up short-term numbers. When a problem is not yours, establish the facts before responding, and step back once the run is clearly finished.
topicRules.study: Build up steadily instead of hunting for methods that promise fast results. Marks swing for reasons effort does not fully control, so put your attention back on understanding the material.
topicRules.romance: Be straightforward rather than managing an image or testing the other person. When a misunderstanding is not of your making, set out the facts instead of rushing to make up for it.
topicRules.family: Carry the part that is genuinely yours and stop short of taking responsibility for other people's choices. Occasional friction at home can be watched for a while before you step in to mediate.
topicRules.relations: A plain motive costs you the least effort. Do not act against your own judgement to keep a relationship smooth, and when someone else's behaviour spills onto you, draw the line before deciding how to respond.
topicRules.finance: Live within your means and keep to the plan you already have rather than chasing opportunities you do not understand. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: Keep a regular routine rather than changing your approach at every small discomfort. If something about your body or mood concerns you, consult a qualified professional; this is not medical advice.
topicRules.general: Hold to an honest motive, move with the timing, and take care of the part you can actually control. Being caught up in other people's trouble is not always avoidable, and the point is not to let it move your principles.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: act on the facts and through proper channels, and adjust when something unexpected lands on you. Avoid: reading the situation through your own wishes, or trying to force control over every result.

hexagrams.name: Dà Xù · Great Accumulating
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Da Xu: Steadfast correctness is beneficial. Not eating at home brings good fortune. It is beneficial to cross the great river.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary praises firmness, substance and radiance renewing their virtue day by day, and the capacity to restrain strength as great correctness. The Xiang image is heaven held inside a mountain, with the noble person gathering the words and deeds of the past to build up character.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Gen above, Qian below. Heaven is contained within the mountain: great strength is stored rather than spent. The commentary praises knowing when to halt, because only restraint lets you keep renewing what you have. The image asks you to take in the recorded words and actions of people who came before and turn them into your own substance. The judgement favours the capable person who is supported rather than living off their own small store, and favours crossing the great water. This is a hexagram about long accumulation bought as passage.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's beneficial steadfastness, good fortune in not eating at home, and beneficial great river crossing are all favorable. The fourth six has supreme good fortune, the fifth good fortune, and the top nine success, with the Image saying “the Way is widely carried out.” The overall assessment is high, hence the rating: Highest Favorability. Yet the first nine's danger and beneficial stopping, and the second's detached wagon axle supports, still call for restraint and pauses while accumulating. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Store your strength now so the road opens later.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: There is danger. It is beneficial to stop.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that stopping when there is danger keeps you from walking into harm. Halting here is prevention, not retreat.
lines.plainLanguage: There is advantage in stopping once you sense danger. The point is not timidity but refusing a head-on push while your strength is still short.
lines.lifeTranslation: When clear resistance appears right at the start, pause and take stock of what you actually have. Filling the gaps first costs less than pressing on and losing ground.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is this resistance telling you that you are underprepared, or just that the start is uncomfortable?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: The wagon's axle supports come loose.
lines.ancientContext: The axle strap has come off the cart, so it cannot move. The Xiang commentary reads the central position as showing that stopping here carries no blame.
lines.plainLanguage: The linkage has failed and the cart will not roll. Being forced to stop is not a fault; it is a signal to repair the thing that broke before travelling on.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a plan stalls halfway, fix the part that actually failed. Throwing more people at a cart with a broken connection does not move it.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What broke here, the driving force or the joint that connects the parts?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Fine horses pursue one another. Steadfastness through hardship is beneficial. Train the wagon and its defenses; it is beneficial to proceed.
lines.ancientContext: Good horses give chase; it favours holding correct through hardship, and practising with the carriage and its defences. The Xiang commentary says movement is possible because your intent aligns with those above you.
lines.plainLanguage: The horses can run, but you must stay correct through the difficulty and be already practised at driving and at guarding the load. That is what makes advance worthwhile.
lines.lifeTranslation: When the chance to speed up arrives, keep your fundamentals and your safeguards in place. Speed is carried by drills done beforehand, not by the push of the moment.
lines.reflectionPrompt: If your pace doubled tomorrow, which basic skill would give way first?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: A young ox's headboard. Supreme good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: A headboard is fitted to a young bull before its horns come through. The Xiang commentary calls this great good fortune with cause for gladness, because early restraint costs little.
lines.plainLanguage: Restrain the calf before the horns are sharp and the smallest effort does the job. That is why the line reads so well. Everything depends on being early.
lines.lifeTranslation: A small fault is cheapest to handle the week it appears. Once it hardens into a habit or spreads into common practice, the price goes up sharply.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which small problem would take you ten minutes to settle right now?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: A castrated boar's tusks. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The tusk of a gelded boar: the charging temper is addressed at its source rather than the tusk being guarded against. The Xiang commentary marks this as an occasion for celebration.
lines.plainLanguage: Faced with the boar's tusk, changing what drives the charge works better than blocking the tusk each time. That is why the line is favourable.
lines.lifeTranslation: For conflicts that keep recurring, find and adjust the condition that keeps producing them. Catching each surface flare-up one by one never ends.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What is really driving this problem that keeps coming back?

lines.original: Nine at the top: How open is Heaven's highway! Success.
lines.ancientContext: Accumulation reaches its limit and the way opens like the great thoroughfare of heaven. The Xiang commentary says the way is now travelled widely, hence success.
lines.plainLanguage: What has been stored breaks into open ground, like stepping onto a broad highway. Long cultivation turns here into a road you can actually walk.
lines.lifeTranslation: When years of preparation finally meet an opening, you can use everything you have. Remember that the restraint and the practice are what paved the road.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which capability you have been building for years fits the opening in front of you?

topicRules.career: Build depth before you push: shore up process, documentation and fundamentals, and settle problems while they are small. Lean on people who know more than you so you can hold the opening when it comes.
topicRules.study: Take in what others have already worked out and organise it into a system of your own. When you hit a wall, repair the underlying concept rather than adding hours to force the pace.
topicRules.romance: Work on your own steadiness and range so the relationship rests on a stable person. Raise small frictions early rather than letting them accumulate past the point of return.
topicRules.family: Take what older relatives have learned and adapt it to how your household actually runs. Set out rules and shares of work in calm times; early agreement costs less than later correction.
topicRules.relations: Seek out people with wide experience and ask questions without defending your position. For recurring conflict, change how the interaction is set up instead of smoothing over each episode.
topicRules.finance: Favour long accumulation and a buffer against risk, and have reserves in place before you expand anything. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: Treat rest, movement and food as a long store you are building rather than something to cram. If your body keeps sending the same signal, consult a qualified professional; this is not medical advice.
topicRules.general: Cultivate and wait. Stop when stopping is right, practise when practising is right, and take the larger step once the accumulation is genuinely in place and the way has opened.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: build up knowledge and capability, set your own limits, and wait for the task that fits. Avoid: collecting without ever practising, or taking on a heavy charge before you are ready for it.

hexagrams.name: Yí · Nourishing
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Yi: Steadfastness brings good fortune. Observe nourishment; seek sustenance for your own mouth.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says nourishment brings good fortune when what is nourished is correct: observe what a person nourishes, and how they nourish themselves. The Xiang image is thunder beneath the mountain, with the noble person guarding their speech and moderating what they eat.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Gen above, Zhen below. A solid line at top and bottom with four open lines between makes the shape of an open mouth, which gives the hexagram its sense of feeding and sustaining. The commentary puts the weight on nourishing correctly: the question is not whether you are fed but by what, and how. The image narrows it to two habits of the same mouth, speech and food, and asks for restraint in both. The judgement says to seek your own sustenance. Several lines show the opposite, going wrong through envy or through feeding against the grain of things.
hexagrams.trendReason: Although the judgment gives good fortune through steadfastness, this depends on nourishing what is right. The first nine brings misfortune, the second misfortune in advancing, and the third misfortune in persistence with a ten-year prohibition on action. Adverse lines are numerous, and the fifth also forbids crossing the great river, hence the overall rating: Neutral rather than Favorable. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Watch what feeds you, and watch what you feed.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Leaving your sacred tortoise, you watch my moving jaws. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: You set aside your own sacred tortoise and watch another's jaw working with envy. The Xiang commentary says plainly that such an attitude deserves no regard.
lines.plainLanguage: You leave your own valuable gift unused and look longingly at what someone else is eating. The fault is in abandoning yourself in favour of admiring another.
lines.lifeTranslation: Rather than measuring yourself against other people's pay and results, take inventory of what you already have and have not yet used. That is the part you can actually act on.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which of your own abilities have you left idle because you take it for granted?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Upside-down nourishment, contrary to the constant way; seeking nourishment on the hill. Advancing brings misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: Nourishment sought upside down, against the usual order, reaching to the high mound. The Xiang commentary says such movement loses its proper kind, so advancing brings trouble.
lines.plainLanguage: The order of who provides for whom has been inverted, and support is sought upward against the normal pattern. Both the source and the method are unsuitable, so pressing forward goes badly.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you need support, ask through the channel that fits. Going over someone's head or around them usually damages the relationship and costs you your standing too.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Has the way you are asking for help skipped the person you should have spoken to first?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Turning against nourishment. Persistence brings misfortune. Do not act for ten years. Nothing is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: Nourishment turned against itself. The Xiang commentary says the way has been deeply violated, which is why the text calls for ten years of no undertaking.
lines.plainLanguage: The proper way of sustaining body and character has been broken. Even holding steady goes badly, nothing is to be undertaken for a long stretch, and there is no advantage. This is the heaviest warning in the hexagram.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you have been draining yourself or others in the same wrong way for a long time, what is needed is a real change of direction and a long repair, not a different technique for carrying on.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What have you kept doing for a long time, knowing it was wearing you down?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Upside-down nourishment brings good fortune. Watching intently like a tiger, desire following desire. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: Nourishment sought upside down again, but here it turns out well: the Xiang commentary credits light given from above. The tiger's fixed gaze and unbroken desire depict sustained focus, so there is no fault.
lines.plainLanguage: Seeking support upward works this time because the support is genuinely being offered. The steady gaze and the continuing want are signs of concentration, and that is what keeps the line clear of fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: When backing really exists, pressing actively for resources is not overreach. What matters is a clear aim and sustained effort rather than asking in bursts and going quiet.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Have you pursued what you want steadily enough for anyone to notice?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Contrary to the constant way. Remaining steadfast brings good fortune. Do not cross the great river.
lines.ancientContext: The usual order is departed from, yet remaining settled and correct brings good fortune. The Xiang commentary attributes this to yielding compliance with the one above. Strength is short, so the great water is not to be crossed.
lines.plainLanguage: The situation is already off the normal pattern. Holding your place without rash movement is what goes well, and the text says outright not to cross the great water. You can hold; you cannot advance.
lines.lifeTranslation: When your resources fall short, keep the current position and rely on support you trust. This is not the moment to launch something that demands a great deal.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Can your present resources really carry the big thing you want to start?

lines.original: Nine at the top: The source of nourishment. Danger and good fortune. It is beneficial to cross the great river.
lines.ancientContext: All nourishment proceeds from here. The weight of the role brings danger, and watchfulness turns it to good fortune; the Xiang commentary calls this great cause for celebration.
lines.plainLanguage: Everyone's sustenance flows through this position. Height and responsibility bring exposure, and it is precisely the caution that makes it favourable, and that makes crossing the great water suitable.
lines.lifeTranslation: When other people depend on you, the responsibility itself is the pressure. Staying alert rather than comfortable is what lets you hold the role.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Who is relying on you right now, and what have you put in place for them?

topicRules.career: Look at what your expertise is actually being fed by and spend your effort on skills that compound. Think before you commit or comment, and stop measuring yourself against other people's packages.
topicRules.study: Choose your material carefully: reading a few reliable sources closely beats skimming many. Cap your intake and leave time to digest, so input does not quietly replace understanding.
topicRules.romance: Mind how you speak, since one careless sentence can outweigh months of care. Ask honestly whether the two of you feed each other or whether it runs one way, and keep your own condition in order.
topicRules.family: Start with the everyday things, meals and sleep and routine. Speech between family members needs the most restraint, and both asking and giving should stay within reasonable bounds.
topicRules.relations: Speak carefully and comment less on other people's private affairs. To judge a relationship, notice whether it leaves both of you more alive or more tired; that reads truer than how warm it looks.
topicRules.finance: Get to the point of supporting yourself before anything else, and treat spending like eating, with limits set by what you can carry. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: This hexagram speaks directly to moderating food: regular meals, an eye on excess, and a workable sleep pattern are the basics of feeding yourself. If discomfort persists, consult a qualified professional; this is not medical advice.
topicRules.general: Come back to nourishing correctly. See clearly what is feeding you and what you are feeding, keep speech and appetite measured, and seek your own sustenance rather than waiting to be given it.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: moderate your speech and your appetite, and choose sources that genuinely sustain you. Avoid: being led by appetite or by flattery, or settling into long dependence on someone else's provision.

hexagrams.name: Dà Guò · Great Exceeding
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Da Guo: The ridgepole bends. It is beneficial to proceed. Success.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary reads the sagging ridgepole as weakness at both root and tip, with firmness in excess yet centred; gentle and pleased movement makes advance worthwhile. The Xiang image is the lake submerging the trees, with the noble person standing alone without fear and withdrawing from the world without distress.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Dui above, Xun below. Four solid lines mass in the middle with a single yielding line at each end, which the commentary describes as weak at both root and tip. Neither end can hold, so the ridgepole bends. This is a load beyond what the structure can carry. The judgement still favours going somewhere, because standing still is not a way out; you have to work your way through. The posture offered is to stand alone unafraid and stay settled even when no one understands. The lines show both a ridgepole holding up well and a crossing that goes over your head.
hexagrams.trendReason: Weak ends and a bending roof beam describe a real danger of excessive load. The third nine's bending beam and the top six's drowning both explicitly bring misfortune, hence the rating: Rather Unfavorable. Yet the judgment's beneficial proceeding and success, along with the fourth nine's raised beam and good fortune, preserve room to find a way through, so it is not the lowest rating. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: The load is beyond the structure; lighten it before it gives.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Spread white thatch beneath. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: White rushes are laid down as a mat before anything is set upon them. The Xiang commentary reads this as the yielding taking the lower place: care upon care, and so no fault.
lines.plainLanguage: Spreading clean rushes underneath before placing the vessel is extreme care. At the opening of a heavily loaded situation, that carefulness is what keeps the line free of fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: At the start of a heavy commitment, make the groundwork and the safeguards a little more thorough than strictly needed. The care that looks excessive now pays out later.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Before this heavy task begins, what is one more layer of protection you could add?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: A withered poplar sprouts new shoots; an older man gains a young wife. Nothing unfavorable.
lines.ancientContext: A withered poplar puts out new shoots; an older man takes a young wife. The Xiang commentary calls this an association that exceeds the norm, yet firm and yielding complement each other, so nothing is unfavourable.
lines.plainLanguage: A dry tree sends out fresh growth. A pairing that looks out of line brings life instead, which is why nothing counts against it. The line is about unusual matches in unusual times.
lines.lifeTranslation: Extraordinary periods allow unlikely combinations, such as pairing an experienced hand with a newcomer so each covers what the other lacks.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which unlikely pairing would actually cover the gap you have?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: The ridgepole bends. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The ridgepole sags and this goes badly. The Xiang commentary points out that no support can be accepted at this stage, which is the real cause of the trouble.
lines.plainLanguage: The beam bends and the structure is heading for failure. The commentary locates the problem in an unwillingness to hear offers of help; standing alone on sheer hardness leaves the danger unresolved.
lines.lifeTranslation: When the load is clearly beyond you, refusing help is the most dangerous move available. Admitting you cannot hold it and asking is what creates room to adjust.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there someone you have not yet asked for help with the thing you are holding up?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: The ridgepole rises. Good fortune. Other entanglements bring regret.
lines.ancientContext: The ridgepole rises rather than sagging, hence good fortune; the Xiang commentary says it does not bend towards what is below. If other attachments pull at it, there is cause for regret.
lines.plainLanguage: The beam arches and holds, so the line reads well. But side interests and entanglements still bring regret. Concentration is the condition attached to the good outcome.
lines.lifeTranslation: Once you have finally got the situation holding, keep your resources on the main line. Starting something new now tends to loosen the structure you just steadied.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What side project is taking the strength you need for the main beam?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: A withered poplar flowers; an older woman gains a young husband. No blame and no praise.
lines.ancientContext: The withered poplar puts out flowers; the Xiang commentary asks how long that can last, and finds the pairing of an older woman with a young man unbecoming. There is neither fault nor praise.
lines.plainLanguage: Flowers on a dead tree are pleasant to look at and cannot last. The arrangement is not wrong, but there is nothing in it worth commending. Visible flourishing without a base under it does not carry on.
lines.lifeTranslation: A brief good result with no underlying conditions behind it is fine to accept, but not to expand on. Check first whether it can happen again.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Could your recent good result repeat itself in a different month?

lines.original: Six at the top: Crossing too far, water covers the head. Misfortune, but no blame.
lines.ancientContext: Wading too deep, the water closes over the head. The Xiang commentary says the misfortune cannot be blamed, since the act came from necessity or from duty.
lines.plainLanguage: The crossing is too deep and the water goes over you, which is a bad outcome. Because it was unavoidable, no blame attaches. The misfortune is real; the absence of blame is a recognition of the intent behind it.
lines.lifeTranslation: Some efforts exceed what you can carry even when the motive is sound, so sound the depth before you step in. If you are already under, getting out comes before working out who was right.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Could you live with the worst case of the thing you are about to commit to?

topicRules.career: Face squarely whether the load now exceeds what the structure can bear, and ask for help, cut scope or add people early. This is not the time for a new front; steady the main pillar first.
topicRules.study: If the schedule is plainly overloaded, cut the scope rather than the sleep. A strong result you cannot repeat is not a reason to add more.
topicRules.romance: You may be under pressure or in an arrangement outside the usual pattern, so say plainly where your limit is. Silent endurance usually damages the relationship more than admitting you cannot hold it.
topicRules.family: Check whether one person has been carrying too much alone for too long and redistribute the load. The carer's own rest belongs on the schedule as well.
topicRules.relations: Isolation comes easily now, so stay self-possessed without shutting the door. Accepting other people's support is the key to getting through; refusing it is the real risk.
topicRules.finance: Examine whether leverage and fixed commitments have passed what you can carry, and reduce the load first. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: This hexagram points straight at overload, so schedule genuine rest and cut the number of things running at once. If exhaustion or low mood persists, consult a qualified professional; this is not medical advice.
topicRules.general: You are in an exceptional period of excess load. Measure the depth before stepping in, start carefully, ask for support, hold the main line and do not press ahead. Standing on your own while still accepting help is what gets you through.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: name the load that is too heavy and put your resources on the one joint that matters most. Avoid: keeping up appearances while the reinforcement waits, or trying to carry every problem at once.

hexagrams.name: Kǎn · The Repeating Pit
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Repeated Kan: With sincerity, the heart alone finds success. Action has merit.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary names this doubled danger: water flows on without filling up, moving through peril without losing its constancy. The heart succeeds through inner firmness, and action has merit. The Xiang image is water arriving wave upon wave, with the noble person keeping virtue constant and practising the work of instruction.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Kan above, Kan below. Two pits stacked on one another make this one of the hardest situations in the book. The judgement says there is confidence and the heart succeeds, which means the outer pit may not release you at once, and what can still get through is your own integrity and steadiness. Action still has merit, so there are things worth doing inside the difficulty. Most of the lines describe falling in, being stuck, or working hard for a small gain, and the top line closes with three years without release. The counsel is to hold your principles and drill the basics rather than rushing for a quick way out.
hexagrams.trendReason: The Judgment commentary explicitly describes repeated danger. The first six falls into a deep pit with misfortune, the third says not to act, and the top remains captive for three years with misfortune. Dangerous and constrained images predominate, with only small gains in the second nine and no blame in the fifth offering respite, hence the rating: Rather Unfavorable. The judgment's sincerity and merit in action mean that purpose can remain open and action possible, not that danger resolves automatically. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Danger comes in layers; keep your footing and take small gains.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Repeated danger. Falling into the deep pit. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says entering the pit at the very start means the way itself has been lost; direction and method went wrong first, which is why the fall keeps going.
lines.plainLanguage: The difficulty has barely begun and you are already in a deeper hole. The commentary puts the cause in losing the proper way, which suggests the trouble began with the opening move rather than with luck.
lines.lifeTranslation: Reaching for a shortcut at the first sign of difficulty tends to land you somewhere worse. Stop and check whether the direction has drifted, then reset the basic method.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How much of your present difficulty comes from having chosen the wrong direction?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Danger within the pit. Seek small gains.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary explains that seeking small gains reflects not yet being out of the centre of the danger. You are still inside it, so only a limited return is appropriate.
lines.plainLanguage: The danger remains, but the firm central position allows small progress within the limits. The commentary is a reminder that you are still in the pit, so the gain is modest and the aim is to stop sliding.
lines.lifeTranslation: With resources and room both tight, shrink the goal to one thing you can finish this week. Small verifiable results serve you better than planning a full reversal.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Within the limits you have now, what is one small thing you could complete?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Coming and going, pit upon pit. Danger and obstruction; entering the deep pit. Do not act.
lines.ancientContext: Pits whether you come or go, danger piled upon danger. The Xiang commentary says such movement ends without merit, which is why the text says make no use of this.
lines.plainLanguage: Forward is dangerous and back is dangerous, with the difficulties layered one on another. Going further only takes you deeper. The text says do not act, and stopping suits better than forcing a move.
lines.lifeTranslation: When every option looks like it ends badly, that usually means the conditions are not yet enough to decide on. Pausing, gathering information and containing the loss is reasonable here.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Would sitting still right now be safer than forcing a decision?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: A jar of wine and two baskets of food, using earthenware. Offer simplicity through the window. No blame in the end.
lines.ancientContext: A jar of wine and two bowls of grain, served in earthenware, with the offering passed in through the window. The Xiang commentary calls this firm and yielding meeting each other, so in the end there is no fault.
lines.plainLanguage: In the middle of danger the ceremony is stripped down and the vessels are plain, but the sincerity reaches the other person by the most direct route. What matters is honesty and simplicity, not presentation, so nothing goes wrong in the end.
lines.lifeTranslation: When resources are short, do not strain to keep up appearances. Say what the situation is and what you need in the plainest form, such as a short message that states both clearly.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What would work better if you simply said it more directly?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: The pit is not overflowing; it has only reached level ground. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The pit is not yet full, only levelling with the ground. The Xiang commentary says the central virtue is not yet fully realised, so the line reaches no fault rather than good fortune.
lines.plainLanguage: The hollow is gradually filling and the situation has moved from bad to level, but not yet to a point where it flows through. No fault means the way out is in sight and not yet reached, so the effort has to hold.
lines.lifeTranslation: The decline has only just stopped, which is exactly when celebrating early or letting go is most costly. Hold the current rhythm a while longer and expand once the base is genuinely level.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you sure this is real improvement, or has it only stopped getting worse?

lines.original: Six at the top: Bound with cords and ropes, placed among thorn bushes. For three years, no release. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: Bound with cords and set among thorn bushes, not released for three years. The Xiang commentary again traces the cause to having lost the way, and uses three years to describe the length of the confinement.
lines.plainLanguage: The danger has run to its extreme: tied up and left in the brambles, unable to get free for a long time. This is the worst line of the hexagram, and the commentary still points at departure from the proper way rather than only at outward bad luck.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you have been stuck in the same difficulty for a long time, treat it as structural rather than a passing dip. Seek outside help and re-examine the underlying cause instead of gritting through.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How long has this gone on, and how much longer will you use the same method?

topicRules.career: You are in layered difficulty, so hold your core duties and standard process and shrink targets to deliverable pieces. This is not the time to expand, change employers, or stake everything on one reversal.
topicRules.study: Go back to the fundamentals and repeat them, the way water runs the same channel again and again. Slow progress is normal; what matters is not breaking the chain rather than covering gaps with a late sprint.
topicRules.romance: The same difficulty may keep resurfacing, so communicate simply and sincerely rather than papering over cracks with large promises. Whether it lifts depends on both of you, and one person cannot carry it alone.
topicRules.family: If the same trouble keeps repeating, state the problem and the boundary plainly and consider help from outside the family. Do not let an unchanged conflict keep accumulating.
topicRules.relations: Cut back on socialising and new commitments and keep your energy for the few people you genuinely trust. Sincerity counts more than presentation now, and a plain clear message often lands better than a polished occasion.
topicRules.finance: Favour holding your position and keeping cash, control your exposure and avoid taking on new debt. This is a general principle rather than investment advice; decide according to your own circumstances and consult a qualified professional.
topicRules.wellness: You may be in a long stretch of depletion, so keep sleep and rest regular and notice whether low mood is persisting. This offers no diagnosis or treatment; see a doctor if you are unwell.
topicRules.general: This is stacked difficulty rather than a passing patch. Stay correct, stay consistent, drill the basics and take small gains instead of quick ones. A steady mind does not mean the outside eases at once, so arrange your safety and your way back first.
