hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: keep to fixed procedures, get through the risk section by section, and ask people who have been here before. Avoid: growing casual because the danger has become familiar, or jumping into something deeper while rattled.

hexagrams.name: Lí · Clinging Brightness
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Li: Steadfast correctness is beneficial. Success. Keeping a cow brings good fortune.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary glosses Li as clinging: sun and moon cling to heaven, grain and plants cling to the earth, and doubled brightness clinging to what is correct transforms the world. The Xiang image is two lights arising in succession, with the great person carrying the light on to shine in all four directions.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Li above, Li below: two lights laid one on the other. The original sense of the name is clinging or attaching, because light needs something to rest on if it is to last. The judgement favours correctness and says that rearing the cow brings good fortune, which puts the weight on staying correct and staying yielding. Brightness without restraint burns the one holding it. The lines move from a careful start, through the excellent central position, to the sun past noon, then to a violent reversal, and close with a campaign undertaken to set the state right. Brightness is good, and it has to cling to what is correct and know when to draw in.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment gives beneficial steadfastness, success, and good fortune in keeping a cow, while the second six has supreme good fortune: the direction is positive. Yet the third nine's lament at old age and sunset brings misfortune, and the fourth's sudden burning, death, and abandonment is among the text's fiercest images of destruction. Even the fifth six reaches fortune through tears and grief. Favorable and adverse images appear together with extreme contrasts, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Light lasts only where it rests on something correct.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Confused footsteps. Treat them with reverence; no blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that meeting confused footsteps with reverence is precisely how fault is kept away.
lines.plainLanguage: At the outset the steps cross over one another and the threads are tangled, so a misstep comes easily. Keeping a careful and respectful attitude avoids fault; the point is not to turn careless because things are hectic.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a new task opens with too many loose ends, slow down and put them in order, taking each detail seriously. That goes wrong less often than pushing several items at once.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In the current rush, which step did you take out of habit rather than after checking?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Yellow radiance. Supreme good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: Yellow is the colour of the centre. The Xiang commentary attributes the great good fortune here to holding the central way.
lines.plainLanguage: Clinging in the colour of the mean, neither to one side nor the other, is the best line in the hexagram. The brightness rests in a correct central position, neither overstated nor dimmed, hence the strong reading.
lines.lifeTranslation: When your output matches your position, without grabbing credit or hiding what you can do, trust accumulates most easily. This is a state to maintain rather than a base to build on in a hurry.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do your current output and your current position actually match?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Radiance of the setting sun. Without beating the earthen pot and singing, one laments great old age. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The brightness of the declining sun. The Xiang commentary asks how long such light can hold, marking the point where fullness turns towards decline.
lines.plainLanguage: The light has passed its height and is sloping west. If you cannot meet that calmly, all that remains is the lament of old age, which does not go well. The line says the state of mind matters more here than the light itself.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a good run is visibly tapering, accept the change early and arrange the next stage instead of propping it up with nostalgia or complaint, which only makes the handover harder.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you still using a past high point to justify a present judgement?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Suddenly arriving, burning, dying, abandoned.
lines.ancientContext: It comes abruptly, burning, dying, cast aside. The Xiang commentary says there is nowhere to be contained, meaning the place to cling to has been lost, which accounts for the violence of the images.
lines.plainLanguage: The arrival is sudden and fierce: like fire, like death, like being discarded. This is the harshest description in the hexagram. Once legitimate attachment and restraint are gone, brightness turns into a destructive blaze.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a situation turns sharply, stop the loss first and cut the link that keeps the damage spreading, then talk about rebuilding. Adding to the position usually just widens the fire. This is a situational note, not a prediction.
lines.reflectionPrompt: If things worsened suddenly, which connection would you cut first?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Tears pouring, grieving and sighing. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: Tears fall in floods and there is grieving lament, yet the outcome is favourable. The Xiang commentary attributes this to clinging to the correct position of the ruler: even in fear, there is something proper to hold to.
lines.plainLanguage: Weeping and worry still turn out well, because the fear is a clear reading of the situation and the attachment is still to a correct place. Facing the difficulty honestly helps more than composure you do not feel.
lines.lifeTranslation: Admitting you cannot hold it, saying the worry out loud and asking for help is not weakness. People willing to look at the real state of things usually find a way out sooner than those who grind on.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which of your worries have you never said out loud to anyone?

lines.original: Nine at the top: The king goes on campaign. There is merit in cutting off the chief; captives are not indiscriminately taken from his kind. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The king sends out a campaign with praiseworthy result, taking the chief offender and not the followers. The Xiang commentary says the purpose is to set the state right, hence no fault. The military image should not be read as a modern instruction.
lines.plainLanguage: Brightness at its height acts, and only the principal wrong is dealt with while the rest are left alone, so there is no fault. What matters is a clear boundary and a legitimate purpose, not widening the reach.
lines.lifeTranslation: When handling a problem that has built up over time, address the actual knot and resist the pull to widen the blame, which draws other people into the damage.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you solving the real problem, or also settling accounts with other people along the way?

topicRules.career: Visibility is high and your work is being watched, so attach the results to legitimate duties and real output. Good runs have a term, so plan the next stage early rather than letting prominence outrun the ground beneath it.
topicRules.study: This suits continuous revision, one light following another without a break. Let understanding rest on clear basic concepts rather than short-term memorising that only looks bright.
topicRules.romance: The heat is noticeable, so keep proportion and honesty and let the relationship rest on principles you both accept. When feeling surges, let it settle before speaking; sharp words in the moment are hard to repair.
topicRules.family: Keep the rhythm of care steady and mild, with attention reaching every member. When conflict flares, cool it before discussing it, and do not make big decisions at the peak.
topicRules.relations: You may easily become the focus, so meet people from a centred position, neither showy nor deliberately hidden. Handle disputes on their own terms and keep unrelated people out of them.
topicRules.finance: Both income and exposure are conspicuous now, so stay correct and keep restraint rather than expanding at the height of momentum. This is a general principle rather than investment advice; decide according to your own circumstances and consult a qualified professional.
topicRules.wellness: You may be burning energy too hard, so schedule fixed rest and time to cool down. Take sharp swings or persistent low mood seriously. This offers no diagnosis or treatment; see a doctor if you are unwell.
topicRules.general: Brightness needs a legitimate place to rest and a sense of limit. Stay centred, keep going, hold proportion and it flows; lose the anchor and let it burn, and fullness can turn to collapse. Watch for the point where the peak begins to tip.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: attach yourself to a legitimate aim, keep the boundaries clear, and let the work stay visible over time. Avoid: chasing the most dazzling performance, or leaning too heavily on a single person or source.

hexagrams.name: Xián · Mutual Influence
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Xian: Success. Steadfast correctness is beneficial. Taking a wife brings good fortune.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary glosses Xian as influence: the yielding above and the firm below respond to each other, stillness meets pleasure, and the man places himself beneath the woman, which is why the judgement is favourable. Heaven and earth influence each other and all things come to life. The Xiang image is a lake on the mountain, with the noble person receiving others through emptiness.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Gen below, Dui above: a lake resting on the mountain, an image of influence and exchange. The name is the word for feeling with the heart radical removed, which suggests a response that is natural rather than calculated. The judgement speaks of marriage in its original setting, and the core of it is that the stronger party is willing to place themselves lower so that both can genuinely meet. The lines take the body from the ground up, from toe and calf to thigh, back and jaw, and warn that influence has to be proportionate. Rushing, following blindly, or stopping at talk all fall short.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's success, beneficial steadfastness, and good fortune in marriage are all positive. Its commentary grounds influence in Heaven and Earth's creation of all things, and the fourth nine's good fortune and vanished regret also favor this direction. Yet the second six warns that rash movement is dangerous and staying brings fortune, the third has regret in advancing, and the top reaches only speech. Impatience, blind following, and empty words weaken influence, hence the rating: Highly Favorable, rather than the highest. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Meet others with an empty mind and no calculation.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Influence in the big toe.
lines.ancientContext: Influence reaching the big toe. The Xiang commentary says the intent is already turned outward, though nothing has yet been put into action.
lines.plainLanguage: The response has only stirred in the toe, the first faint motion of an inclination. The line gives no verdict, which fits: an intention has surfaced and nothing has yet succeeded or gone wrong.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you first feel drawn to a person or an idea, let it stay in the observing stage. Watch for a while longer before deciding whether to commit.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do you understand where this new attraction actually comes from?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Influence in the calf. Misfortune; staying brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: Influence reaching the calf. The calf moves first, which makes rash action easy, hence the unfavourable reading; the Xiang commentary says that staying put and yielding does no harm.
lines.plainLanguage: The response reaches the calf and the leg wants to move forward at once. That haste carries risk, while staying settled goes well. The difference lies not in the feeling but in whether you act on it immediately.
lines.lifeTranslation: Declaring yourself, placing the order or switching careers the moment you feel something carries high risk. Staying where you are and letting the feeling settle is usually steadier.
lines.reflectionPrompt: If you hold off for now, will this feeling fade or become clearer?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Influence in the thighs, clinging to following. Advancing brings regret.
lines.ancientContext: Influence reaching the thigh, which follows the foot rather than moving of itself. The Xiang commentary says the intent lies in following others and what is held to is too low, so advancing brings regret.
lines.plainLanguage: The response reaches the thigh, which can only go where the foot goes. The commentary names the problem directly as an intent set on following others, and advancing that way brings regret because your own judgement is gone.
lines.lifeTranslation: Moving at other people's pace and doing whatever they do saves effort in the short run and slowly carries you away from the direction you actually wanted.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is this decision what you want, or what everyone around you is doing?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Steadfastness brings good fortune and regret vanishes. Restless coming and going; friends follow your thoughts.
lines.ancientContext: Correctness brings good fortune and regret disappears; the Xiang commentary says no harm has yet come from influence. But thoughts coming and going restlessly draw only narrow responses, which it calls not yet broad.
lines.plainLanguage: Stay correct and regret dissolves. If your mind swings back and forth in anxious calculation, what answers you will match that same level. The quality of the exchange follows from whether your mind is settled and open.
lines.lifeTranslation: Constantly guessing what the other person thinks and changing your approach tends to draw an equally unsteady response. Settle your own principles and the relationship steadies more easily.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the thought you keep turning over solving the problem or manufacturing anxiety?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Influence in the back muscles. No regret.
lines.ancientContext: Influence reaching the flesh of the back, which lies behind the heart and does not move at whim. The Xiang commentary says the intent is at the periphery, so the line reaches only absence of regret.
lines.plainLanguage: The response reaches the back, which does not dance to the mood, and so there is no regret. The commentary notes that such stillness can also shade into distance, which is why it stops short of good fortune.
lines.lifeTranslation: Keeping your feelings out of it prevents mistakes, and detaching too far makes people think you do not care. There is still a balance to find between composure and involvement.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your calm a mature restraint, or a way of keeping yourself out of it?

lines.original: Six at the top: Influence in the jaw, cheeks, tongue.
lines.ancientContext: Influence reaching the jaw, cheeks and tongue. The Xiang commentary describes this as an outpouring of talk: words in abundance and sincerity in short supply.
lines.plainLanguage: The response stops at the mouth, leaving only verbal warmth. The line gives no verdict, but the commentary makes the point: however much is said, nothing moves anyone unless it is carried out.
lines.lifeTranslation: A relationship held together by compliments, promises and pleasant phrasing eventually shows through. Doing one thing you said you would carries more weight than saying ten more.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which promise you made recently have you still not delivered?

topicRules.career: This favours building relationships of mutual trust, won by listening openly and being willing to take the lower seat. Do not commit the moment you warm to something, and do not follow other people's practice at the cost of your own judgement.
topicRules.study: Discussion and exchange work well here, so stay open to views that differ from yours. Avoid repeating what you heard, and test and organise it yourself afterwards.
topicRules.romance: This hexagram fits the subject closely, with its emphasis on genuine response and willingness to yield. Early attraction calls for more observing and fewer impulsive declarations, and warm words need actions behind them.
topicRules.family: Receive each other's feelings with an open mind so that everyone is actually heard. Persuading and correcting help less than presence and a concrete response to what someone needs.
topicRules.relations: Connection comes easily now, so stay sincere and keep a reasonable distance. Do not follow along just to belong, and do not let friendship stay at the level of warm talk.
topicRules.finance: Watch for decisions driven by someone else's enthusiasm or by the mood of the moment, and give yourself time to observe first. This is a general principle rather than investment advice; decide according to your own circumstances and consult a qualified professional.
topicRules.wellness: You are sensitive to what is around you and your mood is easily moved by others, so schedule quiet time alone to recover. This offers no diagnosis or treatment; see a doctor if you are unwell.
topicRules.general: Receive others through emptiness and respond with sincerity. Willingness to yield first is what opens the exchange. Watch the three distortions of haste, blind following and talk without action, so that influence becomes a real connection.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: settle yourself before responding to a feeling, and build the exchange on sincerity and respect. Avoid: being pulled along by a passing mood, or trading flattery and pressure for a response.

hexagrams.name: Héng · Duration
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Heng: Success, no blame. Steadfast correctness is beneficial; proceeding is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary glosses Heng as lasting: thunder and wind work together, firm and yielding all respond. Enduring in the way is the way of heaven and earth, which goes on without end, and every ending has a beginning. Sun and moon can shine long because they hold to heaven. The Xiang image is thunder and wind, with the noble person standing firm and not changing direction.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Xun below, Zhen above: thunder and wind reinforce each other, an image of what lasts. Lasting here does not mean staying the same. The commentary points to the sun, the moon and the four seasons: it is because their change has order that they can shine and complete for so long. The judgement affirms the direction of persistence, and the lines mark two ways of losing balance. The first digs too deep at the very start and goes badly. The top one shakes with restlessness and also goes badly. Real duration is a steady rhythm between holding where holding is right and moving where moving is right.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's success, no blame, beneficial steadfastness, and beneficial proceeding are all positive, and its commentary invokes Heaven and Earth's enduring way. Yet the lines' actual situations are weaker: the first six's excessive pursuit of constancy brings misfortune with no benefit, the third nine brings shame and regret, the fourth gains no game in the hunt, and the top six's restless constancy brings misfortune. Only the second nine's vanished regret is clearly good. A lofty meaning meets many misplaced lines; favorable and adverse balance out, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Duration is a rhythm you can keep, not an effort you strain.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Seeking constancy too deeply. Persistence brings misfortune; nothing is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: Digging deep for duration. The Xiang commentary locates the trouble in seeking depth at the very beginning: demanding too much too soon makes lasting harder.
lines.plainLanguage: Wanting to dig a relationship or a project to its deepest point straight away, and to have it permanent from the start, is an excess that goes badly and brings no advantage. Duration accumulates over time and cannot be drawn in full at the outset.
lines.lifeTranslation: Asking for a long-term commitment shortly after meeting, or expecting complete trust in your first week in a job, usually produces the opposite. Let the depth grow at its own pace.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Have you asked for something deep while the relationship is still shallow?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Regret vanishes.
lines.ancientContext: The line text is two words: regret disappears. The Xiang commentary supplies the reason, that this position can hold to the centre over a long period.
lines.plainLanguage: Only the disappearance of regret is stated, which makes this the steadiest line in the hexagram. The commentary credits a long-held middle way, neither slanted nor extreme, which dissolves the regret that might have formed.
lines.lifeTranslation: Keep your daily pace at the middle setting, neither excessive nor slack. Over a long stretch, many of the things you would have regretted simply never happen.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your current pace the kind you could hold for three years?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Without constancy in virtue, one may incur shame. Persistence brings regret.
lines.ancientContext: Not maintaining one's character. The Xiang commentary says such a person has nowhere to be contained, so disgrace may follow and holding to this brings regret.
lines.plainLanguage: Conduct that is good one day and poor the next, with no consistent thread, can bring humiliation and leaves the situation regrettable. The commentary puts it harder still: the inconsistent person ends up with no ground to stand on.
lines.lifeTranslation: Standards that move with your mood and accounts that do not match up will gradually use up other people's trust. Holding a basic standard steadily beats being excellent now and then.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which of your standards have you quietly relaxed lately for convenience?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: No game in the hunt.
lines.ancientContext: Hunting in the field and taking no game. The Xiang commentary says the root cause is remaining long in a position that is not yours, so of course nothing is caught.
lines.plainLanguage: You go out to hunt and come back with nothing. The commentary blames long residence in the wrong position: persisting from a place that does not fit yields little however long you keep at it. Duration has to be applied in the right place.
lines.lifeTranslation: If you have put a long time into something with no result, the thing to examine may not be how hard you tried but whether this position, direction or method ever suited you.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your persistence being spent in the right position?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Constancy in virtue. Steadfastness brings good fortune for the wife and misfortune for the husband.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary reads this through the role divisions of its own era: constancy to one course is favourable for one role, while the person whose duty is to judge and decide does badly by simply going along. Read today, this distinguishes the position that should hold from the position that should decide, rather than prescribing anything about gender.
lines.plainLanguage: Keeping the established conduct and method going is favourable for someone in a role of maintenance, and unfavourable for someone who must adapt to circumstances and carry the responsibility of judgement. The same persistence gives opposite results in different roles.
lines.lifeTranslation: If your role is steady execution, consistency is a strength. If your role is deciding, holding to the old method past the point of fit can cost you. Work out which kind of responsibility you carry first.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does your present position call for holding steady, or for changing at the right moment?

lines.original: Six at the top: Restless constancy. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: Duration turned into agitation, at the top position. The Xiang commentary says that in the end this achieves nothing great, hence the unfavourable reading.
lines.plainLanguage: Duration has been made into constant shaking, with someone in a high position moving restlessly. The commentary is direct: sustained agitation looks active and accumulates no result.
lines.lifeTranslation: Constantly switching direction and overturning yesterday's decision drains the team and drains you. Real stability comes from a predictable rhythm rather than continuous motion.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How much of your recent change was a necessary adjustment, and how much was unease?

topicRules.career: This favours long-term building and steady accumulation, held together by consistent standards and pace. Check, though, whether you have stayed too long in a position that does not fit; a long run without results calls for a change of direction, not more hours.
topicRules.study: A fixed, modest daily amount suits this best, and beats occasional sprints. Do not set a target that is too deep at the start, and do not keep switching methods and materials.
topicRules.romance: What matters is a lasting and steady rhythm together, letting trust build over time. Do not demand heavy commitments early, and do not let a passing mood unsettle what you have already established.
topicRules.family: Set up a predictable daily routine and way of relating so everyone feels secure. Once a rule is agreed, apply it consistently rather than tightening and loosening with your mood.
topicRules.relations: Your credit here rests on consistency between what you say and what you do, so keep basic promises and boundaries. Unpredictability damages relationships most, and when you do need to change something, explain why rather than changing without warning.
topicRules.finance: This leans towards long-term, regular and sustainable arrangements, and away from frequently reshuffling what you hold. This is a general principle rather than investment advice; decide according to your own circumstances and consult a qualified professional.
topicRules.wellness: Build a sleep and exercise pattern you can keep for the long run, with intensity set by what is sustainable. Avoid a short burst of hard training followed by stopping altogether. This offers no diagnosis or treatment; see a doctor if you are unwell.
topicRules.general: Duration has order. Hold your direction and principles and keep the pace at a level you can sustain. Watch both extremes: demanding too much at the start goes badly, and restlessness at the top goes badly too. Duration is a matter of rhythm, not force.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: set a rhythm you can repeat, keep it going over time, and correct the course at regular intervals. Avoid: reversing decisions constantly, chasing novelty, or clinging to a method that no longer fits.

hexagrams.name: Dùn · Retreat
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Dun: Success. Small steadfastness is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says success here comes from the retreat itself: withdrawing at the right moment is the success. The yielding line is steadily growing, so only small matters can be held correct. The Xiang image is the mountain under heaven, with the noble person keeping distance from small-minded people without harsh words, holding dignity instead.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Gen below, Qian above: a mountain standing beneath heaven, the image of knowing when to step back. Retreat here is not flight. It is reading the situation and deliberately opening distance, which is why the judgement calls it successful. Because the yielding force is still rising, only a limited range can be held, so the text grants correctness in small things. The lines run from the danger of leaving last, through a resolve bound as tight as oxhide, to retreats held back by attachment, by fondness, then a graceful one, and finally an unhurried withdrawal with room to spare. The point throughout: leaving early and cleanly is safer than staying on to endure.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment explicitly gives success, the fifth nine a commendable retreat with steadfast good fortune, and the top nine an unburdened retreat with nothing unfavorable. Conditions improve toward the end, showing timely withdrawal as an effective exit. Although the first six warns of danger in late retreat and the third nine of distress from entanglement, the overall direction is positive, hence the rating: Good. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Step back in good time, cleanly and with your dignity intact.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: At the tail of retreat. Danger. Do not proceed.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the danger of being at the tail of the retreat brings no disaster as long as you go no further. The position is poor, but stillness keeps it from becoming harm.
lines.plainLanguage: You have dragged out the leaving until you are last, which is the worst place to stand. Pushing forward now only deepens the danger. Holding still and making no new move is what protects you.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you notice you are the last one still in a situation that has gone wrong, stop every new commitment. Do not throw more time or money at it hoping to recover the position.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What have you known for a while you should pull out of, and kept putting off?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Held with yellow oxhide, which none can loosen.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary reads the yellow oxhide binding as firmness of will. Bound this tightly, nothing can work it loose.
lines.plainLanguage: The resolve is tied as fast as a strap of yellow oxhide. This line is not about being trapped. It is about fixing your own position deliberately, so no amount of persuasion shifts it.
lines.lifeTranslation: Once you have decided to leave or to stay out of something, write the reasons down for yourself. When people keep pressing, answer from those reasons rather than reopening the argument each time.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Would your decision survive being talked at for a third time?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Entangled retreat, with illness and danger. Keeping servants brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary calls a retreat held back by ties a state of illness and exhaustion, fit only for small domestic affairs and not for great undertakings. The master-and-servant wording belongs to its ancient setting and does not reflect present-day values.
lines.plainLanguage: You want to withdraw and something keeps pulling you back, which leaves you tired and exposed. In this state you can only handle the small things near at hand. Taking on anything large will cost you more than it returns.
lines.lifeTranslation: When obligation or loyalty stops you leaving cleanly, shrink your workload to what you can actually carry. Turn down new large commitments for now and revisit them once you have recovered.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What exactly is holding you in place when you already want to go?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Willing retreat brings good fortune for the noble person, but not for the petty person.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary contrasts two responses to the same attachment: the noble person can retreat from what they love, and the small-minded person cannot, which is where the difficulty lies.
lines.plainLanguage: The hard part of this line is stepping back from something you genuinely like. Those with room in them can let go and move on. Those who cannot are held in place by their own fondness.
lines.lifeTranslation: The hardest thing to release is usually the project or the relationship you actually love. People who let go for the sake of the longer run tend to find their next place sooner than those who hold on.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The thing you least want to give up, does it still suit who you are now?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Commendable retreat. Steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the good fortune of an admirable retreat to a will that is properly set. The motive is straight and the timing is right.
lines.plainLanguage: This is the best kind of withdrawal in the whole hexagram: well timed and well executed. Because the motive is sound and the decision is clear, holding correct goes well, with nothing left to sour behind you.
lines.lifeTranslation: Finish the handover properly, say what needs saying, and thank the people who deserve it. Leaving that way is remembered as professional rather than as walking out.
lines.reflectionPrompt: If you left now, how would you want people to describe the way you left?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Unburdened retreat. Nothing unfavorable.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says an unhurried retreat carries no disadvantage because there is nothing left in doubt. The base text keeps the older character for the negative here.
lines.plainLanguage: You have withdrawn to the furthest and most spacious position, with no hesitation left in you, so nothing works against you. Real ease comes from no longer arguing with yourself about whether you should have gone.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you can talk about that chapter some time later without bitterness, you have genuinely left it. That is also when there is room for something new.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What is still unresolved in you that makes you keep glancing back?

topicRules.career: This favours narrowing your front and repositioning yourself: arrange the resignation or the end of the partnership early rather than late. Do the handover properly, because the reputation you leave behind is worth more than a few extra months.
topicRules.study: Drop the surplus courses and activities and pull your attention back to the subjects that matter most. Letting go of a direction that does not suit you is not failure; it frees the hours for what you actually want to learn.
topicRules.romance: If the relationship already feels forced, give each other distance rather than pushing closer. When you do leave, say it plainly and keep your manner respectful, without harsh words and without dragging it out through silence.
topicRules.family: With arguments that keep repeating, step back before you talk again rather than settling who is right on the spot. Keep a reasonable distance from relatives who drain you; your tone can stay warm while the boundary stays clear.
topicRules.relations: Open some distance from people you clash with, without hostility and without losing your composure. Cut down on socialising that leads nowhere and keep your time for those who genuinely support you.
topicRules.finance: This favours consolidating, reducing exposure and pulling resources out of positions you do not understand. This is a general principle rather than investment advice; decide according to your own circumstances and consult a qualified professional.
topicRules.wellness: Step away from a high-pressure environment and arrange rest that is genuinely offline, rather than pushing on while already worn down. Take long-term exhaustion seriously. This offers no diagnosis or treatment; see a doctor if you are unwell.
topicRules.general: Retreat at the right moment opens the way. Once you can see conditions turning, withdraw while you still have room, keeping distance without burning anything down. Leave it until last and the position will be harder than it is today.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: recognise a losing position early, withdraw clearly, and keep your bearing while you do it. Avoid: fighting on out of attachment, trading provocations, or leaving and then drifting back into the same conflict.

hexagrams.name: Dà Zhuàng · Great Strength
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Da Zhuang: Steadfast correctness is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says the great is strong here: firmness in motion, hence strength. It then reads the favourable correctness as meaning that the great is precisely the correct, and that through what is correct and great the nature of heaven and earth can be seen. The Xiang image is thunder above heaven, with the noble person refusing to take a single step outside what is proper.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Qian below, Zhen above: thunder rolling above heaven, the image of force at its peak. Strength itself is neither good nor bad. Everything hangs on the two words in the judgement that make correctness the condition. The lines move from strength gathered in the toes and a rash campaign, to a ram butting a fence and catching its horns, then the fence opening and the cart axle holding firm, and finally back into a deadlock with no way forward or back. The same lesson runs through all of it: force used as a battering ram jams, while force used within what is right keeps moving.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's beneficial steadfastness, the second nine's good fortune, and the fourth's good fortune, vanished regret, and broken fence without entanglement show positive results from correct action. Yet the first nine explicitly warns that rushing ahead brings misfortune, while the third's ram caught by its horns and the top's inability to retreat or advance show forceful collision leading to deadlock. Only hardship bringing fortune offers release. Outcomes vary sharply with adherence to right conduct, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Strength only carries you when it stays inside what is proper.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Strength in the toes. Advancing brings misfortune. There is sincerity.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that strength gathered in the toes shows a confidence that runs itself out. The base text keeps the older form of the locative particle.
lines.plainLanguage: All the force sits in the toes, the lowest point, and the momentum arrives before the standing does. Setting out on a campaign from here does not go well. The confidence is real, but the base under it is too thin to hold.
lines.lifeTranslation: The urge to expand right after a first result is usually the riskiest moment. Shore up the foundation underneath before deciding how far to travel.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your current confidence coming from capability or from momentum?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The line says only that correctness brings good fortune. The Xiang commentary attributes this to the central position, where strength is neither short nor excessive.
lines.plainLanguage: The whole line is two words about holding correct, and that is enough. Standing in the middle position, the strength is balanced, so simply keeping to what is right goes well. Nothing extra is required.
lines.lifeTranslation: When your state is already right, do not add drama to it. Carrying on steadily by the principles you have set is the best available move.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there something in your life that is already good enough just as it is?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: The petty person uses strength; the noble person uses restraint. Persistence is dangerous. A ram strikes a fence and entangles its horns.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary contrasts the small-minded person who relies on force with the noble person who declines to. The ram drives its horns into the fence and traps them there, so the one who leans on strength ends up caught.
lines.plainLanguage: Two people with the same strength: one spends it proving something, the other chooses not to. Ramming through ends like the ram at the fence, horns stuck, unable to go either way, and the harder it pushes the tighter it holds.
lines.lifeTranslation: Increasing the force every time you hit an obstacle usually just wedges you in further. Step back half a pace, look at how the thing is actually built, then decide where to go through.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The thing you are forcing right now, is it jamming harder the more you push?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Steadfastness brings good fortune and regret vanishes. The fence breaks without entanglement. Strength in a great wagon's axle supports.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that with the fence broken open and nothing caught, this is the moment to go on. The line uses the firm axle of a large cart as the figure for ample carrying power.
lines.plainLanguage: Holding correct goes well and the regret clears. The fence that was blocking you gives way of itself, so you are no longer stuck. The strength has moved into the axle of a large cart: it carries and travels rather than batters.
lines.lifeTranslation: When the obstacle loosens, put your energy into the structures that keep things running smoothly, such as process, tooling and people. That is worth more than another demonstration of how strong you are.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your effort going into hitting the wall or into repairing the cart?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Losing the sheep with ease. No regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary explains the loss of the sheep in the open borderland by the unsuitability of the position: this kind of hard force was never meant to be held on to here. The base text keeps two older characters in this line.
lines.plainLanguage: The sheep is lost on flat open ground and there is no regret. The sheep stands for the combative, hard-charging impulse. The position was never right for forcing anything, so losing it is a release rather than a loss.
lines.lifeTranslation: Let go of a position you have been defending at real cost. It feels like a loss on the day, and quite often you are relieved later that you stopped spending yourself on it.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there something whose loss actually came as a relief?

lines.original: Six at the top: A ram strikes the fence, unable to retreat or advance. Nothing is beneficial; hardship brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that being unable to retreat or to advance comes from never having looked carefully. Holding correct through the hardship goes well, because the fault does not last long.
lines.plainLanguage: The ram's horns are caught in the fence: it cannot back out and it cannot get through, and no reading of it looks good. The way out is to accept how hard it is and work it loose slowly, so the deadlock does not become permanent.
lines.lifeTranslation: Once you are stuck, stop using the same move harder. Admit the difficulty, extend the timeline, and ease it free piece by piece. That gets you out faster than one violent pull.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you willing to admit that this is genuinely hard?

topicRules.career: Standing and resources are both high, so advancing suits you, but put the force into systems and carrying capacity. Avoid overpowering people or meeting opposition head-on, which tends to leave you wedged in a standoff.
topicRules.study: There is plenty of drive here, so pair it with a clear plan and a workable rhythm instead of long hours alone. Break a hard topic down before attacking it, rather than hitting the same wall the same way.
topicRules.romance: Your manner can easily come across as too forceful, so listen more and press less, and state your case rather than winning on sheer weight. When an argument reaches deadlock, stopping for the night usually opens more than continuing.
topicRules.family: Do not use seniority or the fact that you pay for things to settle a decision; bring it back to discussion. When the atmosphere is tight, lowering your voice and slowing down breaks the stalemate better than insisting who is right.
topicRules.relations: This is a good time to step forward and take a position, but do not take even one step outside what is proper. Before putting yourself out in front, check that the ground you are standing on actually holds.
topicRules.finance: Strong momentum makes overextension easy, so set your ceilings and your exit points, and do not use leverage to prove a judgement. This is a general principle rather than investment advice; decide according to your own circumstances and consult a qualified professional.
topicRules.wellness: It is easy to run on physical strength and overdraw it, so watch the upper limit on both training and work, and scale back at the first strain or burnout. This offers no diagnosis or treatment; see a doctor if you are unwell.
topicRules.general: The strength is at its height and the outcome depends entirely on how you use it. Correct, measured and within the rules, it moves; used to batter through, it can leave you caught between advance and retreat, where only patient work gets you out.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: aim your strength at a legitimate goal, and check where the limits sit before you act. Avoid: meeting force with force, displaying what you can do, or mistaking being able to do something for being right to do it.

hexagrams.name: Jìn · Advance
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Jin: The honored lord receives many horses as gifts and is received three times in a single day.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary glosses Jin as advance, taking the image of the sun rising above the earth: yielding movement that attaches itself to the great light and rises. Hence the judgement of a peaceful lord granted many horses and received three times in a single day. The Xiang commentary asks the noble person to make their own inner virtue shine.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Kun below, Li above: the sun coming up over the ground, the image of rising. The judgement describes the height of favour, a lord given many horses and received three times in one day, but the commentary stresses that the ascent is a yielding one. You rise by moving with the light, not by grabbing. The lines begin with advance being pushed back while correctness still holds, move on to blessing received from an elder and to broad agreement, pass a warning about the greedy rodent clinging to a post it cannot fill, and reach a line that tells you to stop counting gains and losses. The theme is that rising well matters as much as rising at all.
hexagrams.trendReason: The name means progress, and being received three times in a day depicts valued service; the commentary explicitly describes light rising above Earth. The second six has steadfast good fortune and great blessing, the third others' trust and vanished regret, and the fifth good fortune with nothing unfavorable in proceeding. Positive lines predominate. Although the fourth warns against clinging greedily to position and the top shows a narrow end, the overall trend is upward and open, hence the rating: Good. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Rise like the morning sun, and rise cleanly.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Advancing, then checked. Steadfastness brings good fortune. Without trust, remain generous; no blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that advancing and being pushed back still calls for walking correctly alone. Waiting with composure brings no fault, because no formal charge has yet been given. The base text keeps the older form of the negative.
lines.plainLanguage: You want to move forward and are held down, and you do not yet have people's trust. There is no need to rush into proving yourself. Stay unhurried and keep to your own straight path, and no fault attaches.
lines.lifeTranslation: Having proposals knocked back early in a new place is normal. Do not argue or double your visible effort; do the work in front of you correctly, because trust accumulates over time.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you in a hurry to be seen, or willing to make the work solid first?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Advancing with sorrow. Steadfastness brings good fortune. Receive this great blessing from the royal grandmother.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the great blessing received from the ancestress to being central and correct. Advance carries anxiety, yet correctness brings good fortune. The base text keeps the older locative particle.
lines.plainLanguage: You move forward carrying worry, and holding correct still goes well, with a substantial blessing arriving from an elder. The worry is not a flaw here. It is care about the situation, and it keeps you from slipping.
lines.lifeTranslation: Finishing something thoroughly while carrying a reasonable amount of concern often earns more recognition from seniors than brimming confidence does, and help tends to come from those same people.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Has your worry been making the work more careful, or just heavier?

lines.original: Six in the third place: The many give their trust. Regret vanishes.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that the will everyone endorses is a will to move upward, realised because people believe in it. With that agreement, regret disappears.
lines.plainLanguage: Everyone agrees, and the regret you were carrying dissolves. Getting this far was not done alone. It rests on people being willing to believe in the direction you are taking.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a team genuinely agrees on the goal, a lot of earlier friction resolves on its own. Getting the people who do the work alongside you matters more than convincing the level above.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do the people working with you actually agree with this direction?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Advancing like a large rat. Persistence brings danger.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary traces the danger of the greedy rodent to a position that does not suit. The creature is able at many things and accomplished at none, clinging on where it does not belong.
lines.plainLanguage: The manner of the ascent resembles that rodent: a little of everything and mastery of nothing, holding on to a post that is not properly yours. Held long enough, it becomes dangerous. The problem is not ability but the mismatch with the position.
lines.lifeTranslation: Occupying a role you cannot carry and refusing to let it go accumulates risk over time. Either build the capability to match it or move yourself to a place that fits.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Can you actually carry the position you are in right now?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Regret vanishes. Do not worry over gain and loss. Going forward brings good fortune; nothing unfavorable.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that not worrying over loss and gain means going forward brings cause for celebration. Regret has disappeared and the way ahead is open. The base text keeps the older form of the negative.
lines.plainLanguage: The regret has cleared, there is no need to weigh each gain and loss, and going forward goes smoothly. Letting go of the tally is precisely what allows this line to take a long stride.
lines.lifeTranslation: Stop itemising who got slightly more and put your attention back on the thing you are trying to finish. The road tends to widen once you do.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Has keeping score cost you progress that mattered more?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Advancing the horns. Use this only to campaign against one's own town. Danger, good fortune, and no blame; persistence brings regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that being reduced to punishing one's own town shows that the way has not yet grown bright. There is danger, yet good fortune and no fault, while holding to it brings regret. The military imagery of the original should not be read as instruction for action today.
lines.plainLanguage: You have risen to the very horn of the hexagram, and the only place left to apply force is inside your own house. Handling it this way just about passes without fault, but the scope has narrowed, and staying there for long looks small.
lines.lifeTranslation: When someone's whole effort goes into disciplining their own side while nothing opens up outside, growth has hit its ceiling. The question is which stage to move to, not how to tighten internal control further.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Lately, is your energy going outward into new ground or inward into settling scores?

topicRules.career: Visibility and opportunity are rising together, so make use of the moment when your work is being noticed. Keep the credit tied to real capability, do not sit in a post you cannot hold, and do not buy surface progress with internal politics.
topicRules.study: Progress is clear, so let steady accumulation make your ability visible on its own. When results are held down for a stretch, stay calm; filling the gaps first makes the next push steadier.
topicRules.romance: There is room for the relationship to move forward, so express yourself sincerely and gently rather than pressing for a label. Do not weigh who has given more, because fine accounting wears a relationship down.
topicRules.family: Let good changes be seen and acknowledge how family members have grown. Older relatives are often the source of help here, and asking them openly usually brings real support.
topicRules.relations: Win broad agreement before pushing ahead, because having the direction understood works better than announcing it. Avoid dabbling in everything without taking responsibility, which drains other people's trust.
topicRules.finance: Income and opportunity have room to rise, so act within your means and do not reach for what is not properly yours. This is a general principle rather than investment advice; decide according to your own circumstances and consult a qualified professional.
topicRules.wellness: Your state improves along with your progress, so keep a regular routine and let your energy continue to recover. When anxiety over gains and losses builds up, set it down. This offers no diagnosis or treatment; see a doctor if you are unwell.
topicRules.general: The sun is rising and the way up is open. Move with the momentum and let your real capability show, and it goes through. Cling to a position that does not fit, or spend your strength on internal conflict, and you narrow your own room to climb.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: show your results openly, accept the support offered, and advance steadily through a position you can properly hold. Avoid: grabbing a post before you are ready, keeping score of small gains, or obscuring what others contributed.

hexagrams.name: Míng Yí · Light Obscured
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Ming Yi: Steadfastness through hardship is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary reads light entering the earth as the meaning of the name: cultivated within and yielding without, able to bear great adversity as King Wen did. The favourable correctness through hardship means veiling your own brightness, holding the will straight through inner difficulty as Jizi did. The Xiang commentary asks the noble person governing others to appear unseeing and thereby see clearly.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Li below, Kun above: the light has sunk beneath the ground, the image of ability being suppressed. The judgement is four characters long and says only that correctness through hardship is favourable. The lines set out the whole course of being injured: a bird flying with drooping wings, three days without food, a wound to the left thigh, going deep inside the other side, Jizi feigning madness to survive, and finally a darkness that rose to heaven and then fell to earth. This hexagram does not offer a way to turn the situation around. It offers a way not to be broken by it: hide the light, keep the will straight.
hexagrams.trendReason: Light enters the Earth and is wounded, while the judgment offers only beneficial steadfastness through hardship: the circumstances themselves are difficult. Images of damage run throughout: the first nine's three days without food and the host's criticism, the second six's wounded left thigh, the fifth's Jizi concealing his light through feigned madness, and the top's fall from Heaven into Earth. Though the second's strong rescue horse brings fortune and the third's southern hunt gains the great chief, these are narrow openings within adversity, hence the rating: Bad. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Veil your light, keep your principles, and wait for the turn.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Darkening of the light in flight, wings drooping. The noble person travels, three days without food. There is somewhere to go; the host has words of criticism.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the noble person on the road does not eat as a matter of principle, not for want of food. The base text keeps the older locative particle.
lines.plainLanguage: Like a wounded bird flying with its wings hanging down, the traveller goes three days without eating and is spoken about by the host on arrival. The early stage of a setback is both lean and misunderstood, but the fasting is a choice made on principle.
lines.lifeTranslation: Just after leaving, or just after a setback, resources are thin and talk comes easily. Hold your principles, keep your mouth shut, and you get to the next stretch.
lines.reflectionPrompt: When you are misunderstood, are you defending a principle or your pride?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Darkening of the light, wounded in the left thigh. Rescue with a strong horse. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the good fortune here to yielding in accordance with what is proper. The left thigh is wounded, a strong horse carries out the rescue, and the outcome is favourable. The base text keeps the older locative particle.
lines.plainLanguage: The wound is in the left thigh, not in anything vital, and you can still walk. Calling in strong help in time is what makes this go well. The point is to draw on outside support after an injury rather than grinding on alone.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you are hurt but still standing, find reliable people or resources to cover for you quickly. It restores you faster than gritting your teeth, and it lowers the chance of a second injury.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In this setback, have you let anyone genuinely help you?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Darkening of the light in the southern hunt. Capture the great chief. Do not hasten to impose correctness.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that the intent of the southern hunt yields a great gain, while the line itself warns against haste. The hunting and military imagery of the original should not be read as instruction for action today. The base text keeps the older locative particle.
lines.plainLanguage: Hunting in the south and taking the chief figure is one of the few openings in this hexagram. The line immediately adds its own caution: even once you have found the root of it, do not try to put everything right in one pass.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you finally locate the real source of a problem, resist the urge to operate all at once. Handle it in stages so the people around it can adapt, and the change will hold.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does the root cause you found call for one fix or a staged one?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Enter the left abdomen, obtain the heart of darkening light, and go out through the gate and courtyard.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that entering the left side of the belly is a matter of grasping the intent. Having understood it, one walks out through the gate. The base text keeps the older locative particle.
lines.plainLanguage: You go into the most hidden part of it and see the real intention behind the darkness, and then you walk out. Understanding is what tells you to leave, instead of staying on and guessing.
lines.lifeTranslation: Once you finally see how a place actually works, you usually also know whether you should stay. Leaving after the information is in is a judgement, not an escape.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Have you genuinely understood this situation, or have you just had enough of it?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Jizi's darkening of the light. Steadfast correctness is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that Jizi's correctness lies in a brightness that cannot be extinguished. Jizi was a worthy minister at the end of the Shang, remembered for feigning madness to keep himself from harm.
lines.plainLanguage: Like Jizi, you conceal your light in a dark age in order to survive, and the brightness inside you is not put out. Correctness is favourable here because hiding the light is not the same as abandoning the will.
lines.lifeTranslation: In a place where you cannot speak plainly, keeping a low profile is reasonable self-protection. Just do not switch off your own judgement along with it, because you will need it when conditions change.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The light you have put away, do you still remember what it looked like?

lines.original: Six at the top: No brightness, only darkness. First ascending to Heaven, afterward entering Earth.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that rising first to heaven means shining on all quarters, and falling afterwards into the earth means the standard has been lost. The base text keeps two older characters in this line.
lines.plainLanguage: The brightness is gone and darkness sets in. It rose first like a sun lighting every quarter, and then it fell beneath the ground. The reason for that fall is not luck but the loss of the standard it was supposed to keep.
lines.lifeTranslation: Once a much-admired person or organisation stops keeping the rules it set for itself, the collapse is quicker than anyone's. The higher the position, the more often you should check whether your principles have slipped.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which principle you once insisted on have you quietly relaxed lately?

topicRules.career: Your ability may be suppressed or misread, so build a quiet record of results and avoid head-on collisions. Work out how the place actually operates before deciding whether to stay, and do not make that decision on your worst day.
topicRules.study: Results are not visible for the moment, so put your weight on fundamentals rather than performance. Under a setback, keep the study rhythm unbroken; the ability has not gone anywhere, it is just not being seen yet.
topicRules.romance: Your sincerity can be misconstrued, so explain less and let actions speak. If staying in the relationship requires hiding who you are over the long run, that is worth examining honestly.
topicRules.family: There may be pressure at home that is hard to speak about outside, so start by making a space where people can talk safely. Asking someone you trust for help when you are hurt lasts longer than carrying it alone.
topicRules.relations: Keep your edge concealed, stay out of gossip, and avoid taking sides in complicated company. Decide how close to get only after you understand what someone actually wants, and withdraw calmly if you need to.
topicRules.finance: Conditions are tight, so hold your floor, reduce risk, and protect the capital before thinking about growth. This is a general principle rather than investment advice; decide according to your own circumstances and consult a qualified professional.
topicRules.wellness: Low mood, poor sleep and a sense of being trapped are easy to fall into, so keep your eating and sleeping basic and steady, and tell someone how you are. Take a long stretch of low mood seriously. This offers no diagnosis or treatment; see a doctor if you are unwell.
topicRules.general: The light has sunk for a while, and what counts now is enduring without being bent out of shape: draw in your edge, hold your principles, keep yourself intact. Rushing to prove something or fighting it head-on usually widens the wound. The time to shine again comes when conditions turn.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: protect your important ideas and your own safety, and complete the necessary work quietly. Avoid: open confrontation in a place that is not safe, or trading away what you actually value in order to protect yourself.

hexagrams.name: Jiā Rén · The Household
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Jia Ren: A woman's steadfastness is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary describes each member holding their proper place, and calls an ordered household the starting point for an ordered world: when parent is parent, child is child and each role is filled, the way of the family is correct. The Xiang image is wind issuing from fire, with the noble person making their words carry substance and their conduct hold to a constant standard.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Li below, Xun above: wind rising out of fire, a hexagram about order and division of work inside a group. The judgement speaks in its own period's terms of the one who keeps the interior holding correct, and the core of it is that every member stands in their own place and does that part well. The lines begin by guarding against disorder from the very start, pass through the two failures of excessive severity and unchecked levity, then through prosperity and mutual affection, and end with sincerity and a bearing that commands respect through self-examination. What holds a household together is a long-standing standard and the example you set, not a burst of warmth.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's beneficial steadfastness for a woman is positive, as are great good fortune in the fourth six, good fortune in the fifth nine, and eventual good fortune at the top. Its commentary grounds order in the world in a rightly ordered family. Yet the third nine warns that unrestrained merriment among wife and children ends in regret. Favorability depends on proper limits, hence the rating: Good, rather than the highest. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Words with substance, conduct with constancy, everyone in their place.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Establish boundaries in the household. Regret vanishes.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that setting limits for the household at the outset works because the will has not yet shifted. Guarding against trouble in advance is what clears the regret.
lines.plainLanguage: You establish boundaries and rules for the household at the very beginning, and the regret dissolves. The commentary stresses that the moment to set a standard is before people's habits have drifted, because fixing it afterwards is much harder.
lines.lifeTranslation: For a new team, a new shared home or a new partnership, the cheapest approach is to state the rules in the first week rather than patching them after a conflict.
lines.reflectionPrompt: That rule you keep avoiding, does it not get harder to raise the longer you wait?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Pursue nothing independently; attend to nourishment within. Steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the good fortune here comes from yielding and modesty. Seeking no achievement outward and attending to the provisions within, one rests in the proper place and holds correct.
lines.plainLanguage: You are not pushing for outward accomplishment. You take good care of the daily business in front of you, and holding correct goes well. The value lies not in the scale of what you do but in whether your own part is genuinely done.
lines.lifeTranslation: There is no need to chase new projects or make yourself visible just now. Doing the routine, unwatched work reliably is what builds people's reasons to trust you.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The most unremarkable routine task on your list, are you doing it well enough?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Sternness among family members: regret and danger, yet good fortune. Wife and children laughing without restraint: regret in the end.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that stern voices in the household have not lost the way, while unchecked laughter among family members loses the measure of the house, which is why it ends in regret.
lines.plainLanguage: Running a household too strictly brings regret and some danger, yet it still ends well. Letting it slide into everyone laughing without limit ends in nothing but regret. Between the two, err on the side of too strict rather than losing the measure altogether.
lines.lifeTranslation: Holding people tightly makes them uncomfortable, but saying yes to everything eventually leaves no standard at all. When you have to choose, leaning towards saying it plainly is usually the safer side.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your recent leniency kindness, or avoidance of a difficult conversation?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Enriching the household. Great good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the great good fortune of a prosperous household to yielding while holding the right position. This abundance is not a matter of luck.
lines.plainLanguage: The household is well provided for and the reading is strongly favourable. The commentary points to resting in the proper place and acting in accordance with reason, which is how the abundance was built up rather than seized.
lines.lifeTranslation: In the stage where resources start to loosen up, keep doing the things that got you here. Do not change your rhythm just because there is more room.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How many of the habits that produced this abundance are you still keeping?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: The king approaches his household. Do not worry. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that when the ruler reaches the household, the result is mutual affection between all. Reaching here means moving others by virtue, which is why there is nothing to worry about.
lines.plainLanguage: The one in the senior position moves the whole household by character rather than pressure, so there is nothing to be anxious about and the line goes well. The commentary calls it mutual affection: an order people enter willingly.
lines.lifeTranslation: When things get done well without you watching, trust has been established. What that moment calls for is continuing to set the example, not increasing supervision.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does your influence rest on your authority or on people's willingness?

lines.original: Nine at the top: With sincerity and dignity, good fortune in the end.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the good fortune of a commanding presence comes from turning back on oneself. Sincerity is full and the bearing is worthy of respect, because the demand is made of oneself first.
lines.plainLanguage: You stand on sincerity and carry yourself in a way that earns respect, and in the end it goes well. The commentary is blunt about the mechanism: real authority comes from holding yourself to it first, not from raising your voice at others.
lines.lifeTranslation: The most effective way to get people to keep a rule is to keep it yourself. What you actually do carries far more weight than what you have said.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The standard you ask of others, have you met it yourself?

topicRules.career: Settle the division of work, the authority and the rules first, then talk about efficiency and expansion. Setting an example works better than tightening supervision, and do not wait for an incident before writing the rule.
topicRules.study: Build a stable routine and a fixed review cycle so the schedule is carried by structure rather than willpower. Avoid cramming only before exams, and do not let yourself defer things indefinitely.
topicRules.romance: Daily rhythm and a fair share of the chores matter here; sorting out the small practicalities is what steadies the relationship. Correct less sharply and build trust through consistent behaviour instead.
topicRules.family: This hexagram fits the subject most closely: let each member be clear about their place and their responsibility. A little too strict beats no boundary at all, and the older generation in particular should meet the standard they set.
topicRules.relations: Make the boundaries and expectations plain before deepening a friendship. Let your words carry substance, and avoid the empty courtesies and promises that accumulate into disappointment.
topicRules.finance: Set fixed rules for income and spending and keep a habit of recording them, so that abundance comes from long accumulation rather than short-term moves. This is a general principle rather than investment advice; decide according to your own circumstances and consult a qualified professional.
topicRules.wellness: Hold your condition steady through a regular routine and a settled daily rhythm, and avoid spending yourself indefinitely on housework or other people's needs. This offers no diagnosis or treatment; see a doctor if you are unwell.
topicRules.general: Everyone in their place, words and conduct held constant: set the standard early and meet it yourself first. Watch for the two distortions of letting everything slide and of managing purely by talk, and the order will last.
