hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: let people gather around a clearly stated aim, and prepare for trouble in advance. Avoid: chasing numbers and momentum alone, or leaving responsibility inside the group undivided.

hexagrams.name: Shēng · Ascending
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Sheng: Supreme success. Use this to meet a great person. Do not worry. Advancing south brings good fortune.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says the yielding rises with the season, compliant within and without, with firmness in the centre and an answering response, so there is great success. Seeing the great person needs no anxiety, for there is cause for gladness, and moving south is favourable because the will can be carried out. The Xiang image is wood growing up out of the earth, with the noble person following the grain of their own character and accumulating the small into the high and great.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Kun above, Xun below. A tree grows up out of the ground, which is the sense of Ascending: not a leap but the imperceptible daily gain of a growing thing. The judgement grants great success, tells you not to be anxious, and marks movement forward as favourable. The lines run from a rise granted by agreement, through sincerity offered simply, an advance into an undefended town, a proper ceremony on the mountain, a steady climb by steps, and finally a warning about climbing on in the dark.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's supreme success and fortune in advancing south directly affirm the direction. The first six's trusted ascent and great good fortune and the fifth's steadfast fortune in ascending steps are clearly favorable, while the third's ascent into an empty town meets no doubt in the Image. Obstacles are few. Only the top six warns of blind ascent and depletion, while the second nine requires sincerity. Favorable overall, but knowing when to stop matters at the end, hence the rating: Rather Good. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Grow like a tree: small gains, stacked, in the right direction.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Trusted ascent. Great good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that the rise granted by agreement is very favourable because the will aligns with those above. The ascent is not a matter of climbing by force.
lines.plainLanguage: From the very start the rise is agreed to by others, which is why it reads so well. The key word is consent: you go up because people are willing to let you.
lines.lifeTranslation: Having someone vouch for you at the outset is a rare tailwind. Value that trust, make the first task match their expectation, and the path widens as you go.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What exactly is the person backing you counting on?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: With sincerity, a simple spring offering is beneficial. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says plainly that this sincerity is itself a cause for gladness. The plain yue offering is fitting because the heart behind it is genuine.
lines.plainLanguage: With sincerity within, even the simplest form of expression is appropriate and there is no fault. On the way up, honesty moves people more than display.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you are trying for an opening, effort spent on genuine preparation does more than effort spent on packaging or gifts, and it makes people more willing to work with you over time.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your recent effort going into doing it well, or into looking as if you have?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Ascending into an empty town.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that ascending into an empty town leaves nothing to hesitate over: the way is entirely clear.
lines.plainLanguage: The rise is as smooth as walking into a town with no one defending it. The ease is real, but the line states a condition without pronouncing on fortune, which hints that smoothness itself deserves attention.
lines.lifeTranslation: When something moves unusually easily, ask why nobody is objecting: either you have genuinely got it right, or nobody cares about this piece of work.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your current run down to your capability, or to having no competition?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: The king makes offerings on Mount Qi. Good fortune, no blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that the king making offering at Mount Qi is a matter of according with how things are properly done. The ceremony belongs to the period rather than to present-day practice.
lines.plainLanguage: An offering made at a high place in the proper form reads well and carries no fault. Once you have risen a certain distance, working within the established forms is safer than starting your own.
lines.lifeTranslation: On entering a higher circle, understand its conventions and respect them before you talk about changing anything. Overwriting them with your own approach before you are steady tends to cost you support.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which rules of your new environment do you want to change before you understand them?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Steadfastness brings good fortune. Ascending the steps.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that holding correct and ascending the steps means the will is greatly realised. The climb proceeds one stair at a time.
lines.plainLanguage: Holding to what is correct reads well, and the rise proceeds by steps. This is the most solid stretch of ascent in the hexagram: there are stairs to follow and no need to jump.
lines.lifeTranslation: When there is a clear path of advancement in front of you, working through each level in order gets you there faster than looking for a shortcut, and leaves you harder to dislodge.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What, concretely, is the next step on the path in front of you?

lines.original: Six at the top: Blind ascent. Unceasing steadfastness is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that ascending in darkness at the top only wears things away without enriching them, so the line turns instead to the steadfastness that never rests.
lines.plainLanguage: Already at the top and still climbing blindly, which simply drains you. What is favourable now is not more height but turning your effort towards unbroken, steady correctness.
lines.lifeTranslation: Once you have reached the top of the path you are on, pushing harder upward just spins. Redirecting that energy into deepening your craft or building a new capability means more than defending a ranking.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does the next rung you are still chasing actually mean anything to you now?

topicRules.career: You are in a phase of steady ascent, so accumulate along the existing path and make each level firm before the next. When you reach the top of this particular route, start thinking early about deepening your craft or opening a new field.
topicRules.study: Small daily accumulation suits this best, like a tree gaining height without visible change. Lay the foundation before raising the difficulty; it lasts longer than one attempt at material well above your level.
topicRules.romance: Let warmth build through sincerity and let the relationship move a stage at a time, without skipping the parts that need living through. What you feel is best shown plainly rather than proved through expense.
topicRules.family: Work with the existing rhythm and respect the conventions your elders have set before proposing changes. Improvement between relatives usually comes from small things repeated, not from one decisive conversation.
topicRules.relations: Someone is willing to introduce and vouch for you, so value it and answer it with real work. Entering a new circle, learn the rules and respect the existing order before putting your own ideas forward.
topicRules.finance: Small, regular accumulation suits this, with the emphasis on long compounding rather than a short jump. Even in a good run, confirm the results are genuine and not just unremarked risk. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: Build routines and movement you can sustain, starting small and increasing gradually. If you notice you are pushing on out of habit with no sense of direction, take it seriously; consult a qualified professional, as this is not medical advice.
topicRules.general: The direction is a steady rise: follow the grain of your character, stack the small into the high, and with support around you and little resistance, moving forward suits. Note that once you are high, climbing blindly only drains you without adding anything.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: accumulate through small tasks you can finish, accept guidance, and rise steadily. Avoid: skipping grades for speed, fixating on position, or forgetting when to stop once you are high.

hexagrams.name: Kùn · Confinement
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Kun: Success. Steadfastness brings the great person good fortune and no blame. Words are not believed.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says Confinement is firmness covered over: meeting danger yet staying agreeable, being confined without losing your own ground, which is what allows success and is perhaps only within reach of the noble person. Words not being believed comes from prizing talk, which only runs to a dead end. The Xiang image is a marsh with no water in it, and the noble person who will surrender life itself to carry out the will.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Dui above, Kan below. The marsh has no water: resources are exhausted and movement in every direction is blocked. What matters in Confinement is not whether you can escape but whether you hold on to yourself while you are held. The judgement says that words are not believed, so explaining yourself only makes the position more awkward. The lines run from a stump in a dark valley through confinement amid food and drink with help on its way, a place with injury ahead and thorns behind, a slow arrival held up by a fine carriage, a maiming at the top that slowly loosens, and finally entangling vines that still allow a forward step.
hexagrams.trendReason: The name means deprivation; the Judgment says the firm is covered, and the Image's lake without water depicts exhausted resources. The third six's stone, thorns, and absent wife explicitly bring misfortune. The first's three years unseen depicts prolonged darkness; the fifth includes mutilation. The judgment adds that words are not believed, leaving little room even to explain. Although it offers success, steadfast good fortune and no blame for the great person, and the top six fortune in advancing, these are exits for those preserving integrity under pressure, not favorable circumstances themselves, hence the rating: Unfavorable. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Held fast, keep your ground and let actions speak.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Buttocks oppressed by a tree stump. Entering a dark valley, unseen for three years.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that entering the dark valley is a matter of obscurity itself: the surroundings cannot be seen clearly, so the light stays out of reach for a long stretch.
lines.plainLanguage: Stuck on a bare stump, unable to move, then down into a deep dark valley with no one in sight for a long time. This is the floor of Confinement: not only blocked, but unable to see which way anything lies.
lines.lifeTranslation: In a low patch with no clear direction, hold off on big decisions. Keep the basic rhythm of your days going and choose a route once you can see a little further; that usually beats moving in the dark.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In this low patch, what is the one thing you can still see clearly?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Oppressed amid wine and food. Crimson ceremonial sashes are coming. Sacrificial offerings are beneficial. Advancing brings misfortune, but no blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says there is still cause for gladness within this confinement because the centre is held. The scarlet knee-covers stand for a person of rank, so help is approaching and stillness suits better than haste.
lines.plainLanguage: Confined amid food and drink, comfortable-looking but stalled, with the scarlet robes on their way: help is in transit. Sincere observance suits, a rushed campaign does not, and holding your place carries no fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: When a chance is approaching but not yet in hand, the worst move is to rush out and prove yourself. Finish the work in front of you and stay sincere while the other side closes the distance.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does the opportunity you are waiting on need action from you now, or stillness?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Oppressed by stone, resting on thorns. Entering the palace, not seeing one's wife. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes leaning on thorns to the yielding riding on the firm, and calls returning home to find no wife inauspicious. A boulder blocks the way forward and thorns lie behind.
lines.plainLanguage: A boulder blocks the advance, thorns lie underfoot on the retreat, and the person closest to you is not there when you get home. This is the most severe line in the hexagram: both directions injure, and the way back is gone too.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you hit a wall outside and the support at home has also gone, the thing to do is stop pushing anything forward and repair the relationships still with you. Read this as a description of the situation, not a prediction.
lines.reflectionPrompt: While you have been pushing outward, who at home has quietly stepped back?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Coming slowly, oppressed by a metal carriage. Regret, but completion.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the slow arrival comes from a will directed below, and that although the position is unsuitable there is still someone in support, so an outcome does come.
lines.plainLanguage: Movement is slow and held up by a fine metal carriage: the obstacle is not scarcity but encumbrance and hesitation. The process carries some embarrassment, yet it does reach an end.
lines.lifeTranslation: Being unable to help the person you want to help, or reach the place you want to reach, is usually the weight of what you cannot bring yourself to put down. Slower is acceptable if the direction is right.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is what stops you an obstacle outside, or something you will not set down?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Nose and feet cut off, oppressed by red ceremonial sashes. Gradually release comes. Sacrifice is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the maiming shows a will not yet realised, the gradual easing comes from being centred and upright, and the offering brings blessing. The imagery of mutilating punishment belongs to the period and is not a present-day instruction.
lines.plainLanguage: Injured while holding high office, with even the robes of rank becoming a constraint. Yet by staying centred and straight the bind slowly loosens, and a sincere, respectful attitude suits the moment best.
lines.lifeTranslation: When someone in a senior position gets caught, the damage runs deeper and is harder to talk about. Do not expect to reverse it in one move; stay straight, work the knots loose one at a time, and time works with you.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is part of what binds you now the standing you worked to earn?

lines.original: Six at the top: Oppressed by vines and instability. Saying movement brings regret. Recognizing regret, advancing brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that being bound by creepers shows a position that is not fitting, and that feeling the regret of movement and actually forming that regret makes going forward a favourable act.
lines.plainLanguage: Wrapped in creeping vines and unable to stand steady, you think that any move will be regretted. Yet it is precisely that regret that makes you willing to change, and being willing to go forward reads well.
lines.lifeTranslation: The end of a confined stretch is often a tangle of small entanglements. Admitting the old approach was flawed and setting off in a revised direction beats standing still worrying about which step is wrong.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which move you keep fearing to get wrong is costing you more by not being made?

topicRules.career: Resources and room are visibly tight, so hold your core responsibilities and open no new fronts. Explanations and declarations are unlikely to be believed now; finished work argues better than words do.
topicRules.study: You may hit a stretch where nothing goes in however hard you work, so shrink the target to the smallest unit you can complete daily. Rather than doubting your aptitude, keep the rhythm unbroken until the state returns.
topicRules.romance: Communication is easily misread and more talk makes it stiffer, so lower the volume of conversation and show care through action. If even the closest person has grown distant, repair matters more than establishing who was right.
topicRules.family: Money and feeling may both be under strain at once, so put limited energy into each other's basic needs. Avoid reopening old grievances at the tightest moment; it only makes the position harder.
topicRules.relations: Trust is running low and your explanations get discounted, so explain less and offer actions that can be checked. Notice who is willing to reach out in this period, and remember it.
topicRules.finance: This is a tight phase, so protect cash and essential spending first and avoid decisions aimed at winning losses back. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: The pressure may have been running for some time, so hold the floor on sleep and food and reach out to someone you trust. If hopelessness persists or feelings become hard to bear, take it seriously and consult a qualified professional; this is not medical advice.
topicRules.general: The direction is confinement: resources are dry, movement is blocked, argument does not land, and the point is not to lose your own ground while you are held. Keep your limits and your reserves; the opening usually arrives as a slow loosening.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: hold the limits that matter, conserve your strength, and let actions stand in for argument. Avoid: repeated complaint, promises made under pressure, or trading away a principle to get out.

hexagrams.name: Jǐng · The Well
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Jing: The town may move, but the well does not. Neither loss nor gain; people come and go to the well. Almost reaching, yet not having drawn up the water. Breaking the jar brings misfortune.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says that entering the water and drawing it up is the Well, and that the well nourishes without exhausting itself. The town may be moved while the well is not, which rests on firmness held in the centre; water almost drawn but with the rope not yet complete has achieved nothing; and a broken jar is why the ending is unfavourable. The Xiang image is water above wood, with the noble person encouraging the people and urging them to help one another.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Kan above, Xun below. Water is lifted up through the wooden frame, which is the Well. Its nature is to stay put and remain available: the village can move while the well does not, it neither gains nor loses, and everyone who comes and goes may draw from it. The heaviest line of the judgement is the rope left short and the jar broken at the last moment. The lines run from mud at the bottom that nobody drinks, a leaking pot, a cleaned well that goes unused, a wall relined, cold clear water fit to drink, and finally a well left uncovered for all.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment ends with the broken jar's misfortune, and its commentary says no achievement yet, warning of failure at the final step. The first six's muddy abandoned well, second nine's leaking jar, and third's clean but unused well show neglect, damaged equipment, and unused talent. Yet the fifth's clear cold water and the top's uncovered trustworthy well with supreme good fortune give an excellent ending, while the fourth affirms repair without blame. Neglect gives way to maintenance and eventual good fortune; outcomes depend on sustained care, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: What nourishes others must be maintained, and finished to the last pull.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Muddy well, not drunk from. No creatures at the old well.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary explains the undrinkable mud by the lowest position, and says that the old well without birds is what the times have set aside.
lines.plainLanguage: The bottom of the well is all silt and the water cannot be drunk; an old well long abandoned no longer even draws birds. What goes unused and unmaintained is set aside in time.
lines.lifeTranslation: A skill you have not used for years, or a relationship you have not tended, slowly loses its value. Either clean it out properly so it works again, or admit honestly that it has passed.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which of your abilities has gone unused for a long time?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Shooting small fish in the well's hollow. The jar is worn and leaks.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that shooting minnows in the well hollow shows there is no matching support. The earthenware pot for drawing water is cracked and leaks.
lines.plainLanguage: There is water in the well, but it is only used to catch a few small fish, and the jar leaks besides. The resource is still there; it is being spent in the wrong place and cannot be held, which comes to the same as waste.
lines.lifeTranslation: The capability is not the problem. The problem is that it is aimed at something too small and has no supporting setup. Patch the part that leaks before you redouble your effort, then point it somewhere worth it.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which of your efforts is currently being poured into a leaking container?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: The well is cleaned but unused, grieving my heart. It can be drawn from. If the king is clear-sighted, all share its blessing.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary calls the cleaned well that goes undrunk a cause for sorrow, and says that if the king is discerning and draws from it, both above and below receive the blessing.
lines.plainLanguage: The well has been cleaned and the water is fit to drink, yet nobody comes to draw it, which is painful to watch. The well was always usable; it only needs someone above with clear enough sight, and then everyone benefits.
lines.lifeTranslation: Being ready and still unseen is a wearing stage. Keeping the water clean and staying available gets you further towards the person who understands than announcing how good you are.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Does the right person know about the thing you have already prepared?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Lining the well. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary states the point directly: lining the well with brick is repairing the well, and maintenance is itself legitimate work.
lines.plainLanguage: The shaft is relined and there is no fault. This line says nothing about output and everything about repair: supply pauses now so that the well can supply for a long time afterwards.
lines.lifeTranslation: Spending a stretch doing nothing but tidying, reinforcing and rebuilding the base shows no visible result while it lasts, and it is what lets everything afterwards run. There is no need to be anxious about it.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which foundation should you stop and repair that the schedule keeps pushing past?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: A clear well. Its cold spring water is drunk.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the drinkable cold spring to being centred and correct, which is why the water is pure and fit for use.
lines.plainLanguage: The water is clear and cold and genuinely good to drink. After the cleaning and the relining, the well finally does what it is for: nourishing without running dry.
lines.lifeTranslation: A capability you have maintained for a long time has reached the point of steady output. The best thing now is to keep supplying it and keep the quality up, rather than swapping it for something else.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What have you already made good enough that it only needs to continue?

lines.original: Six at the top: Water drawn from the well; do not cover it. With sincerity, supreme good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that the great good fortune at the top is a great completion. The well is drawn from and left uncovered, and sincerity is kept.
lines.plainLanguage: Once the water is up, the mouth is not covered over, so anyone may draw from it, and sincerity is maintained. It reads very well. A well is valuable for being open, not for being kept private.
lines.lifeTranslation: Opening the experience and resource you have accumulated to those who need it takes nothing from you; it carries the value further and returns for longer.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What experience could you share that you have been keeping to yourself?

topicRules.career: This suits going back to repair systems, process and tooling, the unglamorous base that lets capability supply steadily. Work already in flight should be carried through to the final handover rather than released at the finish.
topicRules.study: Clean out the old foundations before stacking anything new on top, and schedule time for material you have not revised in a long while. The temptation to drop something is strongest near the end, so finish that last stretch.
topicRules.romance: What matters here is daily maintenance rather than novelty, and the understanding built over years is the well that does not move when circumstances do. Say what you feel; preparing and never expressing it is how people miss each other.
topicRules.family: This suits repairing long-neglected patterns and the practical base of the household, and whoever puts in that time carries the hardest and most important part. Resources are best shared openly rather than held by one person.
topicRules.relations: What you have accumulated can nourish the people around you, and sharing it openly is worth more than keeping it back. If you feel ready but unnoticed, let the right person know while keeping your own quality up.
topicRules.finance: Check for outgoings that leak continuously; patching the leaking container is more practical than earning a little more. A stable long-term arrangement beats frequent switching. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: Put rest, food and movement back in order as the basics that let the body supply over the long run. Seeing no result during a recovery period is normal and not a reason to increase the load. If something concerns you, consult a qualified professional; this is not medical advice.
topicRules.general: The direction is the Well: value comes from long maintenance and steady supply, and clarity arrives only after cleaning and repair. Watch the last step, where effort is most often wasted, and keep the result open rather than held privately.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: repair what supplies you and confirm the final stretch actually delivers the result. Avoid: changing only the surface, or easing off once the work is nearly complete.

hexagrams.name: Gé · Change
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Ge: On the si day, trust arrives. Supreme success. Steadfast correctness is beneficial. Regret vanishes.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary describes water and fire putting each other out, two daughters under one roof whose wills do not meet: a tension that cannot hold, which is what change means. Trust arrives only on the appointed day, because a change has to be believed before it stands. The Xiang image is fire inside the lake, and the noble person orders the calendar and makes the seasons clear.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Dui above, Li below. Fire sits inside the lake and the two cannot share the space, so something has to give. Change here means replacing the old rather than patching it: the existing way no longer carries the weight. The key phrase in the judgement is that trust comes on the appointed day. Announcing a change does not make people follow it. The timing has to ripen and the trust has to be built first. The lines run from binding yourself still at the start, through talking a proposal through until it holds, to a transformation so visible it needs no explanation.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment combines four positive terms—origination, success, beneficial steadfastness, and vanished regret—and the commentary strongly affirms Tang and Wu's revolutions as responding to Heaven and people. The fourth nine's sincere change of mandate and the fifth's tiger-like transformation with trust even before divination are powerful favorable lines. Yet risks are explicit: the third warns against rash advance, the top against continuing to push after change, and the first demands restraint at the outset. Conditions and legitimacy may suffice, but timing and trust strongly determine success, hence the rating: Rather Good, rather than the best. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Change what must change, but earn trust before you move.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Bound fast with yellow oxhide.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that being bound with yellow oxhide means there is nothing to be done yet. At the lowest position and the first moment of change, self-restraint is the whole of the task.
lines.plainLanguage: You are strapped tight with tough oxhide. Change has only just begun, your position is the lowest and your leverage the least. What this stage asks is not action but holding yourself still.
lines.lifeTranslation: The moment you first see what is wrong is the moment you most want to announce it everywhere. Keep it in, stay steady, and speak when you carry enough weight for it to land.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do you carry enough weight yet to change the thing you are itching to change?

lines.original: Six in the second place: On the si day, make the change. Advancing brings good fortune and no blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that changing on the appointed day means the action itself carries something good. Timing and legitimacy have lined up, so going forward is favourable and no fault follows.
lines.plainLanguage: You act only when the day has come, and going forward is favourable with no fault. The same move a step early is recklessness and a step late is a missed chance. It holds only on the day it fits.
lines.lifeTranslation: A change you have put off for a long time is usually waiting for the moment when not changing costs more. Once that moment arrives, say the thing and make the swap. Hesitating closes the gap that finally opened.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Has the right moment you are waiting for already arrived?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Advancing brings misfortune; steadfastness brings danger. When talk of change is affirmed three times, there is trust.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary asks where else there is to go once the case for change has been through three rounds. The argument has been aired fully; what remains is to settle it and act, not to press further forward.
lines.plainLanguage: Forcing your way forward brings danger, and even holding correct carries risk. But if the case has been debated three times over and consensus has formed, you have a foundation of good faith. Pushing does not work here. Talking it through does.
lines.lifeTranslation: When your proposal gets challenged, the worst response is to treat the objection as an obstacle and push harder. Take the same case to three different rooms, absorb the objections, revise. Resistance afterwards is far smaller.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How many times has your proposal genuinely been argued through?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Regret vanishes. With sincerity, change the mandate. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the good fortune of changing the mandate rests on the will being trusted. Good faith has to be established first; only then does altering the old order hold.
lines.plainLanguage: Regret disappears. Carrying trust you have already built, you alter the established rules, and the line reads well. What lets you change the mandate is not the authority itself but other people believing in your intent.
lines.lifeTranslation: The people who actually manage to replace an old rule are usually the ones who first convinced everyone they were not doing it for themselves. With trust in place, a large move is accepted. Without it, even a small adjustment looks like a grab for power.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Who do the people around you believe this change is for?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: The great person transforms like a tiger. Trust exists before divination.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the great person changes like a tiger because the markings are brilliant. The transformation has become so plainly visible that no divination is needed for people to trust it.
lines.plainLanguage: The person at the centre is renewed the way a tiger renews its coat, markings sharp and unmistakable, and trust is there before anyone consults the oracle. Change made thoroughly enough speaks for itself.
lines.lifeTranslation: When someone's transformation is large enough to be seen at a glance, they no longer have to spend energy explaining that they have changed. Rather than repeating your resolve, make the change clear enough that no statement is required.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Can anyone actually see the change you keep describing?

lines.original: Six at the top: The noble person transforms like a leopard; the petty person changes the face. Advancing brings misfortune; remaining steadfast brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the noble person changes like a leopard, with fine dense markings, while the small person changes only the face, going along with whoever is above. The second is compliance, not inward change.
lines.plainLanguage: At the closing stage of change, some renew themselves thoroughly while others merely adjust their expression and follow the crowd. Pressing further forward brings danger; settling down and holding correct is favourable.
lines.lifeTranslation: As a reform winds down, some people have genuinely changed their minds and others have simply stopped objecting. You do not need everyone to declare agreement. Bedding the new arrangement into ordinary routine does more than pushing harder.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Has this change reached the point where it should be brought to a close?

topicRules.career: The existing structure or method is visibly tiring, so this is a reasonable time to put a change on the table. Build consensus and trust before you start; forcing it through while people are unconvinced tends to stall.
topicRules.study: Review your study method and timetable and replace the parts that have long stopped working. Make one thorough change and give it weeks to prove itself rather than swapping systems every week.
topicRules.romance: This suits addressing a pattern you have both avoided naming, but timing matters more than courage. Raise it when you are both calm, and change your own behaviour rather than asking the other person to become someone else.
topicRules.family: Friction between old family rules and newer ways of doing things may surface. Explain the reasoning rather than announcing the decision; understanding is accepted far more easily than abolition.
topicRules.relations: Redefine arrangements that no longer fit, clearly but without heat. Some people follow sincerely and others only comply for now, and you do not need to force agreement from everyone.
topicRules.finance: Review and replace habits or fixed outgoings that have long stopped serving you, and confirm the replacement works before you switch. This is a general principle and not investment advice; consult a qualified professional about your own situation.
topicRules.wellness: This suits starting a change to sleep, diet or exercise, though a gradual scale works better. A period of change carries its own load, so leave yourself room to adapt and adjust rather than grind on. This is not medical diagnosis or treatment advice; see a doctor if you feel unwell.
topicRules.general: The direction is change: the old structure no longer holds and replacing it is the right road, but the moment has to be ripe and the trust in place. Watch both ends, rushing at the start and overreaching at the finish, and count it done only when the new way has become ordinary.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: establish the reasons and the trust first, then replace the old arrangement in stages. Avoid: overturning everything before the timing is clear, or changing the label while the problem stays.

hexagrams.name: Dǐng · The Cauldron
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Ding: Supreme good fortune. Success.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary reads the cauldron as an image: wood fed into fire is cooking. The sage cooks to make offering to heaven, and cooks on a larger scale to nourish the worthy. Yielding while the senses stay sharp, rising to the upper place and meeting the firm from the centre, brings great success. The Xiang image is fire above wood, and the noble person makes the position correct and the charge secure.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Li above, Xun below. Fire burns above the wood: this is the cooking vessel. The cauldron is the thing that bears weight and feeds people, turning raw into cooked and private resource into public nourishment. The judgement is only four characters long and pitched extremely high. The lines run from a cauldron tipped over so the old filth can be poured out, through solid contents and strong fittings, to jade carrying-bars at the top. In the middle sits the heaviest warning in the hexagram: legs that snap under a load beyond them spill everything they were carrying.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's supreme good fortune and success rank among the text's strongest verdicts, echoed by the commentary's great success in nourishing sages and worthy people. The fifth six's beneficial steadfastness and top nine's great fortune with nothing unfavorable give an excellent ending; the second and third nines also end positively. The fourth nine lowers the assessment: broken cauldron legs spill the duke's food, bringing misfortune, and the Image questions trust. This points to serious consequences when the entrusted person lacks the capacity for the role. An excellent structure has one severe failure point, hence the rating: Rather Good rather than the best. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Nourish others, but first be able to carry the weight.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: The cauldron overturns its legs. Removing what is spoiled is beneficial. Taking a concubine for her son brings no blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says an overturned cauldron is not contrary to sense, and that pouring out what is foul is favourable because it makes room for what is valuable.
lines.plainLanguage: The cauldron is tipped with its feet in the air. It looks like disorder, yet it is exactly what empties the old residue, and that makes it favourable. Gain arrives through an irregular route, and there is no fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: An embarrassing upset is sometimes the only chance to tip out years of accumulated grime. Rather than rushing to set the pot upright and refill it as before, clean it properly while it is empty.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What did your recent upset tip out that should have gone long ago?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: The cauldron has substance. My rival has an affliction and cannot approach me. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that a cauldron with substance calls for care about where you go, and that a rival hindered by affliction leaves nothing to reproach in the end.
lines.plainLanguage: The cauldron holds something solid. The side opposed to you is occupied by its own troubles and cannot come near, so the line reads well. When you actually hold something of substance, the direction you take matters more, not less.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you have real results in hand and your rivals are too busy to bother you, that quiet is exactly when people pick the wrong direction. Use the undisturbed stretch to think the direction through rather than to expand fast.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Nobody is blocking you right now, so where are you putting your effort?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: The cauldron's handles change, obstructing its movement. Pheasant fat goes uneaten. Rain is coming; regret diminishes. Good fortune in the end.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the altered handles have lost their proper function. The handles exist so the carrying-bar can pass through; once they no longer fit, the whole cauldron is immovable.
lines.plainLanguage: The handles have changed shape, the bar no longer passes through, and the cauldron cannot be moved. Rich pheasant meat sits inside and cannot be eaten. Only when the rain comes do the loss and regret ease, and the end is favourable.
lines.lifeTranslation: Having the ability and the results yet being stuck because one connection does not fit is a wearing position. Hurry does not help here. Repair the connection, wait for outside conditions to loosen, and what you built is still yours.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the thing that is stuck your capability, or just the connection?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: The cauldron's legs break, spilling the duke's food and soiling its form. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary ends with a question: the duke's meal is spilled, so what becomes of the trust? It points at responsibility when a charge is given to the wrong hands or a load exceeds the person bearing it.
lines.plainLanguage: The cauldron's leg breaks and the lord's food is spilled, leaving the bearer drenched and disgraced. When the weight taken on exceeds what you can support, the task is not the only thing ruined; the trust goes with it.
lines.lifeTranslation: Take on something clearly beyond you and the loss when it fails is not only that project but other people's read on your judgement. Saying that you cannot carry it is far more dignified than straining until the pot goes over.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is something on your plate already heavier than you can carry?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: The cauldron has yellow handles and metal carrying rings. Steadfast correctness is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says yellow handles mean holding the centre as the real substance. Yellow is the colour of the mean, and the metal bar is the valuable, solid crosspiece.
lines.plainLanguage: The cauldron is fitted with yellow handles and a metal carrying-bar, the connection correct and firm, and holding steady is favourable. What lets a cauldron do its work is not what has been put inside but whether it can be lifted cleanly.
lines.lifeTranslation: For someone in a pivotal position, the greatest value often lies in making sure other people's work gets caught and carried onward. Being a good connection matters more than competing to be the ingredient.
lines.reflectionPrompt: On your team, are you the contents of the pot or the bar that lifts it?

lines.original: Nine at the top: The cauldron has jade carrying rings. Great good fortune; nothing unfavorable.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the jade bar at the top shows the firm and the yielding regulating each other. Jade is both hard and warm, the very image of the two in proportion.
lines.plainLanguage: The cauldron has a bar of jade at the highest place, greatly favourable with nothing that does not suit. Jade is hard and warm at once: at the top position, strength and softness have been tuned to each other.
lines.lifeTranslation: The people who reach the top and still carry others with them are rarely the hardest ones. They are the ones who can hold firm and also give way. Insist where it counts, yield where it counts, and the force lands correctly.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Right now, which do you have more of, your firmness or your give?

topicRules.career: This suits turning existing capability into results that feed the team, and taking on a more important position. Weigh your own supports before accepting; a charge beyond your load costs you trust as well as the task.
topicRules.study: The work here is cooking the raw: integrating scattered knowledge into a usable system. Rather than gathering more material, digest what you have until you could teach it to someone else.
topicRules.romance: This suits moving a relationship from ambiguity to genuine mutual care, with firmness and softness in proportion. Willingness to give is good, but do not promise care you cannot actually provide.
topicRules.family: You may be the one carrying the household or the income, so check that your own legs are steady. Sharing the weight with other members serves the family better than straining alone until the pot goes over.
topicRules.relations: This suits acting as the joint through which resources and people connect smoothly; a clean connection is worth more than standing out. Be careful not to accept a coordinating role out of proportion to your standing.
topicRules.finance: This suits taking stock of resources and directing them where they genuinely nourish, after checking you could absorb the worst case. This is a general principle and not investment advice; consult a qualified professional about your own situation.
topicRules.wellness: Your physical capacity is the cauldron's leg, and a long overload tends to break it in one go. Eat regularly, sleep properly, and treat recovery as necessary input rather than wasted time. This is not medical diagnosis or treatment advice; see a doctor if you feel unwell.
topicRules.general: The direction is bearing and nourishing: turning resources into something that sustains others, and the shape of it is good. The main risk is a mismatch between capability and position, so working within your means is what keeps this favourable.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: secure the structure that bears the load and set out who does what before you widen the responsibility. Avoid: accepting a heavy charge on an unsteady base, or gathering resources you then fail to use well.

hexagrams.name: Zhèn · Shock
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Zhen: Success. Shock comes with trembling, then laughter and speech. Thunder startles a hundred li, yet the ritual spoon and fragrant wine are not lost.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says thunder brings success: the shock arrives and leaves you apprehensive, and that very caution brings good fortune. Laughter afterwards is possible because a standard has been set inside. Thunder startles for a hundred miles, alarming the distant and frightening the near, and whoever stands firm in it can guard the ancestral hall. The Xiang image is thunder upon thunder, and the noble person keeps a wary heart and examines himself.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Zhen above, Zhen below. Thunder rolls in wave after wave: this is shock. What it describes is sudden impact, a thing landing with no warning, leaving you at a loss before you steady. The strongest image in the judgement is thunder shaking a hundred miles while the officiant's ladle and wine stay unspilled: holding to your own task in the middle of the noise. The lines run from fright followed by laughter, through goods lost and recovered without chasing, to a neighbour struck while you are spared. Shock cannot be avoided; whether you stay standing is the point.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment opens with success, and its commentary treats fear as a cause of blessing. The first nine has good fortune, the second six predicts recovery in seven days without pursuit, the fifth preserves its undertaking without loss, and the top ends with no blame. Yet adverse elements are dense: the second has real loss of wealth, the fourth is stuck in mud without illumination, and the top explicitly warns of misfortune in advancing amid trembling and fearful glances. Gain and loss interweave, depending on self-possession, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Hold your ladle steady; fright well used becomes a rule.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Shock comes with trembling; afterward laughter and speech. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the apprehension when thunder arrives is what brings good fortune, and that the laughter afterwards comes from a standard now being in place.
lines.plainLanguage: Thunder breaks suddenly overhead. First comes fright, then, afterwards, ordinary talk and laughter, and the line reads well. Being afraid is not the failure. Setting yourself a rule because of the fright is the gain.
lines.lifeTranslation: After a scare, some people are left only with the fear while others build a habit of preparation out of it. The difference is whether the lesson was written down as a rule you now keep.
lines.reflectionPrompt: After the last time you were badly startled, what rule did you set yourself?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Shock comes with danger; great loss of valuables. Ascend the nine hills. Do not pursue; regain them in seven days.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the danger when thunder arrives to a yielding line riding above a firm one. The position itself is unsteady, so loss comes first and recovery after.
lines.plainLanguage: The shock arrives with danger and heavy loss of goods, so you climb the high ground for safety. Do not go after what was lost; after seven days it returns of itself. Some losses get worse when chased.
lines.lifeTranslation: When the impact hits, secure yourself first and let the money and the pride sit for a while. Pull back to safe ground and ride it out, and much of it comes back on its own. Rushing to rescue it puts you in the wreck too.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is what you are chasing worth the risk you are taking to get it back?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Shock leaves one dazed. Acting through shock brings no calamity.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the unsteadiness in the shock comes from the position being unsuitable. Precisely because the place does not fit, staying put feels worse, and moving with the shock avoids calamity.
lines.plainLanguage: You are shaken and cannot gather yourself, yet moving along with the shock brings no misfortune. Standing and trembling in a position that does not suit you is worse than shifting out of it.
lines.lifeTranslation: If something keeps you permanently tense, the problem may not be that you lack courage but that the position was never right for you. Moving is often safer than enduring.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your unease coming from the situation, or from the position you occupy in it?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Shock sinks into mud.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the shock sinking into mud has not yet come to light. A firm line caught between yielding ones cannot move, and its force finds no outlet.
lines.plainLanguage: After the shock you sink into mud. The line is four characters with no verdict attached, yet it is the most stalled in the hexagram: the strength is there and cannot be applied, and struggling drives you deeper.
lines.lifeTranslation: A stretch after an impact where nothing you do gains traction is normal. Trying to prove you are still capable usually sinks you further. Stop and get your foot out first.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are you moving forward, or treading yourself deeper in the same spot?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Shock comes and goes with danger. Consider how to avoid loss; there is work to do.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says danger comes and goes because the conduct itself sits in peril, yet the business at hand holds to the centre, so there is no great loss.
lines.plainLanguage: The shock brings danger in both directions, yet there is no serious loss, and the work that has to be done still has to be done. When everything around you is shaking, holding the middle and finishing your own tasks keeps you steady.
lines.lifeTranslation: In an unstable period every direction carries risk, and what helps most is turning up as usual and delivering what you owe. Ordinary order is itself a form of protection.
lines.reflectionPrompt: When things are chaotic, which task should you carry out as normal regardless?

lines.original: Six at the top: Shaking with shock, looking fearfully about. Advancing brings misfortune. Shock reaches the neighbor rather than oneself: no blame. Marriage brings criticism.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the scattered steps show the centre not yet attained, and that danger without fault comes from taking warning when a neighbour is struck.
lines.plainLanguage: You are so shaken your steps scatter and your eyes dart about, and going forward brings danger. The thunder falls not on you but on your neighbour, so there is no fault, though those close to you have some complaint.
lines.lifeTranslation: When someone else is hit first, you can be relieved it was not you, or you can treat it as an early warning delivered free. People who pull back and adjust because of it are often told they are overreacting, and it is worth expecting that.
lines.reflectionPrompt: When trouble lands near you, do you treat it as a warning or as someone else's episode?

topicRules.career: Sudden change or bad news may arrive, so steady the work directly in front of you before responding. When something goes wrong for someone else, treat it as an early warning and check whether the same gap exists in your own setup.
topicRules.study: Your rhythm is easily broken by unexpected events, and exam or assessment pressure may rise noticeably. Turn the fright into a fixed revision habit rather than leaving only the anxiety behind.
topicRules.romance: A sudden event may unsettle things and feelings may swing more than usual. Do not make major decisions in the moment of impact; talk once you have steadied, since overreaction damages the relationship.
topicRules.family: Unexpected news may have to be absorbed together, so someone needs to stay calm and keep daily life running. Children and older relatives feel shocks most, and a steady routine is the best reassurance available.
topicRules.relations: Someone around you may run into trouble first, which gives you a warning. Acting early gets you called over-anxious, and there is no need to argue about it; just make your own preparations.
topicRules.finance: Unexpected losses or expenses may appear, so secure your cash flow and safety buffer first and do not rush to recover short-term losses. This is a general principle and not investment advice; consult a qualified professional about your own situation.
topicRules.wellness: Startle responses, poor sleep and anxiety are more likely, so reduce stimulation and keep a regular routine. If palpitations or panic keep recurring and affect daily life, take it seriously. This is not medical diagnosis or treatment advice; see a doctor if you feel unwell.
topicRules.general: The direction is shock: the impact arrives suddenly, it cannot be dodged, but you can stay standing. Secure safety, keep ordinary order, and turn this fright into a rule you keep afterwards; that is what this hexagram actually offers.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: after the shock, confirm safety and priorities before you resume moving. Avoid: spreading alarm in the confusion, or looking calm while skipping the preparations that matter.

hexagrams.name: Gèn · Stilling
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Gen: Keeping the back still, not grasping the body. Walking in the courtyard, not seeing the people. No blame.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary glosses Gen as stopping: stop when it is time to stop, move when it is time to move, and when neither motion nor stillness misses its moment, the way is bright. To still it is to stop it in its proper place. Upper and lower stand opposed and do not engage, hence not perceiving the body and walking the courtyard without seeing anyone, and no fault. The Xiang image is mountain doubled, and the noble person keeps his thoughts within his own position.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Gen above, Gen below. Two mountains stand one on the other: this is stopping. Gen is not about being motionless but about stopping in the right place, within what is properly yours. The judgement stills the attention at the back, where you cannot see yourself, so your own appetites do not pull you, and you cross the courtyard untouched by other people's affairs. The lines climb the body from the toes to the calves, the waist, the trunk and the jaw, ending in a stopping so settled it is no longer effort. Knowing where to stop matters as much as knowing how to advance.
hexagrams.trendReason: None of the six lines declares misfortune. The first six gives no blame and beneficial lasting steadfastness, the fourth no blame, the fifth vanished regret, and the top nine generous stillness with fortune. Its Image affirms a substantial ending, and the Judgment praises movement and rest timed rightly as a bright way. Difficulties concern discomfort in the process rather than poor results: the second's unhappy heart reflects enforced stopping, and the third's torn back and danger scorching the heart reflect abrupt restraint. A stable ending requires self-restraint through a constrained process, hence the rating: Rather Good rather than the best. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Stop where stopping belongs, and think within your own ground.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Keeping the toes still. No blame. Lasting steadfastness is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says stilling the toes means correctness has not yet been lost. Halting at the very first step, before the motion happens, means no fault has yet formed.
lines.plainLanguage: You stop at the toes, halting before the step is taken, so there is no fault, and long-term steadiness is favourable. The easiest moment to stop is the moment before you have started walking.
lines.lifeTranslation: Calling a halt while the idea is still forming costs almost nothing; turning back after ten steps costs a great deal. Stop the moment it feels wrong, rather than waiting until you can prove you were wrong.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there something you know you should not start, with your foot already raised?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Keeping the calves still, unable to rescue what they follow. The heart is unhappy.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says failing to rescue the one you follow comes from that person not yet yielding and listening. You want to stop it and have no purchase, so the heart is uneasy.
lines.plainLanguage: You stop at the calves. Calves only move as the thighs move, so you cannot rescue the one you follow, and that leaves you unhappy. Seeing the problem without the standing to change it is a heavy position.
lines.lifeTranslation: Following someone else's decision, knowing it is unwise and unable to talk them out of it, is a genuinely frustrating place. Admitting you have no say this time and saving your effort works better than trying to drag along people who are not listening.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Whose decision are you quietly resenting, and was it ever yours to make?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Keeping the waist still, splitting the back muscles. Danger scorches the heart.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says stilling at the waist lets danger smoke the heart. Upper and lower are cut apart, the body cannot coordinate, and the peril reaches straight to the spirit.
lines.plainLanguage: You stop at the waist, the boundary between upper and lower, tearing the sinews of the back, and danger smoulders in the heart. Stopping at the joint that should least be stopped tears the body apart from within.
lines.lifeTranslation: Slamming the brakes at the point where things most need to connect rips the upstream and downstream apart. What you stop should be the start of an action, not the critical handover halfway through.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the point where you want to call a halt the starting line or the handover?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Keeping the body still. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says stilling the trunk means placing the work of stopping on yourself. You ask nothing of others and restrain only your own conduct, so there is no fault.
lines.plainLanguage: You stop at your own body, and there is no fault. Instead of judging whether other people should stop, you first hold your own actions in. This is the most practical approach and the one with the surest grip.
lines.lifeTranslation: Rather than spending effort demanding restraint from your environment or the people in it, take care of your own share. The only thing genuinely in your hands is your own behaviour.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How much of your effort goes into managing others rather than yourself?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Keeping the jaw still. Words have order; regret vanishes.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says stilling the jaw comes from holding the centre correctly. Restraining speech so that what is said has order is the mean in practice, so regret disappears.
lines.plainLanguage: You stop at the jaw, so your speech has order and regret disappears. Stilling at its highest reach turns out to be governing the mouth: not silence, but speaking in order and not speaking too much.
lines.lifeTranslation: Most regrets come from the extra sentences. Order your words before they leave and decide whether they need saying at all; that alone saves a great deal of clearing up.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Lately, do you regret what you said or what you left unsaid?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Generous stillness. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the good fortune of generous stilling comes from ending with substance. At the furthest reach of stopping, nothing floats or wavers, and this is the steadiest resting place in the hexagram.
lines.plainLanguage: You stop with a settled, substantial attitude, and the line reads well. The stopping here is not grudging restraint but being genuinely at ease in the place that is yours.
lines.lifeTranslation: Real restraint eventually stops feeling like endurance and becomes simply not reaching for the thing. Once stopping no longer feels like a loss, that steadiness starts working in your favour.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your self-discipline still endurance, or has it become a habit?

topicRules.career: Pull in your front line and do the work you already hold deeply rather than reaching for ground outside your remit. Stop at the planning stage if you must stop; do not call a sudden halt at a critical handover.
topicRules.study: Concentrate on a few subjects or a single topic and resist opening too many fronts at once. Pace matters less than keeping it going without breaks over a long stretch.
topicRules.romance: Rein in excessive guessing and questioning and put your attention back on your own behaviour. When distance is right, keep it quietly; forcing progress creates tension you do not enjoy either.
topicRules.family: Things settle when each person keeps to their own measure and there is less crossing of lines. Before trying to change a relative, adjust your own approach and the way you speak.
topicRules.relations: Reduce the volume of social contact and keep only the connections that matter; speaking less and in order earns trust more easily. There is no need to take a position or step into disputes that are not yours.
topicRules.finance: Hold back and observe, control spending and expansion, and keep resources inside a safe range. Leave alone what you are not sure of; protecting your capital is a result too. This is a general principle and not investment advice; consult a qualified professional about your own situation.
topicRules.wellness: This suits deliberately slowing down, cutting stimulation and hard training, and letting the body genuinely rest. Suppressing feelings for long builds into a slow burn, so find an outlet for it. This is not medical diagnosis or treatment advice; see a doctor if you feel unwell.
topicRules.general: The direction is stopping: halt where halting belongs, keep your thinking inside your own ground, and the outcome is steady and substantial. The process may feel dull and constrained, and the steadiness you build here buys you room in the next stage.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: stop at the place where stopping belongs, and give body, mind and information room to settle. Avoid: chasing the same things while supposedly resting, or stretching a pause into an escape from responsibility.

hexagrams.name: Jiàn · Gradual Progress
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Jian: A woman's marriage brings good fortune. Steadfast correctness is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary reads Jian as advance by degrees. The advance holds its position, so going forward accomplishes something; the advance is correct, so it can set a state right. The lower trigram stills and the upper yields, so movement does not exhaust itself. The Xiang image is a tree on the mountain, growing slowly yet reaching great height, and the noble person settles into worthy character and improves the customs around him.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Xun above, Gen below. A tree grows on the mountain: this is advance by stages. The whole hexagram runs on the image of wild geese in flight, moving in order from the water's edge to the rock in the stream, the dry ground, the branch, the ridge, and at last feathers fit for ceremonial use. The stages are distinct and none can be skipped. The judgement uses a marriage completed step by step through proper form, and asks you to hold correct. Only the third line breaks away and presses ahead alone, and that is the one that goes badly. Slow is not the problem; out of sequence is.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment explicitly gives good fortune with right conduct. The second six, fifth nine, and top nine have fortune, and the fourth no blame; the Image describes positive long-term cultivation of virtue and customs. Negativity is concentrated in the third nine's husband not returning and pregnancy not bearing a child. Its Image attributes this to leaving the group and losing the Way: avoidable rashness outside the proper sequence, rather than the overall theme. Conditions are favorable but require time and order, hence the rating: Rather Good rather than the best. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Climb one rung at a time and let nothing skip its stage.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: The wild goose gradually reaches the shore. Danger for the young person; criticism, but no blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the young one's danger carries no fault in principle. The risk and the gossip come from being early in a career, not from anything done wrong.
lines.plainLanguage: The goose has just reached the bank at the water's edge, low and not yet secure. At this stage a young person feels exposed and hears some talk, yet there is no fault in it.
lines.lifeTranslation: Being questioned about your inexperience is normal when you first enter a field. What helps is not arguing back but doing the most basic part of the work so well that nobody has a handle on you.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the remark aimed at your ability, or just at how long you have been here?

lines.original: Six in the second place: The wild goose gradually reaches the rock. Eating and drinking contentedly. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says eating and drinking in contentment is not being fed for nothing. The ease was earned by your own footing, so it can be enjoyed.
lines.plainLanguage: The goose moves on to the great rock in the stream and stands firmly, eating and drinking at ease, and the line reads well. The commentary adds that this is not something received for free but security you walked to yourself.
lines.lifeTranslation: After getting through the hardest early stretch, you finally have solid ground and can rest for a while. Enjoy it without guilt, and remember that the rock is where you walked to, not a gift.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How did the solid ground under your feet come to be there?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: The wild goose gradually reaches the plateau. The husband campaigns and does not return; the wife is pregnant but does not bear a child. Misfortune. Defending against raiders is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the husband who marches out and does not return has left the flock, and the wife who conceives and does not bear has lost the proper way. Only turning to defence, so that each protects the other, is favourable.
lines.plainLanguage: The goose jumps a stage to the dry high ground, out of its sequence. So the one who sets out does not return and the one who conceives does not bear, and the outcome is poor. Only defence suits here, not an offensive move.
lines.lifeTranslation: Forcing progress past the steps you owe tends to lose you both ends: the new thing does not land and what you already held slips. Stop expanding and protect what you have and the people around you.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which step did you skip, and are you paying for it now?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: The wild goose gradually reaches the tree; perhaps it finds a level branch. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says finding a flat branch is possible through a yielding, accommodating attitude. The bird bends to the situation and finds somewhere it can rest.
lines.plainLanguage: The goose flies up into a tree, where its webbed feet cannot grip a branch, yet it may find one flat enough to perch on for a while, so there is no fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you are put somewhere that does not suit you, you need neither grit your teeth nor walk out at once. Lower your stance, find the angle the environment allows, and settle before deciding anything else.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In this ill-fitting position, which flat branch could you hold for now?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: The wild goose gradually reaches the hill. The wife does not conceive for three years, but in the end nothing can overcome them. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that in the end nothing overcomes it, and what is wished for is obtained. The goose reaches the high ridge and is separated for a time, yet the proper correspondence holds.
lines.plainLanguage: The goose advances to the high ridge, with obstruction along the way, like a woman who does not conceive for three years. Those obstacles do not finally outweigh the genuine connection, and what was hoped for arrives.
lines.lifeTranslation: A partnership or relationship that genuinely fits can still be misread or kept apart for years. As long as neither side has gone off course, time wears the obstacle down, and nothing drastic is needed to force it back.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the thing you have waited a long time for simply not yet due?

lines.original: Nine at the top: The wild goose gradually reaches the plateau. Its feathers can be used in ceremony. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the feathers serve as ceremonial ornament because the formation was never disordered. This gathers the whole hexagram's theme of sequence into its closing image.
lines.plainLanguage: The goose reaches the highest ground, and its feathers are clean and ordered enough to be used as ceremonial ornament, so the line reads well. The commentary points to the order that was never broken.
lines.lifeTranslation: Someone who came up by the proper route leaves behind more than results: they leave a way of doing things others can use as a standard. That influence comes from having taken no shortcuts.
lines.reflectionPrompt: If someone copied your method exactly, what would you want them to learn from it?

topicRules.career: Advance in stages, cutting the large goal into pieces you can sign off one at a time and settling each before the next. Jumping grades or skipping process tends to lose both ends, and a longer timeline is a fair cost.
topicRules.study: Build the foundation in order, work up by difficulty and revise properly rather than attacking problems above your level. Slow progress with no gaps shows its effect over the long run.
topicRules.romance: Move at a pace you both accept, letting acquaintance, companionship and commitment each take their time. Rushing to define things or pressing for an answer tends to jam a connection that would otherwise work.
topicRules.family: Repair relationships slowly over a long stretch, building trust through small fixed interactions. Flag major arrangements early and talk them through in stages rather than announcing a decision.
topicRules.relations: Build trust in order: make the small things reliable before proposing anything deeper. Take care not to break away from the group to prove yourself, since leaving your support behind adds risk.
topicRules.finance: This suits regular, small, long-term accumulation, with an emergency fund in place before anything else. Steer clear of schemes promising to double money quickly. This is a general principle and not investment advice; consult a qualified professional about your own situation.
topicRules.wellness: Adjust sleep and exercise intensity gradually, changing one habit at a time and holding it for several weeks. Sudden increases tend to cause injury or get abandoned halfway. This is not medical diagnosis or treatment advice; see a doctor if you feel unwell.
topicRules.general: The direction is gradual advance: the conditions are favourable, and the result needs time and the right order. Keep your rhythm, build character and reputation, and note that breaking away to rush ahead is the one clear risk here.
