hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: build capability and relationships in sequence, and settle on each stage before moving to the next. Avoid: skipping necessary steps, pressing for commitment, or changing course because the pace feels slow.

hexagrams.name: Guī Mèi · The Marrying Maiden
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Gui Mei: Advancing brings misfortune. Nothing is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary affirms the union of man and woman as the great meaning of heaven and earth and the end and beginning of human affairs, then names the flaw directly: acting out of delight, in a position that does not suit, with the yielding riding above the firm, so going forward brings misfortune and nothing is favourable. The Xiang image is thunder above the lake, and the noble person thinks through the lasting end and knows where it may fail.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Zhen above, Dui below. Thunder rolls over the lake: a younger woman marries into a place where her standing is not right. The hexagram describes a union whose conditions are inadequate from the start. The lame manage to walk, the half-sighted manage to see, the third line waits for a proper position and settles for a secondary one, the fourth simply delays the wedding, the fifth outshone by her own attendants, and the last closes with an empty basket and a sacrifice that draws no blood. The judgement is blunt. The image offers the way out: think the ending and the failure modes through at the beginning.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's misfortune in advancing and nothing beneficial form a rare double negative. Its commentary attributes this to inappropriate positions and yielding above firmness. The top ends with an empty basket and a slaughtered sheep without blood, an image of total emptiness. Positive terms occur only in the first nine and fifth six, both conditioned on accepting a secondary place without competing over appearances; the second also favors quiet steadfastness. Structural inequality rather than a passing mistake creates the unfavorable factors, hence the rating: Poor. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Where standing is unclear, enthusiasm alone tends to fail.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: The maiden marries as a secondary wife. The lame can walk. Advancing brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary credits marrying as the secondary bride with constancy, and says the lame one walks because each supports the other rather than one straining alone.
lines.plainLanguage: You enter in the secondary role of the attending bride. It is awkward, like walking with a lame foot, yet you can still walk, and going forward is favourable. The commentary puts the key in persistence and mutual support.
lines.lifeTranslation: Joining as a deputy or a stand-in can still amount to something, provided you accept the position and stay in it steadily. Grabbing for the lead role instead leaves you with no footing at all.
lines.reflectionPrompt: If this role did not get upgraded within a year, would you still do it well?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: The one-eyed can see. A secluded person's steadfastness is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says this favours the steadfastness of one who lives quietly, because the constant way has not been altered. The circumstances are limited, the conduct is not.
lines.plainLanguage: Like someone blind in one eye who can still see, you see, but not the whole. This suits a person content with quiet who holds correct, because circumstances do not shift their principles.
lines.lifeTranslation: When your information is incomplete and your say is limited, making large judgements is risky. Quietly doing well the part you can see clearly, and keeping your principles, is safer than rushing to declare a view.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How much of this do you actually see clearly?

lines.original: Six in the third place: The maiden waits to marry, then returns as a secondary wife.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says waiting to marry in this way is not suitable to the position. The expectation does not match the circumstances, so the return is to the secondary role after all.
lines.plainLanguage: You had hoped to wait for a better standing before marrying, the wait yielded nothing, and you enter in the secondary role regardless. The commentary locates the problem in an expectation out of proportion to your situation.
lines.lifeTranslation: Setting your terms above what you can currently trade for tends to land you back where you started, with the waiting time spent for nothing. Assess your actual hand honestly, then decide whether to wait or accept.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the condition you are holding out for in proportion to what you can offer now?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: The maiden's marriage is delayed. A late marriage has its proper time.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the intent behind the delay is to wait and then act. This is not procrastination but a deliberate hold for the fitting moment.
lines.plainLanguage: The set date passes and the marriage has not taken place; a later going has its own time. The commentary reads this as intentional waiting rather than drift.
lines.lifeTranslation: Moving the schedule back yourself when the conditions are not ready is a responsible choice, not a failure. Spell out why you are delaying and what condition restarts it, and others accept it more readily.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What condition has to appear before you restart the thing you postponed?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Di Yi gives the maiden in marriage. Her sleeves are less fine than her secondary wife's. The moon is nearly full. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary notes the sovereign's daughter whose sleeves are plainer than her attendant's, and says she holds the central position and moves by the dignity of her character rather than competing through dress. The moon is nearly full, not yet full.
lines.plainLanguage: The sovereign marries off his daughter and her sleeves are less fine than her attendant's. The moon is nearly full but not quite, and the line reads well. Her standing rests on the centred character, not the appearance.
lines.lifeTranslation: People with genuine weight do not need to outshine those around them, and giving away the spotlight tends to earn more respect. Leaving something in reserve is also safer than using everything up.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Where recently could you have let go of the most visible position?

lines.original: Six at the top: The woman holds an empty basket; the man slaughters a sheep without blood. Nothing is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the top line has no substance and carries an empty basket. The rite is outwardly complete and inwardly hollow.
lines.plainLanguage: The woman carries a basket with nothing in it and the man cuts the sheep without drawing blood. What should have been substance is entirely absent, and no advantage is visible here.
lines.lifeTranslation: A relationship or partnership where the ritual is complete and the substance is empty does not hold. Rather than staging a grander ceremony, admit the content is missing and renegotiate.
lines.reflectionPrompt: In this arrangement, which is fuller, the form or the substance?

topicRules.career: Your title and your actual authority may not match, and pushing outward tends to meet resistance. Settle into the role you have and do it solidly, confirm the scope of your mandate before major moves, and postpone with an explanation if needed.
topicRules.study: Your information or foundation may be incomplete, so this is not the time for large conclusions or a hurried exam attempt. Fill the gaps and keep to your method; deferring the harder target is a reasonable choice.
topicRules.romance: A sudden attraction can push things forward fast while the standing, the expectations and the practical conditions fail to line up. Set out what each of you actually wants, since a formal commitment is no substitute for the daily reality.
topicRules.family: Watch for resentment and comparison arising from unclear roles, and explain the long-term plan before major arrangements begin. Surface harmony with the real issue unspoken is harder to deal with later.
topicRules.relations: You may be in a position with little leverage and limited say. Hold to your principles, judge less, avoid escalating a conflict over pride, and do not use display to prove your standing.
topicRules.finance: Steer clear of arrangements that look attractive but cannot explain their substance; good figures on paper are not solid content. Confirm what the money is for and what protections exist. This is a general principle and not investment advice; consult a qualified professional about your own situation.
topicRules.wellness: Resentment and comparison drain you quietly, so talk to someone you trust rather than holding up an appearance of normality by force. This is not medical diagnosis or treatment advice; see a doctor if you feel unwell.
topicRules.general: The direction is a union where standing is not right: the conditions are inadequate from the start and enthusiasm alone carries real risk. Think the ending and the likely failures through at the outset, accept the secondary position, and make the substance real.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: clarify the standing, the responsibilities and the long-term cost before deciding whether to commit. Avoid: being carried in by enthusiasm, or expecting an unequal arrangement to improve by itself.

hexagrams.name: Fēng · Abundance
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Feng: Success. The king attains it. Do not worry; be like the sun at noon.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary glosses Feng as greatness, arising from clarity that can act. The king reaches it because greatness is honoured, and the counsel not to worry but to be like the sun at noon means shining on all below. Then the warning: the sun at noon declines, the full moon is eaten, and heaven and earth themselves wax and wane with the seasons, let alone people. The Xiang image is thunder and lightning arriving together, and the noble person decides cases and applies penalties.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Zhen above, Li below. Thunder and lightning arrive together: this is fullness at its height. Feng means great, means full. The judgement speaks of success, of the king reaching this state, of having no cause for worry and standing like the sun at noon. Yet the lines keep returning to thick screens and to seeing stars at midday: the more splendid the arrangement, the more of your own light it blocks. A broken right arm, a vast house with an empty hall, three years with nobody seen. When the light is brightest, the shadow is deepest.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment begins with success and gives positive guidance in not worrying and being like the midday sun. The second six, fourth nine, and fifth six explicitly have good fortune; the first nine's blameless equal meeting and worthwhile proceeding are feasible, and the third has no blame. Negativity is concentrated in the top six's three years unseen and misfortune, attributed by its Image to self-concealment. The Judgment's sun declining after noon and moon eclipsing after fullness are timing reminders rather than verdicts. Abundance is clear but must be used promptly, hence the rating: Rather Good rather than the best. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: At full noon the shadows deepen, so decide while you can see.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Meeting a matching partner. Though equal, no blame. Proceeding has merit.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that ten days brings no fault, and that going beyond that span brings calamity. The time limit is stated with unusual precision.
lines.plainLanguage: You meet the partner who matches you, and within a set span there is no fault in the dealing; going forward even earns praise. The commentary adds the other half: past that span, trouble follows.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you meet the right person, settle the matter inside the right window. Opportunities have a length, and once you run past it the favourable terms turn into a burden.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What deadline have you given yourself for the opening in front of you?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Abundant screening; the Dipper is visible at noon. Going brings suspicion and distress. Sincerity opens the way. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that meeting it with good faith means trust awakens the other's intent. Sincerity is what opens the screen.
lines.plainLanguage: The screen is so thick that the Dipper is visible at midday. Going forward now draws suspicion, yet approaching with good faith that awakens the other person still reads well.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you are misread and guarded against, rushing to explain or forcing your way in only deepens the suspicion. Steady sincerity and concrete action let the other person see for themselves, which works better than persuasion.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is someone doubting you while you try to fix it with words alone?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Abundant covering; small stars are visible at noon. Breaking the right arm. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the heavy curtain means great undertakings are not possible, and a broken right arm cannot be used again. This is acknowledging a limit and stopping.
lines.plainLanguage: The covering is heavier still and only a faint star shows at midday. It is as though your right arm were broken and great work were out of reach, and because you recognise that and stop, there is no fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: When your main strength is injured or a key person is absent, admitting you cannot take the big project is not weakness. Taking it anyway is what produces the real fault.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which right arm are you missing while the work stays scheduled at full size?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Abundant screening; the Dipper is visible at noon. Meeting an equal lord. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the thick screen to an unsuitable position and the stars at midday to obscurity, and says meeting an equal counterpart is favourable because it involves actually going.
lines.plainLanguage: The screen is still heavy and the Dipper still visible at noon, so the situation is far from clear. Yet you meet someone of comparable standing who can deal with you as an equal, and the line reads well; the commentary puts the weight on acting.
lines.lifeTranslation: The environment has not brightened, but a partner has appeared who can speak with you on level terms. Go to them yourself. Waiting for the other side to open dims the light another notch.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Who should you be approaching while you wait for them to come to you?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Brilliance arrives, with celebration and praise. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the good fortune here lies in there being real cause for celebration. Bringing in people of talent produces something genuinely worth marking, not merely a good name.
lines.plainLanguage: You draw in people of ability and refinement to help, and blessing and a good reputation follow, so the line reads well.
lines.lifeTranslation: The right move at the height of your strength is to bring better people in rather than keeping all the credit. Making room for them returns both standing and substance.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Who is better than you at this, and should you be inviting them in?

lines.original: Six at the top: Enlarging the house, screening the household. Peering through the door, silent and empty of people. Unseen for three years. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the vast house soars to the edge of heaven, and that peering in and finding nobody is a matter of self-concealment. The isolation is chosen, not imposed.
lines.plainLanguage: The house is built enormous and its door is screened tight. Peer inside and it is silent and empty; three years pass without anyone seen, and the outcome is poor. The commentary calls it hiding yourself away.
lines.lifeTranslation: As the display gets grander, the people leave one by one until only the shell remains. At the height of your strength, leave a door open, and do not use your own elevation to close yourself off.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How long has it been since you let anyone genuinely in?

topicRules.career: You are at a high point for resources and momentum, so settle key decisions and partnerships inside their window. The thicker the layers and the display, the more real information they block, so keep a direct line to the front line.
topicRules.study: Intake is high and results are visible, so use the good state to attack the hardest material. Watch for piling up so much material that the point disappears; periodic distilling beats endless collecting.
topicRules.romance: Warmth and visibility are both high, so this suits taking the relationship a step further. Do not let events and display replace real time together, and dissolve doubts with sustained sincerity rather than one explanation.
topicRules.family: Conditions are comfortable and this suits adding or expanding, though a bigger space does not mean a closer household. Keep fixed time together so that busyness does not hollow it out.
topicRules.relations: This suits widening your circle and actively recruiting people better than you; giving up the stage earns a good name. Watch that a rising sense of status does not thin out the people who tell you the truth.
topicRules.finance: Income and opportunities are plentiful, so build a reserve while there is surplus and keep records of actual cash flow. Avoid raising fixed costs for the sake of appearances. This is a general principle and not investment advice; consult a qualified professional about your own situation.
topicRules.wellness: A dense schedule drains you quickly, so book rest while you still feel good rather than waiting until you cannot continue. Take feeling hollowed out or unmotivated seriously. This is not medical diagnosis or treatment advice; see a doctor if you feel unwell.
topicRules.general: The direction is abundance: conditions are clearly favourable, so decide quickly while the light is good and use what you have in time. Peaks pass as a matter of course, and the main risks here are the screens you build and the isolation that follows.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: make your decisions while the information is clear, and plan for how things hold once the peak passes. Avoid: treating the high point as the normal state, or letting an excess of options delay the handling.

hexagrams.name: Lǚ · The Traveller
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Lu: Small success. The traveler's steadfastness brings good fortune.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says the traveller finds small success because the yielding holds the centre while abroad and defers to the firm, stilling below and clinging to clarity above. It closes by marvelling at how much meaning the time of travel contains. The Xiang image is fire on the mountain, moving with the terrain and never resting long, and the noble person applies penalties with clarity and care and does not let cases pile up.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Li above, Gen below. Fire moves across the mountain: this is being on the road, lodging in a place not your own. The judgement grants only small success and makes even that conditional on holding correct, a more reserved tone than most hexagrams. The lines run through the traveller's whole range: petty grievances that bring trouble on yourself, lodging with funds and a reliable servant, lodging burnt down and the servant lost, shelter and money with an unquiet heart, one arrow spent for a reputation gained, and a nest burnt after laughter. With shallow roots abroad, care, deference and letting small things go are what keep you going.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment combines a limit and a condition: success is small, and fortune depends on right conduct rather than being unconditional. Positives include the second six's loyal young servant and the fifth's eventual praise and appointment. Negatives include the first's self-invited calamity, third's burnt lodging and lost servant, and top's laughter turning to wailing and misfortune. Even the fourth remains unhappy despite obtaining resources and an axe. Favorable and adverse are roughly equal, with outcomes largely dependent on the traveler's attitude rather than external conditions, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Away from home your roots are shallow, so stay light and careful.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: The traveler is petty and fussy, thereby inviting calamity.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the traveller's pettiness brings the calamity of a cramped will. The root of it is a mind already squeezed narrow and filled with small matters.
lines.plainLanguage: At the very start of the journey you are already haggling over trivia, and that is exactly how the trouble is brought on yourself. The commentary locates the cause in a will pressed into too small a space.
lines.lifeTranslation: Spending your first week in a new place arguing over seating, workload and who did more loses you the room quickly. Widen your frame and let the small things pass.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the small thing you are arguing over worth what it costs you?

lines.original: Six in the second place: The traveler reaches lodging, keeping resources close and gaining a loyal young servant.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says gaining an upright young servant means there is nothing to regret in the end. Lodging, funds and a reliable person together make the steadiest state available on the road.
lines.plainLanguage: The traveller finds somewhere to stay, carries enough money and gains a loyal, dependable servant. The commentary says that nothing is left to complain of in the end.
lines.lifeTranslation: Getting a footing in an unfamiliar place needs three things: somewhere to live, money to last and someone you can trust. Missing any one of them makes it hard, so secure all three as soon as you land.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Of shelter, savings and someone trustworthy, which are you short of?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: The traveler's lodging burns, and the young servant is lost. Persistence is dangerous.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary notes the injury first, then the cause: treating those below you as a traveller does means losing them by rights.
lines.plainLanguage: The lodging burns down and the dependable servant is gone, and even holding correct leaves danger. The commentary says the people scattered because of how they were treated.
lines.lifeTranslation: Losing both your base and your contacts in a strange place is rarely bad luck; more often the way you treated people was too hard. When those willing to help you leave, look at yourself first.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Did the person who recently left hint at something before they went?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: The traveler finds a place, obtaining resources and an axe. My heart is unhappy.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the traveller's lodging is not a proper position, so even with funds and tools in hand the heart is not at ease.
lines.plainLanguage: The traveller finds a place to rest for now and obtains money and an axe, yet the heart is not easy. The commentary says the reason is that this was never the right position to hold.
lines.lifeTranslation: Decent pay, reasonable conditions and a persistent unease usually mean this is not where you want to be. Admitting that and planning the next step works better than talking yourself into contentment.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The conditions are fine, so what is the real reason you are not happy?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Shooting a pheasant, losing one arrow. In the end, praise and appointment.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the reputation and the appointment come from reaching those above. What was lost is slight and what was gained sits higher up.
lines.plainLanguage: Shooting at the pheasant costs you one arrow, and in the end it brings reputation and appointment. The commentary says the intent reached upward, so a small loss bought a large return.
lines.lifeTranslation: Being willing to spend a little to be seen usually beats saving that cost. What matters is aiming in the direction of the people who actually decide.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which arrow are you willing to lose in order to be seen?

lines.original: Nine at the top: A bird's nest burns. The traveler first laughs, then wails. Losing an ox through carelessness. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says a traveller placed at the top is in a position that by rights burns, and that losing the ox through carelessness leaves not even news of it in the end.
lines.plainLanguage: The bird's nest is burnt, and the traveller laughs first and then wails aloud. The ox is lost through carelessness, and the outcome is poor. The commentary says a guest perched at the top is exposed from the start.
lines.lifeTranslation: Climbing to the top as an outsider and then losing your head tends to burn down the place you were living in. The better the wind, the more worth remembering how shallow your roots here really are.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the height you are standing at matched by your roots in this place?

topicRules.career: You may be posted out, changing jobs or otherwise holding a guest position with shallow roots and limited room. Settle the basics and build goodwill with colleagues rather than rewriting rules or competing for resources on arrival.
topicRules.study: This suits short courses, study trips or sitting in on other fields, aimed at broadening your view rather than producing results at once. Organise notes as you go and avoid packing the schedule so tightly that nothing is absorbed.
topicRules.romance: Distance, time apart or a temporarily undefined status may all feature. Speak plainly and allow for the other person's circumstances, since quarrelling over small things burns through both your patience faster.
topicRules.family: Relocation, living apart or a member being away may be on the table. Confirm the floor for housing and living costs, and keep regular contact so whoever is away still feels part of it.
topicRules.relations: You are in a new circle, so be deferential, observe before joining in, and treat everyone who helps you well. Looking down on the ground level or losing your measure when things go well is what unravels connections you worked for.
topicRules.finance: Liquidity matters more than returns here, so keep enough cash and emergency funds and avoid tying money up where you cannot reach it soon. This is a general principle and not investment advice; consult a qualified professional about your own situation.
topicRules.wellness: Changing surroundings and constant movement disrupt your routine, so fix the basics of sleep and meals and watch how your body handles the new environment. Take ongoing insomnia or fatigue seriously. This is not medical diagnosis or treatment advice; see a doctor if you feel unwell.
topicRules.general: The direction is travel: the success available is limited and most of the outcome rests on your own manner. Hold correct, stay deferential, see the situation clearly before acting, and note the two dangers here, pettiness and losing your head when things go well.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: keep a modest, alert manner, travel light and respect the rules of where you are. Avoid: making a display in unfamiliar ground, getting drawn into petty affairs, or mistaking a temporary base for a foundation.

hexagrams.name: Xùn · The Gentle
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Xun: Small success. It is beneficial to proceed and beneficial to meet a great person.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary reads doubled Xun as an order stated and stated again: strength that settles gently into a central, correct place, so the intent can actually travel. Because the yielding lines all follow the firm ones, success here is small. The Xiang image is wind following wind, with the noble person repeating the instruction before acting on it.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Xun above, Xun below. Wind upon wind, and the sense of the hexagram is entering by yielding. Wind gets everywhere not by force but by seeping in. The judgement grants only small success: the road is passable but its range is limited, and it still favours having somewhere to go and seeing the person who can decide. The lines run from hesitation at the threshold, through excessive self-lowering that still works because the heart stays centred, to careful reform announced before and tracked after, and finally to yielding so far that you lose your own means. Gentleness is a method of entry, not a reason to give yourself up.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment limits success to small progress, unlike hexagrams of great success; beneficial proceeding and meeting a great person add positive conditions. The lines are evenly mixed: the second nine's fortune without blame, fourth six's vanished regret and three kinds of game, and fifth nine's steadfast fortune with nothing unfavorable are clearly positive. The first's advance and retreat reveals doubt, the third's repeated submission exhausted purpose, and the top's lost resources and axe with misfortune is the strongest warning. Opportunity and excessive compliance coexist; judgment of limits determines gain and loss, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Enter by seeping in, state your case clearly, and keep your own ground.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Advancing and retreating. A warrior's steadfastness is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that advancing and retreating shows a doubting will, and that the steadfastness of a soldier is favourable because it brings that wavering will under order.
lines.plainLanguage: You stand at the door, half in and half out, unable to settle. What suits here is the soldier's kind of correctness: plain, decisive, and enough to shut the wavering down.
lines.lifeTranslation: Excessive caution in a new environment leaves you stuck where you are. Set one simple rule for yourself and follow it a few times; acting clears hesitation faster than more thinking does.
lines.reflectionPrompt: After days of turning this over, is what you lack information or resolve?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Submission beneath the bed. Employ scribes and shamans in great numbers. Good fortune and no blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the good fortune of this repeated appeal to holding the central position. The behaviour is lower than it needs to be, but the heart still keeps its measure.
lines.plainLanguage: You bow so low it is as if you were under the bed, and you keep going through intermediaries to make yourself heard. It looks excessive, yet because you hold your own measure inside, the outcome is favourable and without fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: Lowering your posture in a forceful environment, and asking someone to relay for you, is not humiliating. As long as you know what you are there to win, a low stance is a tactic rather than a surrender.
lines.reflectionPrompt: When you lower your stance, is your own limit still in place?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Repeated submission. Regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the regret of repeated submission comes from a will that has run dry: there is nothing left to put forward as your own.
lines.plainLanguage: You give way again and again until the position becomes uncomfortable. The trouble is not the bowing itself but that there is no longer any view of your own behind it.
lines.lifeTranslation: Accommodate people long enough and you lose the ability to say what you want. Next time you are asked to concede, state your own view first, then decide whether to concede.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The last time you went along with someone, was it agreement or just fatigue?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Regret vanishes. Three kinds of game taken in the hunt.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary closes with the word merit: the hunt that yields three kinds of game is the line where something real is achieved. The three kinds are enough for sacrifice, for guests and for the kitchen.
lines.plainLanguage: Earlier regret disappears, and a single hunt brings back three kinds of game, enough to serve several purposes. This is the rare line in the hexagram where actual results arrive.
lines.lifeTranslation: People willing to go in low and work a job through from the start usually come away with several things at once: experience, contacts and reputation. Do not count only the most obvious return.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Besides money, what did the last thing you finished actually give you?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Steadfastness brings good fortune, regret vanishes, and nothing is unfavorable. No beginning, but an ending. Three days before geng and three days after geng. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the good fortune here to a position both correct and central. The three days before and after the day of change stand for full explanation beforehand and steady follow-up afterwards.
lines.plainLanguage: Holding correct brings good fortune, regret disappears, and nothing is unfavourable. The start is rough but the finish is sound. When you change a rule, explain it well in advance and keep watching how it lands afterwards.
lines.lifeTranslation: Do not spring a new process on people. Let them hear why it is changing before it changes, then go back and check how it is working. Resistance drops sharply when you do both.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Have the people affected by your change actually understood the reason for it?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Submission beneath the bed, losing resources and an axe. Persistence brings misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says bowing under the bed at the top position shows that the way has run out, and that losing your goods and axe is dangerous even if you hold to it. The axe stands for the means by which you earn and decide.
lines.plainLanguage: At the highest place you press yourself under the bed again, and you lose the very things you live and decide by. Holding to that position without changing it is where the danger lies.
lines.lifeTranslation: Concede far enough and you hand over your expertise and your say along with everything else. That is no longer modesty. The signal to stop is the moment you start thinking it makes no difference whether you are there.
lines.reflectionPrompt: To keep the peace, have you given away something you should have kept?

topicRules.career: Advance by working your way in rather than pushing head-on: say clearly what you want, then let the practice settle layer by layer into daily routine. When a rule changes, explain before and follow up after, rather than announcing it cold.
topicRules.study: Take difficult material through repeated exposure and gradual depth instead of one hard push. A modest posture helps when you ask for help, but bring your own question rather than simply nodding along.
topicRules.romance: Approach gently and let the other person get used to you at their own pace. Watch for the habit of always deferring; a long stretch with no view of your own wears the relationship thin.
topicRules.family: Say difficult things in stages and in a level voice, giving relatives time to absorb them. Discuss changes to household rules or shares of work before applying them, then keep asking how people find it.
topicRules.relations: A soft approach opens most doors, and an introduction through a mutual contact suits this time. Note that repeated retreat gets read as having no position, so speak plainly when a position is called for.
topicRules.finance: Build up in small, spread-out steps rather than committing heavily at once, and take particular care not to hand your own financial decisions to someone else for the sake of harmony. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: Long-term self-suppression to fit an environment builds a tiredness you cannot name. Choose regular, gentle activity to recover, and keep one outlet where you can say what you actually feel. This is not medical advice; consult a qualified professional if something concerns you.
topicRules.general: The direction is entry by yielding: soften the posture, state things clearly, and let the change seep through in layers. Progress accumulates slowly and stays modest in scale. The real risk is yielding past the point where your own view and your own means still exist.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: communicate clearly and repeatedly, advance by soft pressure, and keep your own view intact. Avoid: restating things endlessly without a point, or yielding until you no longer hold any power to decide.

hexagrams.name: Duì · The Joyous
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Dui: Success. Steadfast correctness is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary glosses Dui as delight, held up by firmness at the centre and gentleness on the outside, and insists that delight must accord with correctness to stand. Lead people through gladness and they forget their toil, even their fear of death. The Xiang image is two lakes joined and feeding one another, with friends discussing and practising together.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Dui above, Dui below. Two lakes lie side by side, and the hexagram is about pleasure and about speech. Its root sense is to be glad: to say aloud what pleases you, and to be the reason someone else is glad. The judgement is short, granting success and favouring correctness. Delight is good in itself, but it only holds if it rests on honest ground. The lines move from open, unbiased warmth, through pleasure built on trust, to deliberate ingratiation that turns out badly, hesitation between two sides, trust placed in someone who is eroding you, and finally pleasure you were led into. Delight that came from flattery is the first to collapse.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment directly affirms progress, and its commentary highly praises joy's influence as making people forget toil and death. Most lines are favorable: harmonious joy in the first nine, sincere joy with vanished regret in the second, and joy after distinguishing affliction in the fourth. Negatives concern flawed motives for pleasing: the third's approaching joy brings misfortune from an inappropriate position, the fifth trusts what strips away and faces danger, and the top's induced joy lacks illumination. Conditions are positive, with risk in pleasing to win approval, hence the rating: Rather Good rather than the best. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Gladness built on candour lasts; flattery buys goodwill only once.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Harmonious joy. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the good fortune of harmonious delight comes from conduct that has not yet attracted any suspicion.
lines.plainLanguage: You meet people evenly, taking no side, and the pleasure that follows is favourable. What matters is that the conduct is plain enough to leave nothing to doubt.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you first join a group, the same courtesy to everyone is what gets you accepted. Not rushing to pick a side is the most valuable thing you hold at this stage.
lines.reflectionPrompt: When you are good to people, are you quietly tallying the return?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Sincere joy. Good fortune; regret vanishes.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the good fortune of trustworthy delight rests on a will that can itself be trusted. The gladness is not performed.
lines.plainLanguage: Pleasure that grows out of dealing honestly with people is favourable, and earlier regret falls away with it, because the gladness is genuine rather than staged.
lines.lifeTranslation: You do not need to be a good talker. If everything you say holds, people come to you on their own. Credit repairs a relationship better than eloquence does.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Of the things you promised recently, how many did you actually do?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Approaching joy. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the misfortune of coming forward to please to a position that does not fit: both the motive and the standing are out of place.
lines.plainLanguage: You step up to win someone's favour, and it goes badly. The position was never the right one, so the harder you court approval the more the strain shows.
lines.lifeTranslation: Accommodating people past your own limits to be liked looks warm for a while, then stops being taken seriously. If you want weight, build something worth weighing first.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Have you agreed to something you did not want, just to be liked?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Considering joy, not yet at peace. Distinguishing affliction brings happiness.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary marks the gladness of this line as an occasion for congratulation. To shut off the harmful part, in the sense of holding a boundary, is what produces it.
lines.plainLanguage: You weigh one side against the other and cannot settle. Once you can seal off the part that is doing harm, the gladness arrives.
lines.lifeTranslation: Being pulled by two kinds of people makes unease normal. Rather than trying to offend neither, work out which side is costing you and put distance there.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Of the two choices holding you up, which one is draining you?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Trusting what strips away. There is danger.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary notes that the position here is properly correct. Precisely because the standing is sound, the danger clearly comes from the party trusted rather than from the place you occupy.
lines.plainLanguage: You give your trust to a side that is wearing you away, and danger follows. Nothing is wrong with where you stand; the error is in whom you trusted.
lines.lifeTranslation: You are in the right role and have handed your trust to someone who depletes you. You do not have to doubt your judgement in general, but you do have to look at that one relationship again.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there someone you keep giving to who has never given back?

lines.original: Six at the top: Induced joy.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says only that this drawn-out delight is not yet bright. No judgement of fortune is attached: pleasure arrived at by being led is simply not creditable.
lines.plainLanguage: Someone else pulls you along into the pleasure. The text attaches neither good nor bad fortune, and the commentary says only that such gladness has no brightness to it. It is not yours.
lines.lifeTranslation: You get taken to the lively occasion you did not want to attend, and you are present without being there. You need not cut it off at once, but you can ask whose enjoyment this is.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How much of your recent enjoyment did you actually choose?

topicRules.career: The atmosphere is easy and communication flows, which suits work that needs consensus and mutual instruction. Hold your professional judgement, and do not endorse a plainly flawed proposal to keep a meeting pleasant.
topicRules.study: Explain material to classmates and question each other; being able to say it aloud is the test of understanding. Keep the discussion from becoming mutual comfort, and still name the mistakes that need naming.
topicRules.romance: Interaction is enjoyable and closeness comes easily, so build it on candour rather than flattery. If you notice yourself constantly adjusting to the other person's tastes, stop and check whether the exchange is even.
topicRules.family: Arrange relaxed time together and raise difficult subjects inside that good atmosphere. Swallowing grievance for the sake of harmony is not harmony; saying how you feel is.
topicRules.relations: Your standing with people is good and conversation lands well, which suits widening cooperation. Distinguish those who deal with you honestly from those who only consume your goodwill, and step back from the latter.
topicRules.finance: Warm company and good feeling loosen the purse, so fix a ceiling before joining a gathering or a shared venture, and check any enthusiastically recommended opportunity one layer deeper. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: Mood runs bright, and time with other people restores you, so plan for it. A forced smile accumulates its own cost, so allow yourself to go quiet when you cannot keep it up. This is not medical advice; consult a qualified professional if something concerns you.
topicRules.general: The direction is gladness and exchange: conditions are positive, and dealing honestly brings real support and real openings. Watch the motive. Straining to be liked wears away the goodwill it took you so long to build.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: exchange views frankly and share good feeling in ways you can sustain. Avoid: over-promising to keep people happy, or using a light atmosphere to dodge the real problem.

hexagrams.name: Huàn · Dispersion
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Huan: Success. The king approaches his temple. Crossing the great river is beneficial; steadfast correctness is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary explains the success of Huan by firmness arriving without being cornered and yielding taking its proper place outside, and says the king reaches the temple because he stands at the centre. Crossing the great water works because you ride on wood. The Xiang image is wind moving over water, with the former kings making offerings and founding temples to gather scattered hearts.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Xun above, Kan below. Wind blows across the surface of water, and the hexagram is about things coming apart. Its root sense is scattering: ice melting, ripples spreading, people drifting away. Yet the judgement grants success, because dispersal is not only loss. What should scatter is private interest, blockage and the closed circle. So the text asks for a shared centre, for the nerve to cross the great water, and for correctness. The lines move from timely rescue while the horse is still strong, through finding something to lean on, letting go of self-concern, dissolving your own faction, issuing a decision that cannot be recalled, and finally putting distance between yourself and harm. Scattering the right things gathers people better than gripping does.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment opens with success and adds beneficial river crossing and steadfastness: a rare positive invitation to action amid dispersal. The lines are also mostly positive: the first's strong rescue horse brings fortune, the second regret vanishes, the third has no regret, the fourth supreme fortune, and the fifth and top no blame. None explicitly brings misfortune, danger, or regretful limitation. Yet the third's purpose turns outward, and dispersion inherently involves uncomfortable loss and separation. The overall rating is Rather Good, with benefits arising from actively letting go rather than grasping tightly. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Let the blockage go and the space it leaves is where people return.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Rescue with a strong horse. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary explains the good fortune of this first line with a single word: compliance. You move with the trend while it is still forming, rather than straining against it.
lines.plainLanguage: At the very start of the scattering you set out to help while the horse is still strong, and it goes well. What matters is moving with the current and moving early.
lines.lifeTranslation: A crack in a relationship or a team is easiest to work on while everyone still has energy. Wait until people are worn out and the same words will not go in.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there something that would be far easier to handle now than in a month?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Amid dispersion, run to support. Regret vanishes.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that hurrying to the support obtains what was wished for. The word here means a bench or rest that can bear your weight.
lines.plainLanguage: As things scatter, you move quickly to something you can lean on, and the regret disappears. The commentary reads this as finally getting the thing you wanted.
lines.lifeTranslation: When the situation is chaotic, secure one place to stand first: a steady income, one person you trust, a fixed daily rhythm. The rest can wait.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Inside the present mess, which one thing could you steady first?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Dispersing the self. No regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says dispersing the self is possible here because the will was already directed outward rather than inward.
lines.plainLanguage: You let go of your grip on your own gains and losses, so no regret follows. The reason is plain enough: what you cared about was never yourself.
lines.lifeTranslation: Move your attention off the question of whether you are losing out and onto the work or the people, and a great deal of knotted feeling loosens by itself. This is not self-sacrifice; it is a different angle on the ledger.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Will the thing you are counting now still matter in a year?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Dispersing one's group. Supreme good fortune. Dispersion creates a mound, beyond ordinary thought.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary calls the dispersal of one's own faction brilliant and great. Breaking up the small group gathers a hill instead, a result beyond ordinary calculation.
lines.plainLanguage: You break up the small circle you belonged to, and this brings the highest good fortune. What gathers afterwards is a hill, an outcome most people would not have thought of.
lines.lifeTranslation: Release the circle that only protects its own and your scope widens, with more people willing to come near. It looks like loss in the short run and reads as expansion later.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the circle you are guarding protecting you or confining you?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Dispersing a great proclamation like sweat, dispersing the king's holdings. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the absence of fault to holding the correct position. A great proclamation goes out like sweat, which cannot be drawn back in, and the ruler's own store is dispersed to settle people.
lines.plainLanguage: You issue a major decision the way the body gives off sweat: once out, it cannot be recalled. At the same time you release what you had accumulated for yourself, and no fault attaches.
lines.lifeTranslation: Anyone announcing a significant decision has to stop reversing it once it is said. If you are also willing to give up your own advantage first, people believe you mean it this time.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What have you given up yourself before asking others to cooperate?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Dispersing blood, going far away and emerging. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary states the point of this line in two words: keeping harm at a distance. The word read as blood is taken as anxiety or injury, and the departure is a far one.
lines.plainLanguage: You disperse the injury and walk a long way out of it, so no fault attaches. This line is simply about leaving, and leaving far enough not to be caught by the backwash.
lines.lifeTranslation: Some environments that drain you do not need to be fought, only left. Go cleanly and go far, and do not keep the one thread that lets you be pulled back.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there a place you should have left long ago and have not?

topicRules.career: This suits breaking up rigid divisions and departmental turf so information and people can move again. Think a major announcement through before making it, because it cannot be taken back, and say at the same time what you yourself will carry.
topicRules.study: Drop a stuck method entirely and start again with a different approach or a different setting. Step outside your usual circle and discuss the material with people from other backgrounds to expose blind spots.
topicRules.romance: There may be a stretch of distance or separation, and there is no need to pull the person back at once. Let the attachments and misunderstandings disperse first; the space is what makes a healthier reconnection possible.
topicRules.family: Use a shared commemoration, observance or family ritual to draw distant members back together. Allow children and older relatives their own space too; closeness is not a matter of holding tighter.
topicRules.relations: Break up the circle that shuts others out and extend goodwill outward, and more people will come near. At the same time leave relationships that injure you, decisively rather than by dragging it out.
topicRules.finance: This suits spreading an over-concentrated position and clearing out assets sitting idle so the money can move again, once you have confirmed you can absorb the change. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: Release what has been held tight for a long time, through walking, stretching or travel that gets things moving. If something will not leave your mind, saying it aloud or writing it down helps disperse it. This is not medical advice; consult a qualified professional if something concerns you.
topicRules.general: The direction is passage through dispersal: once private interest, blockage and closed circles scatter, the road opens, which is why the judgement grants success. Move early, and keep one support you can lean on.

hexagrams.name: Jié · Limitation
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Jie: Success. Bitter limitation cannot be maintained steadfastly.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary grounds the success of Jie in firm and yielding each keeping their share, with firmness at the centre, and says bitter limitation cannot be held because that road has run out. Heaven and earth have their limits and so the four seasons come about; limit by institution and you neither damage wealth nor harm people. The Xiang image is water above the lake, with the noble person setting measures and weighing conduct.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Kan above, Dui below. Water stands over the lake, and the hexagram is about limits. The character means the joint of a bamboo: one clear segment after another. A lake holds water, but only so much, and past that it spills. The judgement says limitation brings success, then immediately adds that bitter limitation cannot be held to. The lines run from staying inside the courtyard because the way is blocked, to failing to go out when the way is open and suffering for it, to regret with nobody to blame, to limits that feel settled, to limits so well judged they taste sweet, and finally to limitation pushed into pain. Set the limit where you can hold it for a long time: too loose and it spills, too tight and it snaps.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment gives success, then limits it by warning against bitter restriction. The lines likewise span both ends: the fourth six's peaceful limitation succeeds, and the fifth nine's sweet limitation brings fortune and worthwhile proceeding. The first and third have no blame. Yet the second nine's staying behind the gate brings misfortune through lost timing, and the top's bitter restriction brings misfortune because its way is exhausted. Fortune depends entirely on appropriate measure: remaining indoors is blameless in the first line and unfortunate in the second, differing only in timing, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Set the limit where you can hold it; too loose spills, too tight snaps.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Not leaving the inner doorway and courtyard. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that not leaving the inner courtyard is a matter of knowing what is open and what is blocked. The courtyard here is the inner one, closer in than the outer gate.
lines.plainLanguage: You do not even step out into your own inner courtyard, and no fault attaches, because you know clearly whether this is a time that is open or a time that is shut.
lines.lifeTranslation: Holding still when the timing is wrong is judgement rather than idleness. The test is whether you can say what you are waiting for, or are simply afraid to move.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is your holding still a judgement or an avoidance?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Not leaving the outer gate and courtyard. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that not going out of the outer courtyard misses the moment utterly. The act is the same as in the first line; the difference is that the gate is now open and still not used.
lines.plainLanguage: Again you do not go out, and this time it goes badly. The gate could be walked through and you stay inside, so the moment is missed completely.
lines.lifeTranslation: Caution stops protecting you and starts costing you. When the conditions around you are all in place and you are still finding reasons to delay, that is not steadiness but a miss.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there an opening where everything is ready and you are still waiting?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Without restraint, there is sighing. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary asks who else there is to blame for the sighing that follows a lack of limits. The absence of fault means the fault cannot be laid on anyone else.
lines.plainLanguage: You will not set a limit, and sighing is what is left. The text says no fault, and the commentary makes the sense blunt: there is nobody else to blame for this.
lines.lifeTranslation: The regret after a late night, an overspend or an overstated promise usually has no other author. Admitting that is unpleasant and it is the only place a change can start.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How much of your latest regret came from your own indulgence?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Peaceful limitation. Success.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the success of settled limitation comes from following the correct way already laid down above. The measure is not something forced into place by your own effort.
lines.plainLanguage: You sit comfortably inside the limit, and it goes well. The reason given is that you are following an established correct way rather than gritting your teeth to hold a line of your own.
lines.lifeTranslation: A good limit should feel steady rather than like a daily fight with yourself. If a rule takes fresh resistance every day to obey, it is probably cut wrong for you.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Do the rules you set for yourself leave you settled or exhausted?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Sweet limitation. Good fortune; proceeding has merit.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the good fortune of sweet limitation to holding the central position. A measure that stays central is not bitter but sweet.
lines.plainLanguage: The limit is judged so well that it is actually pleasant, which brings good fortune, and going forward earns esteem. Everything rests on staying central.
lines.lifeTranslation: The best self-discipline is the kind you enjoy: eating about right, spending about right, working about right. Reach that level and other people copy you without being told.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there a good habit of yours that you genuinely enjoy?

lines.original: Six at the top: Bitter limitation. Persistence brings misfortune; regret vanishes.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says bitter limitation held to is dangerous because the way has run out. Yet the text also says regret disappears, so bearing the hardship willingly at least leaves nothing to regret.
lines.plainLanguage: Limitation pushed to the point of pain is dangerous if you keep holding it, because the road ends there. The text still says regret disappears: hardship accepted willingly leaves no remorse behind.
lines.lifeTranslation: Economising or disciplining yourself to the edge of what you can bear does not last. If this is a stretch you genuinely have to walk, at least put an end date on it.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The thing you are gritting through now, until when do you plan to keep it up?

topicRules.career: Set clear systems, clear responsibilities and a ceiling on workload, so the team runs on rules rather than endurance. When the moment to act does arrive, take it; excessive caution lets openings slip away.
topicRules.study: Fix a study rhythm that is regular and sustainable, since working in segments beats a single sprint. If the plan makes you want to give up every day, it is too tight and should come down to a load you can carry.
topicRules.romance: Set boundaries that are clear and comfortable for both of you, so the relationship has room to breathe. Too strict and it suffocates, too loose and resentment builds; the measure is what leaves both of you settled.
topicRules.family: Work out household rules and shares of work together so everyone has something to follow. The rules should fit the present situation, and any rule causing lasting misery should go back on the table.
topicRules.relations: Keep the frequency of contact and the amount you give within what you can sustain over time. Say no early when you need to; leaving it unanswered does more damage than declining.
topicRules.finance: Set a spending ceiling and expense categories so the system does the work instead of willpower, and leave reasonable slack, because severe economising rarely lasts. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: Build a regular rhythm of sleep and food, judged by whether you can keep it up rather than by how strict it is. If your current demands on yourself already hurt, lower the intensity and set an end date. This is not medical advice; consult a qualified professional if something concerns you.
topicRules.general: The direction is limitation: with boundaries and rhythm in place, things can move. Fortune turns entirely on the measure, since too loose spills and too tight snaps. The right setting is the one you find comfortable yourself.

hexagrams.name: Zhōng Fú · Inner Truth
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Zhong Fu: Good fortune extending to pigs and fish. Crossing the great river is beneficial; steadfast correctness is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary describes the structure as yielding within and firmness holding the centre: pleased and gentle, such trust transforms a whole state. Trust that reaches even pigs and fishes is auspicious. Crossing the great water works because the wooden boat is hollow, and it is the hollowness that floats. The Xiang image is wind over the lake, with the noble person deliberating over cases and staying execution.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Xun above, Dui below. Wind moves over the lake, the water answers, and inside and outside respond to one another. This is the hexagram of trust. Zhong Fu means sincerity that grows from the centre rather than being arranged for show. The judgement says the sincerity that reaches even pigs and fishes is what counts, that such trust is what lets you cross the great water, and that correctness is required. The lines move from settling the heart on one thing, through a crane calling and its young answering, unsteady feeling in front of a rival, leaving a companion to go upward, trust that binds people together, and finally a sound that climbs to heaven while the substance stays on the ground. How far sincerity travels depends on whether it is real or merely loud.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment's three statements are positive, and its commentary highly praises transformation of the state and response to Heaven. The first nine has prepared good fortune, the fourth six and fifth nine no blame, and the second's answering cranes provide one of the text's warmest images of response. The top nine lowers the assessment: a cock's cry rising to Heaven brings misfortune, and the Image questions how reputation beyond substance can last. The third's alternating drumming, stopping, weeping, and singing also shows unsettled feelings. Inner conditions are good, with a final risk of unreality, hence the rating: Rather Good rather than the best. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Sincerity grows from the centre; never let volume outrun substance.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Preparedness brings good fortune. Other attachments prevent peace.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the good fortune of weighing things carefully at the start rests on a will that has not yet shifted. Where something else is also being sought, there is no rest.
lines.plainLanguage: At the beginning of trust, settle your own heart and weigh the matter properly, and it goes well. Keep another option in mind and you will not be at ease.
lines.lifeTranslation: Before starting anything that depends on long-term trust, confirm that this is genuinely the only thing you want to do. People with a foot in two boats sleep badly in both.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What fallback are you still holding onto behind the thing you just agreed to?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: A crane calls in the shade; its young answer. I have a fine cup of wine and will share it with you.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the young answering comes from genuine willingness in the heart, not from anything applied from outside. A crane calls from a hidden place and is answered.
lines.plainLanguage: A crane calls where nobody can see it and its young answer of their own accord. I have good wine and will share it with you. A true call finds a response without any performance in front of an audience.
lines.lifeTranslation: Work seriously where nobody is watching and the people who understand will come to you. Rather than trying to be seen by everyone, keep what is worth sharing for those who actually answer.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Who responded to you recently without you having promoted anything?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Finding a counterpart: now drumming, now stopping, now weeping, now singing.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes this swinging between drum and halt to a position that does not fit. The received text of the commentary differs slightly from the line text and is kept as it stands.
lines.plainLanguage: You meet a match for yourself and swing between attacking and stopping, weeping and singing, entirely led by the other side. The trouble is not that the rival is strong but that you are standing in the wrong place.
lines.lifeTranslation: When someone or something sends your feelings up and down, hold off on reacting. Usually you have put yourself in a position that was never yours to contest from.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Who or what has been swinging your mood several times in a single day?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: The moon is nearly full; the horse's mate is lost. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary explains the lost pair of horses as cutting the tie to one's own kind in order to turn upward, which is why no fault attaches. The moon is nearly, not quite, full.
lines.plainLanguage: The moon is close to full but not yet there, and the horse that ran alongside is gone. Leaving the old companion to give your attention upward brings no fault.
lines.lifeTranslation: Moving to a higher place sometimes means leaving the people who walked beside you. It is not betrayal; the directions have parted, and a proper goodbye serves better than dragging each other along.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there a partnership that has quietly reached the point of going separate ways?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: Sincerity binds closely. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the binding quality of this trust holds because the position is properly correct: there is standing enough to carry the connection.
lines.plainLanguage: Sincerity binds those above and below firmly together, and no fault attaches. It works because the place you occupy is legitimate to begin with.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you are the person holding everyone together, what carries it is not technique but people believing what you say. Promise less and deliver more exactly, and the link holds.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The last promise you did not keep, does the other person still remember it?

lines.original: Nine at the top: A cock's cry rises to Heaven. Persistence brings misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary asks how a sound climbing to heaven can last. The bird's cry rises while the bird does not, and reputation detached from substance cannot be sustained even if held to.
lines.plainLanguage: The cry has gone up into the sky and the bird has not followed. When trust at its far end becomes nothing but volume, holding to it carries danger.
lines.lifeTranslation: When your reputation, slogan or claim is running ahead of what you have actually delivered, the trouble is waiting behind it. The move is to fill in the substance, not to raise the volume again.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How far apart are the version you tell others and the version you have delivered?

topicRules.career: Integrity and professional reputation are your strongest assets, which suits work requiring deep trust from the other side. Keep your external claims tight against actual delivery rather than borrowing against future vision.
topicRules.study: Commit to a field you genuinely care about and go deep with others who share it, since asking openly gains you more than displaying. Do not treat certificates as ability; go back and fill in the fundamentals.
topicRules.romance: Sincerity gets noticed here, and this is a good time to say plainly what you feel. Do not let gifts or elaborate phrasing stand in for the real thing; what registers is consistency, not packaging.
topicRules.family: This suits saying honestly the things you have carried for years, and being generous about past faults rather than settling who was right. Listen more than you judge, and leave room for the quietest person to speak.
topicRules.relations: Your sincerity draws people on the same wavelength, so you need not work the network deliberately. If one relationship keeps swinging your mood, check first whether you are standing somewhere you should not be.
topicRules.finance: Weigh the credibility of the people involved rather than their pitch, keep your distance from promises of high returns, and put accounts and agreements in writing. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: Care for yourself quietly and single-mindedly, through a regular routine and time alone to settle. Playing a role that does not match what you feel inside accumulates a real cost. This is not medical advice; consult a qualified professional if something concerns you.
topicRules.general: The direction is inner truth: a genuine intention carries through barriers and draws a response, and an open, hollow mind is what floats a heavy load. Watch the far end, where only volume is left, and keep restoring the substance.
