hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: build credit through real action, and understand the other person before stating your own position. Avoid: substituting fine words for substance, or asking for trust while refusing to be checked.

hexagrams.name: Xiǎo Guò · Small Exceeding
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Xiao Guo: Success. Steadfast correctness is beneficial. Small matters are possible; great matters are not. The flying bird leaves its call. Going upward is unsuitable; going downward is suitable. Great good fortune.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary reads Xiao Guo as the small exceeding and thereby succeeding, provided it keeps correct and moves with the time: the yielding lines hold the centre, so small matters go well, while the firm lines are out of place, so great matters cannot be undertaken. The flying bird leaves its cry behind, and going down accords while going up runs against. The Xiang image is thunder above the mountain, with the noble person erring slightly towards respect, towards grief in mourning, and towards thrift in spending.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Zhen above, Gen below. Thunder sounds on the mountain top and the sound does not carry far, so this is the hexagram of going a little past. Xiao Guo is about scale: in harmless small matters such as respect, mourning and thrift, it is better to do slightly more, but in great matters do not cross the line at all. The judgement uses the bird leaving its cry to say that downward is right and upward is not, and that a lower posture is what brings fortune. The lines run from a bird flying high too early, through reaching the grandmother rather than the grandfather, refusing to guard a little more and being harmed, keeping within bounds, dense clouds that do not rain, and finally overshooting altogether. This is a season for gathering in: make the task small and the posture low.
hexagrams.trendReason: Although the judgment gives success, beneficial steadfastness, and great good fortune, that fortune explicitly depends on staying low rather than rising. The commentary directly rules out great undertakings. Three lines bring misfortune: the first's flying bird, the third, and the top's calamity. Only the second and fourth offer no blame. Outcomes depend entirely on maintaining small proportions: lowering brings passage, raising brings misfortune. Both possibilities coexist with a sharp contrast, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Overdo the small things a little; do not cross the line on the large ones.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: A flying bird brings misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says of the flying bird that nothing can be done about it, a phrase close to a sigh. Rising at the very start goes against the instruction to stay low.
lines.plainLanguage: Right at the beginning you fly high like the bird, and misfortune follows. You went up when the time asked you to go down, and by then there is no repairing it.
lines.lifeTranslation: Competing for visibility and position before you have found your footing carries the most risk. The opening will wait for you; the fall may not find anyone there to help you up.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Are your feet steady under the step you are rushing to take?

lines.original: Six in the second place: Passing the grandfather, meeting the grandmother; not reaching the ruler, meeting the minister. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that not reaching the ruler is right, because a minister should not go past the ruler. Stopping here is exactly why no fault attaches.
lines.plainLanguage: You pass the grandfather and meet the grandmother; you aim for the ruler and reach only the minister. Stopping there brings no fault, because you were never meant to go past.
lines.lifeTranslation: Asking to see the decision-maker and getting the contact point instead is usually not a failure. Making your case clearly through the right level is both safer and more effective than forcing your way up.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is the level you want to skip really one you need to skip?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Failing to take exceptional precautions, someone following may harm you. Misfortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary exclaims at how severe this misfortune is. Refusing to exceed in the matter of guarding means those who follow may do the injuring.
lines.plainLanguage: You will not take the extra precaution at the point where extra precaution belongs, and the people close by turn out to be the ones who harm you. In this season, guarding is precisely the small thing you are allowed to overdo.
lines.lifeTranslation: The moment you decide everyone around you is on your side and no safeguards are needed is usually the most exposed. Putting contracts, access and responsibilities in writing is not distrust; it gives the relationship somewhere to retreat to.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What did you skip confirming because you assumed nothing would go wrong?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: No blame. Do not exceed; meet what comes. Advancing brings danger: be watchful. Do not persist forever.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary notes that the position is not fitting, so meeting without exceeding cannot be forced, and warns that advancing brings danger and that no single approach should be held to forever, since this state of affairs will not last.
lines.plainLanguage: No fault attaches, because instead of forcing your way past you meet things as they come. Going forward carries danger and calls for caution, and no single method should be kept in place indefinitely.
lines.lifeTranslation: Do not push and do not force; what is meant to meet you will. Remember too that the present workaround suits only the present, and should change when the conditions do rather than hardening into permanent policy.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Which temporary workaround have you started treating as a fixed rule?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Dense clouds, no rain, from our western outskirts. The duke shoots with a corded arrow, taking what is in the cave.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the clouds bring no rain because they have already risen too high. The prince takes with a corded arrow whatever is hiding in the burrow, which is a modest catch rather than a great one.
lines.plainLanguage: The clouds bank up thickly and no rain falls, drifting in from the western outskirts. The prince can only draw out what is hiding in the burrow: there is a result, but a small one.
lines.lifeTranslation: When every condition looks present and nothing comes of it, you have usually set yourself too high to touch the ground. Take the small gain and stop holding out for the downpour.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How many small gains has waiting for the big one already cost you?

lines.original: Six at the top: Not meeting, but overshooting. The flying bird is caught. Misfortune: this is calamity and error.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that not meeting but exceeding shows one has already gone too high. Calamity and self-inflicted trouble together mean the harm comes from both outside and inside.
lines.plainLanguage: What should have met you does not, and you sail straight past it; the bird flies far off and misfortune follows, compounded from outside and from your own hand. The end of small exceeding is exceeding too far.
lines.lifeTranslation: Pressing on after you have already gone past the mark rarely costs you only one thing. Stopping, admitting the error and bringing people back matters far more than adding another push.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is there something you have known for a while you have overshot?

topicRules.career: This suits handling detail, repairing process and strengthening safeguards, not launching a large project that needs heavy resources. Communicate upward through the usual levels, since going over someone's head tends to backfire.
topicRules.study: Advance in small steps and accumulate daily, working the basic problems until they are automatic. Do not take on material far above your level; progress looks slow and the error rate drops noticeably.
topicRules.romance: Put your care into small things, where one extra kindness or one more question is enough. This is not the time to press for a major commitment or a declaration; a lower posture works better than a raised one.
topicRules.family: This suits everyday matters and small adjustments to household habits, which is where your relatives feel the effort. Postpone major questions of dividing property, moving house or money arrangements; raising them now tends to go badly.
topicRules.relations: Stay modest and restrained, leave room in what you say, and let go of winning every point. Rather than widening your circle, look after the few relationships you have, while keeping a basic guard against anyone approaching with unusual warmth.
topicRules.finance: Economise, trim spending and tidy up small outgoings rather than committing heavily or increasing leverage, since staying within your means matters more than the return. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: Lower the intensity and lengthen recovery, since modest exercise and a regular routine serve better than a hard challenge. Do not let small accumulating symptoms drift; handling them early saves trouble later. This is not medical advice; consult a qualified professional if something concerns you.
topicRules.general: The direction is small exceeding: you may go slightly further in respect, thrift and precaution, while great matters call for holding back and waiting. Downward accords and upward runs against, so judging the measure is the work of this stretch.

hexagrams.judgmentGuidance: Worth doing: attend carefully to small matters, keep a low posture, and control the size of each move. Avoid: leaping over levels on a big undertaking, or ignoring a warning because the small things are going well.

hexagrams.name: Jì Jì · After Completion
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Ji Ji: Success in small matters. Steadfast correctness is beneficial. Good fortune at first, disorder in the end.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says the success of Ji Ji is the success of small things, and that correctness is favoured because firm and yielding are each properly placed, this being the one hexagram in which every line sits in its correct position. Early good fortune comes from the yielding line holding the centre; the disorder at the end comes from stopping once the crossing is made, when the way runs out. The Xiang image is water over fire, with the noble person anticipating trouble and guarding against it in advance.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Kan above, Li below. Water sits over fire, the pot is on and the heat is right: the crossing has been made. Ji Ji is the only hexagram where all six lines occupy their correct places, and it looks complete, yet the judgement grants only small success and says plainly that it begins well and ends in disorder. Completion is itself the dangerous moment, because the order starts to loosen as soon as you decide you have arrived. The lines run from dragging the wheel and wetting the tail, through a loss that returns of itself in seven days, a three-year campaign won at the cost of exhaustion, rags kept ready against a leak, a small offering that suits the season better than a great one, and finally a crossing that soaks the head. The time to start guarding is the moment it is done.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment gives both ends: small success and beneficial steadfastness are positive, yet initial fortune ends in disorder. Its commentary explicitly locates danger in stopping, when the way becomes exhausted. No line says misfortune, but none offers supreme fortune either: the first nine's no blame, second six's recovery in seven days, and fifth nine's real blessing are positive. The third's three-year conquest is exhausting, the fourth stays vigilant all day, and the top wets its head in danger. The most correct arrangement has the least momentum; outcomes depend on continuing after completion, hence the rating: Neutral. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: The moment it is finished is the moment to start guarding it.

lines.original: Nine at the beginning: Dragging the wheels, wetting the tail. No blame.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says that dragging the wheel is without fault in principle, meaning the slowing is a deliberate restraint rather than a mistake.
lines.plainLanguage: You hold the wheel back so the cart does not run, and the tail gets wet in the crossing, with no fault attaching. Slowing down right after getting across is a choice you made.
lines.lifeTranslation: Just after reaching a goal is when it is easiest to press the advantage further. Tapping the brake yourself, and allowing the moment to look less impressive, is what protects what you gained.
lines.reflectionPrompt: After finishing something, do you usually rest first or start the next thing immediately?

lines.original: Six in the second place: The woman loses her carriage screen. Do not pursue; regain it in seven days.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the recovery in seven days comes from holding the middle way. The lost item is the screen on a carriage.
lines.plainLanguage: A woman loses the screen from her carriage, and there is no need to chase it: in seven days it comes back. Keep the proper rhythm, neither panicking nor pursuing, and what was lost returns in the ordinary course.
lines.lifeTranslation: When something is lost, an opening passes, or someone misreads you, chasing it often pushes it further away. Give it time and carry on as usual, and most things settle back where they belong.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What would happen to the thing you are chasing if you simply left it alone?

lines.original: Nine in the third place: Gaozong campaigns against the Gui Fang, conquering them in three years. Do not employ petty people.
lines.ancientContext: Gaozong is King Wu Ding of Shang, and the Guifang were a northwestern people. The Xiang commentary gives one word, exhaustion, to a victory that took three years, and the text warns against employing small-minded people afterwards.
lines.plainLanguage: Gaozong campaigns against the Guifang and takes three years to prevail, and the commentary offers only one word: worn out. After the war, be careful whom you appoint, and keep out those who serve only themselves.
lines.lifeTranslation: Some fights cost you so much that winning leaves you depleted. What matters more is who holds the ground afterwards; the wrong successor can lose three years of work in a season.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Whose hands are the results you worked so hard for in now?

lines.original: Six in the fourth place: Fine clothing turns to rags. Be watchful all day.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the day-long vigilance rests on genuine doubt: the wariness has a basis. Fine silk and worn rags are carried on a boat to plug leaks.
lines.plainLanguage: Rags are kept aboard, ready to stop a seam from leaking, and the watch is kept all day. The surface looks calm and the crack is already there beneath it.
lines.lifeTranslation: A system still running does not mean nothing is wrong. Get the backups, the spare capacity and the fallback plan ready, because that unease you cannot articulate usually has a cause.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What is the thing that faintly worries you and that you have not put into words?

lines.original: Nine in the fifth place: The eastern neighbor's slaughtered ox does not equal the western neighbor's simple spring offering, which truly receives blessing.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says the eastern neighbour's ox does not match the western neighbour's timing, and that receiving the blessing in substance is great good fortune arriving. The western offering is a plain and modest one.
lines.plainLanguage: The eastern neighbour slaughters an ox for a grand rite and gains less than the western neighbour's simple offering, because the latter truly receives the blessing. The difference is not scale but whether it suits the season.
lines.lifeTranslation: The same intention needs only a sentence when the timing is right, and cannot land however elaborate it is when the timing is wrong. Before you spend the effort, ask whether this is the moment for it.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is now actually the right time for the thing you are about to do at full scale?

lines.original: Six at the top: Wetting the head. Danger.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary asks how such a state can last. At the first line only the tail was wet; at the top the head goes under, the crossing having gone from shallow to deep.
lines.plainLanguage: You cross until the water covers your head, and it is dangerous. What began as a wet tail ends with you fully in the water, and that cannot be held for long.
lines.lifeTranslation: When you find you are wholly submerged in one thing with no room to breathe, that is not commitment but the signal before you go under. Find the bank now and stop going forward.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What in your life has already risen above your neck?

topicRules.career: A stage has been completed, so the work now is to take stock of risk and strengthen handover and backup rather than expanding at once. Be especially careful about people, since who holds the ground matters more here than who opens it.
topicRules.study: You have a working foundation, and the temptation to stop because you roughly know it is exactly where the slide begins. Schedule review and testing to find what only looks familiar.
topicRules.romance: The relationship has settled and daily life turns easily into habit. Create new shared experiences deliberately, and watch the small cracks you have been passing over with the assumption that they already understand.
topicRules.family: When things look harmonious is precisely when latent issues should be handled: shares of care, money arrangements, the health of older relatives. Talking early is far calmer than talking after something has happened.
topicRules.relations: Your position and role suit you at present, so hold your bounds and do not overstep. If someone misunderstands you or a relationship cools for a while, time is often more effective than explanation.
topicRules.finance: The structure looks solid, which makes this the time to review insurance, emergency reserves and diversification rather than enlarge a position. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: You have just come off a hard stretch, and tiredness often surfaces late. Plan rest and a check-up rather than waiting until something is plainly wrong. This is not medical advice; consult a qualified professional if something concerns you.
topicRules.general: The direction is after completion: everything is in place, and the structure is at its most correct just as the momentum is at its weakest. Treat completion as a new start, anticipate trouble and guard in advance, so the good beginning does not run into disorder.

hexagrams.name: Wèi Jì · Before Completion
hexagrams.originalJudgment: Wei Ji: Success. The little fox almost crosses, but wets its tail. Nothing is beneficial.
hexagrams.ancientContext: The Tuan commentary says Wei Ji still succeeds because the yielding line holds the centre. The small fox almost across wets its tail because it has not yet left the water and cannot carry through to the end, so nothing is gained. Though none of the six lines sits in its correct place, firm and yielding still answer one another, and that is where the hope lies. The Xiang image is fire above water, with the noble person carefully distinguishing things and settling each in its proper place.
hexagrams.plainLanguage: Li above, Kan below. Fire sits over water, fire burns upward and water runs down, so the two never meet: the crossing has not been made. The sixty-four hexagrams close here, which says that nothing ever truly ends. Not one line is in its correct place, which looks like the worst case, yet the judgement opens with success, because firm and yielding still answer each other and nothing has hardened into its final shape. The lines run from a tail wet through rushing, through dragging the wheel and holding correct, a premature campaign that goes badly while the crossing itself remains worth doing, three years of effort finally rewarded, the light of the noble person resting on trust, and finally drinking that goes past the measure. Unfinished is not failure. Put things where they belong and leave the rest to time.
hexagrams.trendReason: The judgment starts with success, and the commentary twice gives positive reasons: the yielding attains the center and firm and yielding respond. Though all six lines occupy inappropriate positions, response remains possible. The second nine's steadfast fortune, fourth's fortune with vanished regret and rewards after three years, and fifth six's steadfast fortune, no regret, and sincere noble radiance provide strong support. Negatives cluster at the ends: the wet tail without benefit, first six's regret, third's misfortune in advancing, and top's sincerity losing what is right. These arise from controllable rashness or excess rather than an externally hopeless situation, hence the rating: Rather Good. This is the app's interpretation of the text, not a guarantee of outcomes.
hexagrams.coreMessage: Not yet ashore is not defeat; sort things, place them, and keep going.

lines.original: Six at the beginning: Wetting the tail. Regret.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says wetting the tail shows that one does not know one's own limit. Regret here is awkwardness and falls short of misfortune.
lines.plainLanguage: You have barely entered the water and the tail is already wet, which is awkward. The problem is not luck but not knowing how far your capacity actually extends.
lines.lifeTranslation: Trying to arrive in one move at the very start leaves you struggling at the first stage. Make an honest estimate of what you can carry now, then decide how large a step to take.
lines.reflectionPrompt: How far beyond your current ability is the thing you are planning?

lines.original: Nine in the second place: Dragging the wheels. Steadfastness brings good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the good fortune of correctness here to occupying the centre and conducting oneself properly, advancing by restraint.
lines.plainLanguage: You hold the wheel back so the cart moves slowly, and holding correct brings good fortune. Knowing how to slow down before the crossing is what keeps you steady.
lines.lifeTranslation: At the stage before anything is finished, pace is usually more useful than drive. Set your speed to what you can hold for the long run, and then do not stop.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Can you keep your current pace until the work is finished?

lines.original: Six in the third place: Before completion, advancing brings misfortune. Crossing the great river is beneficial.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary attributes the misfortune of campaigning before the crossing to a position that does not fit. The line then says crossing the great water is favoured. The two halves have long been read together: attacking with present means goes badly, while the crossing itself remains possible, depending on timing, standing and method.
lines.plainLanguage: You set out to campaign before crossing, and it goes badly, yet crossing the great water is still favoured. Two outcomes sit in one sentence, and the difference lies in what standing and what method you use.
lines.lifeTranslation: The same task can go wrong when forced and work when the approach or the timing changes. When you are blocked, check whether the thing is wrong or your current position is.
lines.reflectionPrompt: Is this blocked because the direction is wrong or because of where you are standing?

lines.original: Nine in the fourth place: Steadfastness brings good fortune; regret vanishes. Use force to campaign against the Gui Fang. After three years, receive rewards from the great state.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says correctness and the disappearance of regret come from the will being carried out. The campaign against the Guifang again lasts three years, as in the third line of the preceding hexagram, but here a reward is explicitly granted.
lines.plainLanguage: Holding correct brings good fortune, regret disappears, and a vigorous campaign against the Guifang earns the reward of a great state after three years. Long effort pays off because the intention was actually carried through.
lines.lifeTranslation: Things that genuinely matter rarely show a result within a year. If you believe the direction is right, give it three years' worth of patience, because the reward waits for the people who stay.
lines.reflectionPrompt: What have you worked at for a long time and are close to abandoning just before it shows?

lines.original: Six in the fifth place: Steadfastness brings good fortune and no regret. The noble person's radiance, with sincerity. Good fortune.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary speaks of the radiance of the noble person's light: it does not only illuminate the one who holds it but spreads outward with warmth.
lines.plainLanguage: Holding correct brings good fortune and no regret. The light of the noble person comes from sincerity within, which is why it is favourable. It is not a glare but a warmth that spreads.
lines.lifeTranslation: The credit you build through how you deal with people eventually speaks for you. There is no need to perform; keep your integrity intact and the light reaches others by itself.
lines.reflectionPrompt: If someone put in one good word for you, what would you want it to be?

lines.original: Nine at the top: Sincerity in drinking wine. No blame. Wetting the head: sincerity loses what is right.
lines.ancientContext: The Xiang commentary says drinking until the head is wet shows one does not know moderation. Sincerity while drinking carries no fault, but the excess costs even that sincerity its rightness.
lines.plainLanguage: Drinking in good company with genuine feeling carries no fault, but drink until your head is soaked and you lose the measure, however sincere you were. The last line of the sixty-four is about restraint.
lines.lifeTranslation: Celebrating is right, and celebrating past the point turns into something else. When you reach a milestone, let yourself enjoy it, and draw the line before you start.
lines.reflectionPrompt: The last time you relaxed too far, what were the circumstances?

topicRules.career: You are in an unfinished transition, so sort people, tasks and resources back into place and let each role fit. Results need long investment to surface, so do not let go on the final stretch.
topicRules.study: You are halfway, where not seeing the end makes self-doubt easy. Cut the large goal into sections you can actually finish, and advance at a steady rather than an explosive pace.
topicRules.romance: Nothing has settled into shape, and that is exactly why the possibilities remain. Speak honestly and give the other person time, without forcing a conclusion and without losing the measure when the mood is good.
topicRules.family: A good deal is still unresolved, so clarify responsibilities and roles before arguing over detail. Long-term care or living arrangements need patience, and not settling it in one go is normal.
topicRules.relations: This suits working out afresh who fits where, and putting the right people into the right relationships. Rather than hurrying to declare a relationship a success or a failure, let each side settle into its own place.
topicRules.finance: Things are not yet stable, so separate the necessary from the discretionary, direct money to purposes that suit it, and keep a pace you can maintain. This is not investment advice; check anything specific yourself and weigh what you could afford to lose.
topicRules.wellness: Recovery is still underway, so go step by step without rushing, and do not return to full intensity the moment you feel better. Keep a measure in both rest and celebration. This is not medical advice; consult a qualified professional if something concerns you.
topicRules.general: The direction is before completion: you are not ashore, and because nothing has set, there is room to turn things around everywhere. Distinguish carefully, place each thing where it belongs, and hold restraint and patience through the last stretch.
